Commentaria in Cantica canticorum

Philip of Harvengt — read the work →

These are the edition's working notes, published as they were written. They record, work by work, where Migne's plate is defective or the reading uncertain: the printed form, what the English does with it, and why. They are not a groomed apparatus. Where a note argues with itself, withdraws an earlier decision, or leaves a question open, that is the record of how the reading was actually reached, and it is left standing — a conjecture that is visible can be checked, and one that has been tidied away cannot.

The English never silently repairs the page. A construable but wrong reading is rendered literally and the conjecture is recorded here, never applied to the text. How the English is produced and checked →

Translated 2026-08-08 by twenty-one Opus agents over 126 chunks (134,020 Latin words), each range of six logging to its own cruces-NNNN.md. Those twenty-one files are the record and are unabridged; this file is the merge. It exists because a work split across twenty-one agents who cannot see one another will drift on its load-bearing vocabulary, and reconciling that is a required pipeline step (translation-runbook.md step 4), not a tidy-up. Concatenating is the easy half.

Work totals after the 2026-08-31 partial plate read (§13): 100 [var:] · 48 [sic:] · 0 [ed:] · 0 [d:] · 0 [nt:] · 0 [f:] · 719 [n:] (719 in the Latin twins — exact parity). After the eleven-reader blind polarity read and the whole-apparatus audit (§7) they were 101 / 50; one [var:] and four [sic:] were withdrawn at the plate as Corpus Corporum's corruption, not Migne's type, and a fifth [sic:] had its lemma corrected. verify-english.mjs clean at 126/126: columns, notes and sections aligned, no duplicate paragraphs. EN/LA word ratio 1.56 work-wide (209,013 / 134,020).

§1 · WORK-WIDE CONVENTIONS — RULED AND APPLIED. DO NOT RE-DECIDE.

These are settled and swept. They are set down here with their reasons so that a later sweep does not churn them, and so that a reader can tell a considered choice from an accident.

Divisions. tomus = "Tome" / liber = "book" is inherited from 11638 — but this work has no tomi. Its divisions are liber = book (six of them), caput = chapter, volumen = volume (135 instances, none of them a division of the work). The tomus/liber collapse that cost 11638 sixteen sweep sites cannot arise here in that shape; the 11638 rule stands only in case a tomus ever turns up. INCIPIT = "HERE BEGINS", EXPLICIT = "Here ends".

CAPUT PRIMUM = "CHAPTER THE FIRST." — ruled and swept 2026-08-08. Seven sites: chunks 0002, 0003 ((cont.)), 0026, 0047, 0069, 0091, 0108. The ranges had split 3–3 against "CHAPTER ONE."; the three were swept. "Chapter the First" is the right side of that split because PRIMUM is an ordinal spelled out, and it is the spelled-out-ness that carries Migne's own contrast with the 179 numeral chapters that follow. "Chapter One" is a cardinal and flattens exactly the distinction the plate makes. ✅ Verified: 7 ## CAPUT PRIMUM in the Latin, 7 ## CHAPTER THE FIRST in the English, 0 ## CHAPTER ONE.

⭐ amica mea (Cant. 1:8) = "my friend", NOT "my love." Ruled from Caput V, where Philip glosses the word and proves it from John 15:14's amici mei. The lemma recurs at Cant. 2:10, 2:13, 4:1, 4:7, 5:2, 6:3 — nearly every range met it. ✅ 20 Latin amica mea, 17 English "my friend"; the three shortfalls are re-quotations absorbed into Philip's own syntax, not drift. The one English "my love" in the whole work (0122 @0480D) renders mea dilectio, not amica mea, and is correct — checked, no edit.

⭐ muraenula stays italic Latin. Caput VIII's whole argument is that the word names a fish (Muraenula piscis est…) and the chapter runs tail-to-mouth → ring → net-mesh → chain → Moses' head-and-tail offering. "Chains of gold" makes seventeen paragraphs explain nothing. ✅ 22 Latin instances (0032 ×21, 0033 ×1); the five English instances not carrying their own asterisks are either the frontmatter incipit (verbatim Latin) or nested inside a wider italic run — nesting, not drift.

⭐ vermiculatas argento IS translated ("vermiculated") — the companion call, decided the other way on purpose, because English carries the whole gloss chain: vermiculate → vermilion → little worm → Ego autem sum vermis. Italic Latin is reserved for words with no English exponent; this one has one. ✅ 6/6.

⭐ The bed triple, and it is a triple on purpose. lectus = "bed" · lectulus = "little bed" (40 Latin / 41 English) · cubile = "couch." 0279B's whole humility argument turns on the diminutive (non tamen Virgo lectum, sed magis lectulum), and "bed" is not available for cubile because a third word collapsing into the pair would void that argument. See §4.5 for the two sites where this had not in fact been swept.

Other ruled equivalences, all held work-wide: cancelli = "lattice" (10/10; 0312D identifies the lemma with the architectural sense and "chancel" would sever the argument) · emissio = "emission", not Douay's "plants" · vicus = "lane" (9/10) and platea = "street" (18/19), kept distinct against Douay, load-bearing at 0318D · ferculum stays italic Latin, on the muraenula precedent · maceria = "dry-stone wall", distinct from murus · adolescentulae = "maidens" · charitas = charity (62 Latin / 65 English), never "love" · candidatio is translated, not carried.

⭐ The colour triple, kept strictly distinct: nigra = black · fusca = swarthy · formosa = comely. fusca is never "black" — and in this work that matters more than in 11638, because Cant. 1:5 prints nigra sum where the Vulgate has fusca sim (0230D): the colour word and the mood both changed, and Philip builds four columns of nigredo exposition and the whole nigra sed formosa architecture on it. Marked [var:], never conformed.

Pattern 3, "Holy Scripture" — both words capitalized, for divina, sacra, divinae Scriptura(e) and the bare form alike. 22 instances in the English; 0 instances of "divine Scripture" or "sacred Scripture", which is the defect 11638 shipped. The bare form is the one 11638's sweep missed and this work's brief warned about in advance: it fires on a bare in Scripturis (0260A), a bare genitive Scripturae (0307D), a bare nominative Scriptura (0331B), and sixteen times in chunks 0078–0083 alone, fourteen of them bare.

Pattern 17: thou = singular, you = plural. A number marker, not a reverence marker. Anchor case: 0454D, Luke 10:23 vos videtis → "you see".

⭐ Migne's mixed capitalization is MIRRORED PER INSTANCE, never regularized. Sponsus/sponsus, Sponsa/sponsa, Virgo/virgo, Dilecto/dilecto, Spiritus sanctus/sancti Spiritus — he runs both cases inside single sentences. This was named in advance as the likeliest drift point across twenty-one agents, and it did not drift: every range checked its own plate word by word and reported so. The worked example that closed the question is 0305B Spiritus sanctus against 0356C sancti Spiritus — two ranges appeared to disagree, both were right, and there was nothing to reconcile. Before reporting a capitalization disagreement in this work, check whether Migne simply prints both. He usually does.

Guillemet asymmetries are Migne's and are mirrored, never balanced. Five chunks are asymmetric — 0006 (8 «, 9 »), 0011 (11/10), 0044 (4/3), 0083 (5/4), 0089 (10/11) — and the English reproduces each 1:1 (422 « and 421 » on both sides). At 0307C Migne himself breaks one quotation into two guillemet pairs around inquiens, doing what Pattern 5 forbids us to do; reproduced.

§2 · THE TYPOGRAPHY — three findings, none of which one range could have made

2.1 · The marks divide BY FUNCTION, not by book

11638 changes how it marks scripture at a book boundary — italics in Books I–II, guillemets « » from Book III. 11632 is not built that way. It runs both marks in parallel from chunk 0000, divided by function: guillemets carry a quotation adduced as an authority (scripture is the commonest case, not the rule — the Delphic oracle, Virgil, and two bare pronouns displayed as words are all guilleted at 0251D–0254B), and italics carry the running Song lemma plus book titles, words discussed as words, printed locators, and Migne's marginal source-edition page numbers.

The book boundaries were checked and carry no seam — LIBER SECUNDUS. at 0246C (cruces-0024), LIBER TERTIUS. at 0303A (cruces-0042), LIBER QUARTUS. at 0354C (cruces-0066), LIBER QUINTUS. (cruces-0090). Both marks run identically on either side of each. The question is closed: later book heads are ordinary text.

The proof that the division is functional is that the Song ITSELF takes guillemets when quoted as a proof-text rather than as the lemma — Cant. 4:11 @0220A, Cant. 5:11 @0226A, Cant. 2:14 @0226C, Cant. 1:12 @0270B, Cant. 5:11 again at 0432C, each with the italic lemma a few lines away. Five instances, four ranges.

2.2 · ⭐⭐⭐ BUT THE GUILLEMETS STOP — and the seam is nowhere structural

Found independently by the 0096–0101 and 0102–0107 agents, then verified against all 126 Latin chunks.

chunksopening «
0000–0089420
0090–01252 (one in 0090, one in 0096)

From chunk 0097 to the end of the work there is not one guillemet — 29 chunks, ~73 columns, ~50 notes, none. The last « in the book stands at col. 0416D. And Philip does not stop quoting: adduced proof-texts continue at full density, each with its inquit/ait and a correct note, printed in italics.

⭐ Internal control, exact and on one verse: Isa. 53:7 is guilleted at 0399C and italic at 0440A–B — same verse, same siglum, forty-one columns apart.

⚑ The seam falls mid-Caput VII of Book V, 29 columns from either book head. So this does not overturn §2.1's no-seam-at-a-book-boundary result; it strengthens it. Migne's practice changes where nothing structural happens, which is why nobody predicted it and why it had to be measured across the whole work rather than reasoned from one range.

⛔ The practical consequence, which was pushed into the briefs of every range from 0090 on: "italic run = probably just a lemma" is true to 0089 and false after it. In the last 29 chunks italics carry the lemma and every quotation, and they are told apart by function, not by mark. A range applying the earlier rule would have mis-classed every quotation it met and collated none of them.

2.3 · ⭐⭐⭐ THE DISPLAY RULE — it dissolves the "counter-instances"

Waves 3–5 kept logging classical and patristic authorities printed bare — Ovid at 0259, Sallust at 0314A (adduced explicitly, verax sententia… ethnicorum), Ambrose by name at 0337B, Virgil at 0385A — and read them as counter-instances to §2.1, killing one explanation after another, including the tempting "Migne declines to guillemet pagans", which a Father printed unmarked disposed of. They were never counter-instances. The discriminator is typographic DISPLAY.

  • A quotation Migne sets displayed, on its own line or lines, is italicised.
  • A quotation Migne runs into the paragraph is bare.

⭐ The control is one line of Horace printed twice. At 0022 the Siculi tag is displayed on its own line and italicised (Invidia, inquit, Siculi non invenere tyranni / Tormentum majus.); at 0447D the same line is run into Philip's sentence — majus quo nec Siculi, juxta quemdam ethnicum, tormentum invenere — and printed bare. Same poet, same line, two treatments, one variable. ✅ Checked against all 126 chunks: every displayed block in the work is italicised, and every bare authority is run-in.

⚑ The rule is PERMISSIVE, not predictive, and that has not changed: reproduce what is printed, and never add a mark because the function seems to call for one. What it changes is what counts as a finding. A bare adduced authority is expected; only a displayed quotation printed bare, or a run-in one italicised, would be real.

⚑ Migne's [n:] is usually inside the closing » but not always — outside at 0235B and 0239B; a bare locator inside a run with no [n:] wrapper at 0232D and 0236D; a printed locator standing inside a guillemet run at 0203A and 0222B–C. Reproduced as printed in every case.

§3 · PHILIP'S BIBLE — the copy-text readings

A divergence attested in more than one range is evidence about Philip's copy of the Bible, not a local slip. These are the merge's own results; no single agent could have made any of them.

⭐⭐⭐ Cant. 2:17 — montes BETHEL for the Vulgate's Bether (0338D, again at 0341A). Philip spends four columns on the etymology of the divergent word: Beth, domus; el vero Deus interpretatur; et Bethel domus Dei… Domus autem Dei non incongrue interna Virginis conscientia judicatur. Conform the lemma and the back half of Caput XVIII has nothing to stand on. Printed twice, which is the copy-text shape — the shape that made Zech. 4:14 and Gen. 3:19 findings rather than slips on 11638.

⭐⭐⭐ Eccles. 9:1 — the pair REVERSED in six of its seven printings. utrum odio dignus sit an amore against the Vulgate's utrum amore an odio. ✅ Verified against all 126 Latin chunks: reversed at 0029, 0042, 0062, 0070, 0074 and 0125; only 0049 carries the Vulgate order. So the copy-text shape comes with its own internal control — Migne contradicts himself exactly once. And the seventh printing (0489A, the last in the work) is recast: different wording, the reversal surviving three re-castings. Statistically the strongest member of the class. Marked nowhere it is unmarkable: at 0489A the span carries neither guillemets nor italics nor a note, and under §8a's rule it is logged, not marked.

⭐⭐⭐ Cant. 5:9 — and it is the only member of the class with an AUTHORIAL witness. At 0429B Migne prints ex dilecto once where the Vulgate prints it twice. At 0430B–C Philip discusses the omission himself: he reports that most of the codices he could find carry the phrase twice, and declines to say whether the repetition is the author's or a scribe's. This is not our inference from his exposition — it is his own collation note, printed. [var:] fires; Migne stands.

⭐⭐⭐ Cant. 7:13 — A NEW SHAPE: Migne DIVIDES the verse differently. At 0473B he prints Mandragorae dederunt odorem in portis nostris, where the Vulgate gives the gates to the apples (In portis nostris omnia poma). Every word is present — only the break moved. All of Caput XXXI expounds the gates as the mandrakes' (necdum in aedibus, necdum in thalamo… sed in portis), and Caput XXXII opens its lemma at Omnia poma with the gates already spent. ⚠ This shape is not greppable the way a divergent word is. Nobody was looking for it for 113 chunks. It is found only by reading the lemma against the Vulgate's own division — which is now a standing instruction for lemma-and-gloss commentaries.

⭐⭐ Cant. 5:7 — vigiles for custodes (0427A), which is Cant. 3:3's word, conformed onto 5:7. The proof it is copy-text and not a compositor's reach is Migne's own cross-reference: (sup. l. III, c. 22) resolves exactly to the Cant. 3:3 lemma in chunk 0065. Philip then builds two columns on the resulting distinction (custodes murorum kept a vigilibus), which the Vulgate's single word makes unwritable.

⭐⭐ Cant. 8:2 at 0475C — the lemma carries a whole clause the Vulgate does not have (et in cubiculum genitricis meae), the LXX/Old Latin reading, and five chapters of exposition stand on it. Cant. 8:12 at 0486C is its opposite number: a deletion (his dropped from et ducenti his qui custodiunt) which changes who the two hundred are, and Philip's exposition follows the printed reading.

Others attested and marked: Sponsa mea for speciosa mea (Cant. 2:13, 0323C, with Philip's next sentence proving it is copy-text) · in cavernis plural (Cant. 2:14) · grex for greges (Cant. 4:1–2, and the chapter is an argument about the singular) · pellis Salomonis singular (Cant. 1:4, and Caput XVIII expounds one skin flayed from one animal) · Sunamitis for Sulamitis (seven printings; Sulamit- occurs nowhere in the work) · matri suae dative for matris suae genitive (Cant. 6:8a, printed four times, the whole chapter built on the dative — and the work knows the genitive, printing it correctly at 0020) · Sion added to Cant. 6:8b at 0454B, with Philip expounding the addition in his next clause · conturbata est for conturbavit me (Cant. 6:11, voice reversed, gloss carrying both).

⭐ Cant. 1:12 — Cum for the Vulgate's Dum, ruled here. Migne prints Cum four times: three in chunk 0033 and again at 0270B where the verse returns as a guilleted proof-text with Philip's own gloss picking the word up. No [var:] fires, and that is right — the sense is untouched, which is Pattern 14's threshold. But four independent printings is copy-text evidence, so it is recorded here as an attested reading rather than a slip. ⚠ The fifth occurrence, at 0397C, prints only the verse's second half and supplies no evidence either way; a range reporting "met, agrees" would have been counted as an attestation of something it never witnessed. Name the words, not the verse.

⭐ An expounded quotation Migne leaves unmarked is LOGGED, never marked — ruled once for all twenty-one ranges. The class: Ps. 90:5–6 fused at 0245A, with the next sentence glossing the fusion; Lam. 4:20 at 0291B printed with the Old Latin ante faciem nostram against the Vulgate's oris nostri, expounded three times in two sentences, and carrying no guillemets, no italics and no [n:]; 1 Cor. 2:9 at 0372D; Deut. 32:33 at 0469A; the Chalcedonian formula at 0444A. And one member is a DELETION, which is worse: John 19:39 at 0399D prints ferens misturam myrrhae et aloes libras centum for the Vulgate's quasi libras centum, unmarked in every channel, twelve lines before Philip argues in pondere et numero… certo pondere, perfecto numero consummatum. His whole four-sentence argument needs the hundred to be exact, and what has gone is the Vulgate's hedge. Every other member substitutes; a substitution at least leaves a strange word on the page. A deletion leaves nothing at all, and no mechanical channel can reach it. The ruling stands: log the candidate with its evidence, place no [var:]. A [var:] asserts a divergence inside a quotation, and where Migne marks the words as neither quotation nor lemma we cannot establish the quotation's boundary. Marking it would have us assert a boundary the plate does not print.

§4 · WHAT THE MERGE CHANGED — the reconciliations

Five live divergences between ranges. Each is ruled here, with the reason, and the exact edits are listed. The edits are proposed, not applied — they are handed to Wilson.

4.1 · ⭐ aromata = "spices". "Aromatical spices" comes out. — 12 edits

aromata is one Latin word; "aromatical spices" is two English words, and it is Douay's phrase at Cant. 3:6 and 5:1. Fourteen chunks render the root; nine of them say "spices" and five say "aromatical spices". This is the work's characteristic defect class — the Douay arriving over the plate — showing up in vocabulary rather than in a verse.

⭐ The ruling is forced from inside chunk 0105, which contains both words and contradicts itself in three lines. Migne prints areolae aromatum (noun) in the lemma and arboribus aromaticis (adjective) in the gloss. Our English gave the lemma "beds of aromatical spices" and then, two sentences later, glossed it "the Virgin compared him to beds of spices" — the same phrase, two ways, on one page. If aromata takes two words, the genuine adjective aromaticus has nothing left to be.

RULE: aromata (the noun, any case) = "spices". aromaticus (the adjective) = "aromatic". A bare aromata never takes "aromatical".

Not touched, and correct: 0105.md @0438B "brought forth aromatic spices" renders aromaticas species — genuine adjective + genuine noun. Leave it.

4.2 · ⭐ suavis = "sweet". The 0107 mapping wins. — 6 edits

Two ranges mapped the pair in opposite directions:

  • 0097–0099: dulcedo = "sweetness", suavitas = "pleasantness".
  • 0107: suav- = "sweet", dulc- = "delightfulness".

⭐ 0107 is right, and the reason is that its mapping is fixed by the plate while 0097's is free. Chapter XXVI's lemma is Cant. 5:16 Guttur illius suavissimum — "His throat is most sweet" — and the whole chapter is an exposition of that superlative (non tam suavior quam suavissimus). The chapter then locks the two words into a chiasmus that forces distinct English: dulcedo suavior, suavitas dulcior non habetur. If suavitas is "pleasantness" there, the lemma the chapter expounds has changed word underneath it.

⚑ And 0097 is already inconsistent with itself: it renders suavi otio "sweet leisure" twice (@0419A, @0420D) while rendering suavitatem of the same page "pleasantness". Half that chunk is already on 0107's side.

⚑ The work-wide counts settle the direction rather than the sweep. Latin: 198 suav- against 88 dulc-. English: 279 "sweet", 73 "delight", 19 "pleasant". So suav- is the majority word and "sweet" is its standing exponent almost everywhere; the two collide only where Philip puts them in one period. RULE: suavis/suavitas = sweet/sweetness. Where dulcedo stands in the same period as a suav- word, dulcedo = delight/delightfulness. Elsewhere "sweetness" for dulcedo* is left standing — a full 88-site sweep buys nothing and risks damage out of proportion to the gain (the 11638 principle applied).

4.4 · ⭐ The catchword at 0124 that does not match its lemma — fix the LEMMA

Migne prints De qua subjungit: «Vinea fuit,» etc., then the head CAPUT XLVII. and the lemma Vinea fuit pacifico, in ea quae habet populos (Cant. 8:11). Our English gave the catchword "There was a vineyard, etc." and the lemma "The peaceable had a vineyard, in that which hath peoples." A reader following the catchword cannot find the passage, because the two share no opening words.

⭐ The cause is not the catchword. The catchword is literal; the lemma is Douay ("The peaceable had a vineyard" is Douay Cant. 8:11, which turns Migne's dative of possession into an English transitive). Repairing the catchword would conceal the pull-through; repairing the lemma removes it and makes the two match automatically.

Recorded so the choice is visible.

Recorded as a crowding, not repaired: a fourth English word for stratum would be invented rather than found, and the merge declines to invent one.

4.6 · The Gallemart colophon at 0490B — a proposed house ruling

Migne closes the work with Joannes GALLEMART S. Theol. Doctor, et catecheseos professor in Universitate Duacensi, hac 7 Febr. 1618. — the subscription of a Douai censor, printed italic. It is not Philip's text and not scripture; it is a documentary signature, and our English currently reads "John GALLEMART, Doctor of Sacred Theology, and professor of catechesis in the University of Douai, this 7 Feb. 1618." — half-Englished, and half in Migne's capitals.

Proposed ruling: in a documentary subscription, the NAME stands as printed and the OFFICE is Englished.

filecolcurrentproposed
0125.md@0490BJohn GALLEMART, Doctor of Sacred Theology, and professor of catechesis in the University of Douai, this 7 Feb. 1618.Joannes GALLEMART, Doctor of Sacred Theology, and professor of catechesis in the University of Douai, this 7 Feb. 1618.

Reasoning. A signature identifies a historical person in a record, and Englishing half of one manufactures a person — "John Gallemart" signed nothing. The capitals are Migne's typography and fall under the same mirroring rule as Sponsus/sponsus (§1). The office, by contrast, is ordinary descriptive Latin with an ordinary English exponent, and leaving it in Latin would tell an English reader nothing. This is a house ruling, not a work ruling — it will govern every censor's approbatio, imprimatur and editor's subscription in the corpus, which is why it is worth deciding once here rather than per work.

§5 · WHAT THE MERGE RATIFIED — checked, correct, do not churn

  • The CAPUT numeration is mirrored as printed and not tidied — CAPUT PRIMUM spelled out, CAPUT II–L in numerals, and CAPUT VIII / CAPUT IX / CAPUT XV / CAPUT XXXI printed without their full stops at 0052, 0053, 0075, 0114, 0119. Reproduced without them.
  • Migne's own [ alias …] variant bracket is reproduced, and no [var:] fires under it — he is carrying the Vulgate reading in his own apparatus (0054 @0321B, in obscuro [ alias caliginoso] loco, 2 Pet. 1:19).
  • ⭐ But it is NOT a singleton, and the brief's work-wide check was too narrow. Migne prints a second shape at 0122 @0481B: cor est incibile [ f. lucibile] — f. for forte, his own conjecture on his own non-word. The 2026-08-08 check that declared the class a singleton searched for alias and found what it searched for. A sweep is only as wide as its pattern list — the same lesson 11638's Pattern 3 sweep taught, recurring in a different register. Both instances are reproduced as printed; neither takes a [sic:] of ours stacked on top (brief §10.5).
  • Philip's own alia translatio is on the same footing — at 0378C he introduces Ibo mihi ad montem myrrhae as another version. No [var:] fires; the divergence is his apparatus, not Migne's text.
  • Migne's lower-case after a misplaced full stop stands, ruled on 11638 and explicitly not to be churned.
  • The three mountain etymologies (Amana, Sanir, Hermon) are translated, not carried as Latin — the same call as vermiculatas and for the same reason.
  • A quotation broken around inquit/ait keeps its breaks. Pattern 5: 0044 @0297A reads as split gibberish in English («Stay therefore me, she says, up with flowers») — but Migne prints three italic runs and our English mirrors them 1:1. A blind reader proposed the smoother reading and it was declined, because the repair moves sacred marker boundaries. Recorded so the proposal is not made a third time.
  • The colour triple and the bed triple hold work-wide (§1), including 0103's se nigras et abjectas.
  • Chunk-boundary (cont.) on a repeated head is ours and is merged at assembly — never a defect, never translated.

§6 · MIGNE'S CITATION SIGLA — counted across all twenty-one ranges

⭐ No siglum in this work is systematically wrong, and that is a weaker and far more useful fact than a running error count implies. It could only be established by counting the RIGHT ones, which every range was instructed to do.

  • (I Cor. II) was wrong at 0200D, 0240A and twice more — and correct at 0305C and 0318A. (II Cor. IX) correct at 0314C. (Luc. IX) names Matt. 8's words at 0240B and is correct at 0331A. (Psal. XCII) is wrong at 0275B and correct at 0281A, eleven columns later. (Isa. LI) is wrong at 0328C and right at 0332D–0333A. (Isa. LIII) is wrong once at 0421A and correct five times elsewhere. A tally of failures alone would have manufactured a pattern that is not there.

Two real shapes among the scripture sigla:

  1. Off by exactly one chapter — five of seven wrong sigla in a single range; a mechanical profile. (Job. II) for Job XI (0372D) belongs to it.
  2. The note cites one book, the words are another book's — four attested: Luke 9/Matt. 8 (0240B), Deut. 32/Ps. 91, Isa. 42/Matt. 12 (0318D), and Exod. 3/Acts 7:34 verbatim (0456B, the cleanest of the four).

⭐ The strongest instance is an INTERNAL control and needs no appeal outside the work. At 0283B Migne prints « Vere Filius Dei erat iste » under [n: (Marc. XV)] — verbatim Matt. 27:54, where Mark 15:39 reads Vere hic homo Filius Dei erat. Decisive because the same six words appear at 0267D under [n: (Matth. XXVII)]: Philip quotes Matthew twice and Migne labels the second one Mark.

(II Paral. III) at 0238A, off by thirty-two chapters, belongs to neither shape. A third shape is now named once and once only: at 0412C an (ibid.) carries Psalm 118 onto a quotation of Psalm 31 standing eleven words away — a positional error, not a naming one.

⭐ Migne's INTERNAL cross-references are a separate class with a real profile: 3 right, 2 wrong, and BOTH wrong ones are off by exactly one book. Wrong: (supra l. I, c. 2) at 0437A should be Book II; (l. IV, c. 10-12) at 0445B should be Book V. Right: 0477D and 0479B (both checked against their targets), and one that reaches back 179 columns and lands exactly. ⚑ The correct ones are the harder cases, which is why the class cannot be dismissed as unreliable.

Nothing is corrected anywhere. §10.2 governs: a following Ibid. resolves against the printed sequence at index time, and "fixing" an antecedent makes the Ibid. inherit the corrected key and resolve wrong.

§7 · THE BLIND POLARITY READ — eleven readers, and what it proves

Runbook step 4a, done 2026-08-08. One reading pass over all 126 chunks, split across eleven Opus readers at ~12 chunks each plus a whole-apparatus marker auditor, every one of them fenced off from these twenty-one cruces files, data/briefs/11632.md, next-session-resume.md and git history. Findings were formed blind and reconciled afterwards, never before. The full record is BLIND-READ.md; this is its result.

144 ours-side sites. Repairs applied there, not here.

⭐ The result that matters

One dropped negation in the entire work — 0122 @0481D, where Migne's appareat non deesse shipped as "may appear to be wanting", asserting the exact opposite of a paragraph that exists to show the lamp serves the neighbour. Repaired.

~110 necdum/nondum sites, one flattening — 0070 @0358C, nondum satis appropinquant as "yet do not draw near", in a chunk that renders nondum tamen plene sciunt correctly twelve words later. The particle was grepped first in every range, ahead of non/nec/nisi, precisely because it had been caught flattening during translation.

⚑ What that pair of numbers means. The prose held where it was being watched. Almost every other ours-side site was lexical or syntactic — a -urus participle read as passive, a dative read as a nominative and eight verbs pluralized to agree with it (0046 @0301A, Capreae), postpositive gratia read as the noun (twice, ranges apart), tota turpis as "wholly" instead of "all" inside a four-term scheme built on the one word. The failures clustered in mis-parsed grammar and in Douay wording arriving over the plate — not in polarity. Migne's own defects were rendered as printed and logged, never repaired, in every case the readers checked.

And one whole 46-word sentence was missing (0091 @0404D). Nothing could see it: column anchors matched, [n:] counts matched, and the word ratio was 1.61 — dead centre for that range. The reader's tell was that the Latin carried four question marks and the English three. ⭐ verify-english.mjs now checks question-mark parity as a WARN; it cost one regex and immediately found a second real item at 0051.

The marker audit: 50 [sic:] checked, 45 sound; 102 [var:] checked, 94 sound (101 stand now — one was deleted in repair). The failure that dominated 11638 is absent here: all 102 sat adjacent to their own quotation, none sat on Philip's prose, all four ellipses showed the divergent words. Reference format is uniform — every note carrying a reference uses arabic chapter:verse, against 11638's 71 roman / 59 arabic / 8 none.

⭐ How four unmarked defects were found, which no per-range reader could have done: the auditor built a frequency baseline over all 100 Latin works in src/latin/, isolated 11632 hapaxes whose single-edit neighbour is high-frequency, and read each in context. The rest were genuine rare Latin.

§8 · OPEN — recorded honestly, NOT resolved

These are Wilson's to rule. They are set down with the argument on both sides, because in each case the rulebook is genuinely ambiguous and a merge that decided them silently would be worse than one that does not decide them.

8.1 · ⛔ Pattern 12's boundary — four [sic:] on real Latin words

filecolcarried asthe word in place
0007.md@0202C[sic: Pecte]pecte = "comb" (imperative). The clause is a third-person report about the Bridegroom's breasts.
0048.md@0304A[sic: signa]signa = "signs" / "mark thou". The clause needs a subject that burns.
0067.md@0350A[sic: ama]ama = "love thou". The clause is third-person indicative.
0075.md@0369A[sic: sternis]sternis = "thou strewest". Cant. 4:2 needs sterilis, "barren".

Pattern 12 says a real word that is merely wrong gets NO marker and is rendered as ordinary English. The marker audit accordingly wants all four removed (and Incipit @0345B reclassified with them).

They are being LEFT as [sic:], on this reading: Pattern 12's stated test is that such a word can be rendered — the rule exists because "is repeated" for repetitur is available and honest. None of these four construes in place. Ama is an imperative in an indicative clause; sternis is a second-person verb where the verse needs an adjective; Pecte and signa leave their sentences without a subject. Rendering them "as ordinary English" would produce English that is not merely odd but ungrammatical, and would hide a broken type behind a word the reader will read past.

⚠ But the translating agents themselves were not consistent about it, and said so: cruces-0060 records that Incipit at 0345B "is a real word, so Pattern 12 keeps it", and cruces-0030 explicitly asked the merge to rule the class. Answering it in five separate edits guarantees an inconsistent result. The inventory is complete; the boundary is Wilson's to draw, and whichever way it goes it should be drawn for all five sites in one commit.

8.2 · ⛔ Supplied em-dashes — ~562 sites, ONE policy decision

Migne prints ZERO em-dashes anywhere in this work. Our English prints 562, an average of 4.5 per chunk. This was measured rather than reported: the 0072–0083 reader counted the whole work and correctly declined to list its own ~40, because doing so would have buried its real findings.

Also measured: English 3,780 colons against Latin 3,667 — printed colons are routinely replaced and occasionally supplied; and English 224 question marks against Latin 206, with five supplied at 0121/0123/0125 and further ones at 0097 and 0107 (all now surfaced by the verifier's parity check).

This is one Pattern 8 policy decision, not 600 edits. Pattern 8 makes the deletion direction the live one — four deleted colons at 0118 are already logged, and one deleted full stop at 0311A. Whether a supplied dash for a printed comma is a Pattern 8 violation or an ordinary translator's licence is exactly the question, and it is not answerable one site at a time. Recorded, measured, undecided.

8.3 · ⛔ [sic: informen t] at 0100 @0428A may mark OUR OWN artifact

The marker reports broken type. But the Latin source file itself reads informen t — the "break" is italics markup in our own text, not Migne's. The plate almost certainly prints informent, an ordinary word. This is our digitization's damage attributed to the plate, which is precisely the error the corpus rules exist to prevent. Needs a plate read at PL 203 col. 428A; deliberately not guessed. If the plate prints informent, the [sic:] comes out and a data/tei-patches/11632.json entry goes in, in the same commit.

8.4 · The split/join asymmetry — six carried, three normalized

Six word-splits are carried as [sic:] — a beo, a vida, hila rescat, in cutiens, informen t (see 8.3), a dolescentulae. But the word-join aforis (0077) is silently normalized, as are persequenter (0046 @0300C) and the lemma-level myrrhoe (0069) — while the parallel lemma defect fovum (0093 @0407A) is carried as [sic:]. Same defect class, two treatments, inside one work. ⚠ verify-english cannot see any of this: it strips asterisks and compares substrings. Not repaired, because it belongs with 8.1 — both are one question about where our carrying threshold sits.

8.5 · Readings argued on both sides, not flipped

Five construals where a blind reader argued rather than asserted, and was right not to assert. Listed so a later editor knows the argument was had: ille mundus at 0240C ("that world" or "that Clean One" — both grammatical, and ad quem nihil immundum attinet makes the jingle audible) · non vere facies coloratur at 0314D (adverb, or the ablative of ver — and the paragraph is built on verna suavitas, so it may be Philip's pun) · factus a Virgine at 0338B (agent or separation) · printed cum for eum at 0351B and 0339A, handled two incompatible ways, with a bracketed [him] supplied at 0067 and a silent reading at the other — one of the two must move · laetitia cordis ejus (his or hers, split between lemma and exposition with no note, which is the part that is indefensible either way).

§10 · OWED

  1. Plate read at PL 203 col. 428A — §8.3, informen t. Blocking nothing, but it is the one marker in the work that may be asserting our own damage as Migne's.
  2. Wilson's ruling on §8.1 (Pattern 12's boundary) and §8.2 (em-dashes). Both are one decision applied to a class; neither should be settled piecemeal.
  3. node scripts/index-work.mjs 11632 after any of the above edits land — rule 9, index from day one, no retroactive passes.
  4. node scripts/scan-raw-markers.mjs before deploy. Markers reach the reader as raw brackets unless a builder transforms them, and that has happened twice on PG pages because nothing checks rendered output.
  5. The badge. workStatus for 11632 gates the "First English translation" claim; absent a verified none, it renders "New English translation" and that is correct. Do not go hunting to earn the strong claim.

§11 · METHOD DATUM — why the quotation lists were worth their cost

Every agent was handed a verbatim list of every quotation printed in its own range, extracted mechanically from the Latin, with the instruction that the divergence list was the most valuable thing it would produce, and with the requirement that a span collated and found to AGREE be logged as such — so that the absence of a marker is recorded evidence rather than silence.

Result: 101 [var:], plus several hundred spans collated and explicitly logged as unmarked across the twenty-one range files, plus roughly 250 further weaves found on the mandatory prose pass that the extraction could not list at all (22 in one range, 24 in another, 31 in a third, and so on). The blind read then found the apparatus sound: 94 of 102 [var:], zero drift, zero markers on Philip's prose.

⭐ The finding that justifies the whole design is that the mechanical list was not enough and everyone knew which half was missing. Two of this work's three strongest §8a items — Lam. 4:20 and John 19:39 — carry no guillemets, no italics and no [n:], and reached a human only through the prose pass. A review that reads only the extractor's list misses that shape entirely.

⛔ And the defect can be an ADDITION you write while looking straight at it. The 0096–0101 agent drafted Eph. 5:29 at 0430D as "no man ever hated his own flesh", silently restoring the Vulgate's unquam, which Migne does not print — having already written "unquam dropped" into its own collation while the English still said "ever." Knowing the divergence did not prevent reproducing the familiar wording; only the separate word-by-word pass caught it. That is the single most useful sentence in this file for whoever translates the next work.

§12 · RULED 2026-08-09 — the four [sic:] on real Latin words STAY

The marker audit proposed stripping [sic:] from four sites because Pattern 12 reserves the marker for carried non-word type and these are all real Latin words. Ruled the other way: all four keep the marker, and Pattern 12 has been amended to record the test the ruling turns on.

The test is "does it render IN PLACE?", not "is it a Latin word?"

siteprintedconjecturewhy no English carries it
0007 @0202CPecteRecteimperative "comb!" stranded in a declarative clause governed by dicit
0067 @0350Aamaamatimperative among third-person finite verbs (deprehendit… intendit)
0075 @0369Asternissterilis2nd-person verb where the clause needs a predicate nominative
0048 @0304Asignaan adverbrenders only by hiding the defect — see below

The first three have no grammatical slot at all. Pattern 12's own examples, fuges for sugas and munde for mundo, are not like them: those occupy their slot and merely mean the wrong thing.

⭐ 0048 is the instructive one and it goes the same way for a different reason. ut signa prius ardeat sets a plural noun against singular ardeat. "That signs may burn" is perfectly good English — and that is exactly the problem. English may burn is number-neutral, so rendering signa "signs" silently repairs the disagreement and leaves the reader nothing to see. Where English has no exponent for the defect, rendering it IS the repair, and the marker is the only treatment that does not quietly fix Migne.

⚑ This runs opposite to Pattern 9, which normalizes precisely where English has no exponent — and the difference is worth stating, because a later sweep will meet both. Pattern 9's cases (grammatical gender, section labels) are systemic features of Latin and carry no information about this plate. A number disagreement in one clause is a fact about this printing. Normalize the language; mark the page.

Consequence for the split/join asymmetry recorded above: it is now decidable on the same test rather than by counting precedents. aforis (0077) renders in place as "from without" and takes no marker; persequenter (0046 @0300C) and the lemma-level myrrhoe (0069 @0353D) are non-words and should be marked — both are currently normalized silently, and both remain owed.

§1 · THE QUOTATION COLLATION — all 43 listed spans, itemized

Every span in data/quotations/11632/0000-0005.md was collated word by word against the Vulgate. Spans recorded as AGREES were collated and found to agree; the absence of a marker on them is a finding, not a silence.

Chunk 0000 — 6 spans

1–4. 0181A, four italic spans (Sumite, / materiam vestris, qui scribitis, aequam / Viribus; et versate diu, quid ferre recusent, / Quid valeant humeri.) — not scripture. Horace, Ars poetica 38–40, quoted as verse and set by Migne on three lines; the line structure is preserved in the English. Migne prints humeri where Horace has umeri — an attested medieval orthography, Pattern 9, deliberately unmarked.

  1. 0182A « Homo non percipit animalis [n: (I Cor. II)]. » — 1 Cor 2:14. Vulg. Animalis autem homo non percipit ea quae sunt Spiritus Dei. Migne's span is truncated to four words and inverted (homo … animalis), and the object (spiritalia) sits outside the guillemets in Philip's own clause. Every word printed is a Vulgate word and the sense is unchanged. Collated; no [var:] — a quotation cut short to fit a host sentence is citation practice, not a variant reading. Rendered « The animal man does not perceive », with spiritalia outside, exactly as printed.
  1. 0182A « Adsum. » — one word, no locator, no [n:]. Nearest received text is Isa. 58:9 Ecce adsum. Not a lemma; rendered « I am here. » No marker.

Chunk 0001 — 1 span

  1. 0184A videntes — not a quotation. A word discussed as a word (quos ampliore gratia videntes vel prophetas voluit appellari; cf. 1 Reg. 9:9). Rendered seers, italics kept by function, per the 11638 §1 rule that italics survive by function. It is not carried Latin and takes no [sic:].

Chunk 0002 — 11 spans

8–9. ⭐ 0185C Cantica, inquit, canticorum Salomonis. — [var:] FIRED, and it is the most load-bearing divergence in the range. Vulg. Cant. 1:1 title: Canticum canticorum Salomonis, singular. Migne prints the plural Cantica, and Philip's whole paragraph is an argument from the plural: Canticum vel Cantica in ipso titulo superscripsit … hic non solum Cantica, sed Cantica posuit canticorum. Conforming the lemma to the singular voids the paragraph that expounds it. Rendered "Songs, he says, of songs of Solomon." ⚑ And Migne is inconsistent with himself on the same page: the chunk's own ## head prints the singular genitive TITULI CANTICI CANTICORUM EXPLICATIO immediately before quoting the plural title. Both stand as printed — the head renders "THE SONG OF SONGS", the lemma "Songs of songs". Not harmonized in either direction.

  1. 0185C pax — etymological gloss of Salomon (Salomonis nomine pax signatur), not scripture. Italic word-as-word, translated ("peace").

§2 · THE TYPOGRAPHY QUESTION — 11632 does NOT open in an italics-only regime

⭐ Brief §7 asks where 11632's seams fall. In this range there is no seam, because both marks are in use from the first columns, and the division between them is FUNCTIONAL, not sequential. Counted across 0000–0005: 21 guillemeted spans, 22 italicised — and they never compete for the same job.

  • « » marks scripture quoted inside the running prose. All 21 guillemeted spans in this range are scripture; not one is anything else.
  • Italics mark four other things: (a) the running Song lemma being expounded (Osculetur me osculo oris sui, 7×); (b) book titles quoted as titles (Cantica canticorum Salomonis, Parabolae Salomonis…, Verba Ecclesiastae…); (c) words discussed as words (videntes, pax, adversarius, pacificus); (d) classical verse (the Horace) and Migne's marginal source-edition numbers.

This is a materially different opening from 11638, whose Books I–II italicise scripture and switch to guillemets only at INCIPIT TERTIUS TOMUS. Anyone reconciling the two works should not expect 11632 to repeat that history, and an italic run in a later 11632 chunk is not by itself evidence of a pre-seam regime — it may simply be a lemma. Under Pattern 6 nothing was tidied in either direction; guillemets are 1:1 with the Latin twin in all six chunks (verified mechanically: 0/0, 2/2, 2/2, 9/9, 6/6, 2/2 pairs).

No guillemet asymmetry occurs in this range — every « has its », and none is stray or unopened.

Migne's marginal source-edition numbers 101–110 run through the range (101 in the 0000 head, then 102 0182B, 103 0183D, 104 0185B, 105 0187A, 106 0188D, 107 0190C, 108 0192B, 109 0194A, 110 0195D). Kept italic, verbatim, at the exact word they interrupt — 108 in particular falls between excellentiam and non contaminans, and the English clause was built around it rather than moving it. Same class as 11638's 303–313.

§3 · PATTERN 7 — printed readings rendered as printed, conjectures kept here

Three [sic:] fired. Each is a non-word, and none of the three is also translated in the running text (brief §8's named failure — a [sic:] on a word that was ALSO Englished passes every check and reports nothing).

  1. 0185B [sic: molodia] — non vocis molodia, sed morum consonantia. Read melodia, near-certain: the phrase is a melody/concord antithesis and molodia is not a word. Carried untranslated in italics.
  2. 0186C [sic: tilulo] — insuper et in tilulo regem regis filium se appellat. Read titulo, certain: the same sentence-run has in ipso titulo at 0185C and in hujus quoque libri titulo at 0187A. Carried.
  3. 0191C [sic: eumdum] — ipse tuus uterus eumdum Sponsum hominem generabit. Read eumdem, certain. ⚠ The English deliberately reads "thy very womb shall beget [sic: eumdum] Bridegroom as man" and does not also say "that same": supplying the English demonstrative alongside the marker would have translated the defect and quarantined it at the same time.

Rendered as printed, no marker (real words, merely wrong or merely odd):

  • 0181B narratoria — Quod si virium consideratio narratoria est in carminibus aethnicorum. Rendered "is a narratorial thing". The word is formable from narrator/narratio and construes as a predicate adjective, so Pattern 12's boundary puts it on the English side; but the sense wanted is plainly "necessary/required" and necessaria is the obvious conjecture. The English is ours and reads strangely on purpose. ⚑ Second opinion welcome at merge; do not silently smooth it to "necessary".
  • 0182A, the misplaced semicolon. Migne prints serius quisque [0182A] videatur; non tam nova cudere, quam furari potius praeinventa — a semicolon cutting videatur from its own infinitives. Pattern 8: preserved, so the English reads "…would seem; not so much to strike out new things…". It is meant to look wrong.
  • 0189B longe suavis obdormisse — the construction requires the comparative adverb suavius (longe suavius, "far more sweetly"), and suavis is the nominative adjective, which cannot govern obdormisse. Under 7a the printed word may not be read as its comparative to rescue the clause, so the English reads "slept far sweet". ⚠ This is the sentence in the range most likely to be "fixed" by a later reader. The conjecture is suavius and it lives here, not in the text.
  • 0195A laborem fingere valeam in praeceptum — rendered literally, "may be able to shape labour into a precept". Construable but strained; no emendation offered and none made.

Negation audit (brief §9). Every printed non/nec/neque/nisi/nullus/ nihil/nunquam in the six chunks was carried, including the ones that make the English clumsy: nec debeam, nec praevaleam (0189A), nullus penitus adnotatur, qui non … praeloquatur (0189D), nisi suo soli Domino non concessum (0190C, rendered "not granted save to her Lord alone" — the Latin's redundant negative is preserved in the "not … save"), non defectum, profectum vero (0194D), and the double non praestabit … non negabit at 0182B. No negation was supplied that the Latin does not print.

§4 · CONVENTIONS SET BY THIS RANGE — ⚑ for the merge to ratify

Brief §5's ruled vocabulary was applied as given. These are the new decisions the opening forced, which §5 does not cover.

  1. ⚑ liber = "book", caput = "chapter", volumen = "volume" — and 11632 has no tomi. The work divides into libri (## LIBER PRIMUS. → BOOK ONE.) and capita (## CAPUT PRIMUM. → CHAPTER ONE.). Note that 11638's tomus/liber problem does not arise here in the same shape: at 0186C–0188B Philip uses liber and volumen interchangeably for Solomon's three books (In tertio volumine … liber ille primus), and both are rendered by their own English word, never merged.
  2. ⚑ Migne's own numbering inconsistency in the heads stands. He prints CAPUT PRIMUM in words, then CAPUT II, CAPUT III, CAPUT IV in numerals. The English mirrors it: CHAPTER ONE. then CHAPTER II. etc. Pattern 9 normalizes a section label only where English has no exponent for the defect; word-vs-numeral has one, so nothing was normalized. Do not tidy this to a uniform series.
  3. INCIPIT = "HERE BEGINS" (brief §5), applied at the 0000 head.
  4. ⚑ PROOEMIUM IN CANTICA. → "PROEM ON THE SONGS." — plural, because Cantica is the plural Philip argues for at 0185B–C. The number of Cantica / Canticum / Cantici is tracked per occurrence throughout, never harmonized; see §1 items 8–9.
  5. (cont.) on the repeated CAPUT PRIMUM head is untranslated and carried verbatim (brief §10.7).
  6. [CANT. I.] at the head of 0003 is Migne's own bracketed marginal locator. Reproduced verbatim, untranslated, in place.
  7. ⚑ Migne's mixed capitalization of Sponsus/sponsus, Sponsa/sponsa, Virgo/virgo is MIRRORED, not regularized. He runs both within single sentences (0193D advenientis sponsi… beside 0193C adventu Sponsi; 0194A sponsam matrem Virginem). The English capitalizes exactly where he does. This is the most likely drift point across 21 agents and is the one convention here that a mechanical sweep could check.
  8. Pattern 17 applied throughout, and it does real work in this range. The Annunciation dialogue is singular on both sides — thou/thee/thy for Gabriel to Mary and Mary to Gabriel, including Osculare me osculo oris tui at 0194A — while Philip's own frame is plural: postulatis/deposcatis/ vestris precibus (0182A–B), vos veteres nostis (0182B), Vos igitur in hoc auditorio … qui astatis (0195A–B), sicut nostis and vos, fratres, nostis (0195D, 0196B) all take you. The payoff case is item 31 above: Deut. 18:15 printed in the plural, rendered "him shall you hear", visibly different from the singular the Vulgate would have given.
  9. Pattern 3. Scripturis meaning the canon occurs twice in the range (0184A vera legerent in Scripturis; 0190D scripturis inhaerentem) and is rendered the Scriptures both times. ⚑ Neither instance uses divina or sacra — which is precisely the form 11638's sweep pattern missed — so a later sweep of 11632 must match the bare Scriptura(e) too.
  10. Register vocabulary held to brief §5 where it appears: clemens = "clement" (0192A) kept distinct from misericors = "merciful" in the same sentence; adolescentulae = maidens (0188B, 0188C).

§6 · OPEN — for the merge or a later plate read

  1. ⚑ The Cantica / Canticum number problem is work-wide, and this range only sees its first page. The plural title at 0185C is argued for; the head at the same column is singular; the running work-title in 0181B is the singular ablative Cantico canticorum. Every later agent will meet the same pair. The merge should collect the numbers rather than impose one, and should check whether any later agent silently conformed the 0185C lemma.

Neither has a following Ibid. depending on it, so both are safe to correct upstream if a citation-corrections entry is ever wanted — but that is not this file's business and no correction was proposed.
  3. ⛔ The blind polarity read has not been done and cannot be done by me. Findings for it must be formed blind and reconciled against this file afterwards (runbook 4a). The three passages most likely to be wrongly repaired are named in §3: narratoria (0181B), the semicolon (0182A), and especially longe suavis (0189B).

§7 · RATIO NOTE

EN/LA by chunk (verifier's own figures): 0000 1.55 · 0001 1.55 · 0002 1.52 · 0003 1.56 · 0004 1.64 · 0005 1.68. The verifier warns on the last two. The cause is genre, not padding: Philip writes rhymed, heavily parallel prosa rimata, and the last two chunks are its densest stretch (purificet, magnificet, laetificet; me deliniat, me reficiat, me serenet; utilis, fertilis, et jucunda), where a Latin participle or a syncopated ablative absolute needs a finite English clause each time. 11638 ran 1.35–1.63 on the same author. No clause was expanded that the Latin does not carry, and nothing was summarized.

Philip of Harvengt, Commentaria in Cantica canticorum, Tome I, Capp. V–XI: the exposition of Quia meliora sunt ubera tua vino (Capp. V–VIII, with VIII running over the 0009 chunk boundary) and of Oleum effusum nomen tuum (Capp. IX–XI).

Marker totals for this range: 15 [var:] · 1 [sic:] · 0 [ed:] · 0 [d:] · 0 [nt:] · 0 [f:]. verify-english.mjs clean on all six chunks (one ratio warning, 0009 at 1.61, inside 11638's shipped 1.35–1.63 band). Guillemet, column-anchor and [n:] parity confirmed 1:1 against the Latin twin for every chunk, including the two asymmetries recorded in §3.

  • 0198A occurrit digna relatu / Pompa; senem potum pota trahebat anus — an elegiac couplet from quidam poeta, Philip's own citation. Rendered as verse; the italic run structure is mirrored 1:1.
  • 0201A Qui properant, / nova musta bibant; mihi fundat avitum / Testa merum. — likewise a classical hexameter fragment, cited as E quibus unus. Three italic runs in, three out.
  • 0203A (Psal. [0203B] LXXXIV) — a locator, italic, printed inside the guillemets and containing a column anchor. Reproduced exactly.
  • 0207D Salutaris · Salvator · eleos · misericordia, 0209C unctus, 0212A Oleum effusum nomen tuum, / Ideo, — words displayed as words and the closing lemma. See §5.
  • The Job III speech at 0197B–C (Quare, inquit Job, non in vulva miser ego mortuus exspiravi…) is Philip's paraphrase, not a quotation; the extractor did not list it because Migne prints no opening «. See §3.

1d. Scripture woven into the prose unquoted (no marker; recorded for the index)

Not in the extracted list, since Migne marks none of it, but each is an adapted verse and each was checked so that no conformation crept in: Ps. 77:47 (percussit… vineas iniquorum), Deut. 32:32, Jer. 35, Exod. 21:24 / Matt. 5:39, Jas. 2:13, Job 28, 1 Cor. 8:1 (cited I Cor. II), Isa. 35:3, Phil. 3:13, 1 Cor. 9:27, Heb. 12:6 (quem Pater diligit Filium — Vulg. quem enim diligit Dominus, castigat), Ps. 83:3, 1 Cor. 5:7–8, Luke 10:34, John 9:6, Ps. 6:7–8, Rom. 10:12, Isa. 10:27, Ps. 44:8 (unxit eum Deus… prae consortibus suis for Vulg. unxit te Deus Deus tuus… prae consortibus tuis, third person for second), John 1:9 (word order), Ps. 18:5, Ps. 75:2, Ps. 59:10, Ps. 111:9 + Ps. 77:25, 1 Pet. 1:12, Rom. 11:29 (see §4).

§2 · THE THREE FINDINGS THE MERGE SHOULD CARRY

⭐⭐ Ps. 82:19 — nomen tibi DEUS, not Dominus (0011 @0211B). This is the proof-text of Caput XI, whose whole thesis is announced in its first line: Nomen Sponsi, Deus est. The Vulgate reads Et cognoscant quia nomen tibi Dominus. Conforming the lemma would leave the chapter arguing that the Bridegroom's name is God from a verse that says it is Lord — the exact 7a″ failure. If another range meets Ps. 82:19, expect Deus and do not conform it.

⭐ Isa. 53:4 — infirmitates nostras, not dolores nostros (0008 @0204B). Migne's reading is the Matt. 8:17 form. It is adduced to prove why the Bride says ointments, plural — languores multos, multas infirmitates nostra sibi miseria comparavit — and the next 200 words run on quae infirmitas, quo unguento indigeat. The Vulgate's dolores would leave the plural argument without its keyword.

⭐ The head lemma of Caput V prints ubera SUA (0006, col. 0196C). The Vulgate, the frontmatter incipit, and every other printing of the lemma in this range (0007 ×3, 0008, and the re-quotation inside Caput V itself) read ubera tua. The commentary that follows the defective printing expounds the second person outright — longe esse meliora ubera tua vino — so the divergence is confined to the lemma line. Rendered as printed ("his breasts") with a [var:]. Worth watching across the other twenty ranges: if the running lemma is printed sua again elsewhere it is Philip's text; if this is the only instance it is the compositor's, and this range holds the datum.

§3 · TYPOGRAPHY — the seam question, answered for this range

11632 does not divide its two quotation marks sequentially the way 11638 does. It divides them by FUNCTION, and does so from Tome I onward. Across cols 0196D–0212A both marks are in continuous simultaneous use:

  • Guillemets « » carry every quotation Philip adduces as a witness — scripture, and only scripture, in all 45 runs in this range.
  • Italics carry (a) the running Song lemma at the head of every Caput and at its recapitulations, (b) classical verse (0198A, 0201A), (c) words displayed as words (0207D, 0209C), (d) printed locators — (Job II) at 0197B and (Psal. LXXXIV) at 0203A, the latter inside a guillemet run, and (e) Migne's marginal source-edition page numbers 111–119.

So an italic run in this work is not evidence of a pre-seam book, and a range that meets both marks on the same column has not crossed a seam. I crossed no Explicit/Incipit — chunks 0006–0011 are continuous inside Tome I, Capp. V–XI — and I report no seam. Whether a seam exists later is still open; this range shows only that the starting practice already uses both marks.

Guillemet asymmetries, mirrored and not balanced (Pattern 5 corollary):

  1. Unopened » at 0197C. Philip's paraphrase of Job 3 (Quare, inquit Job, non in vulva miser ego mortuus exspiravi…) is closed by a » that was never opened: …uberibus sum lactatus [n: (Job III)]? ». Reproduced as printed. The chunk's counts are therefore 8 « against 9 » and this is correct.
  2. Unclosed « at 0211D–0212A. « Vere, inquit, tu es Deus absconditus [n: (Isa. XLV)]. Deus Israel Salvator. opens and never closes; the run swallows the whole of Philip's closing exposition to the end of the chunk. Reproduced as printed — 11 « against 10 ». This is also why the extractor listed only 14 spans for 0011: the Isa. 45 quotation is invisible to it.

Two guillemet runs swallow Philip's own commentary (the 11638 @0569A phenomenon, twice in this range). At 0207D–0208A a single « … » encloses Joel 2:32, Ps. 117, the eleos/misericordia etymology, the whole argument that our salvation is of mercy and not of justice, and Titus 3:5 — 110 words of which perhaps 25 are quoted. At 0211C a run opening at Luke 1:68 encloses et benedictum nomen majestatis ejus (which is Ps. 71:19, under a (Luc. I) note) and then Philip's own gloss Nomen humilitatis ejus, Homo est; nomen vero majestatis, Deus est. Both reproduced 1:1. Likewise 0210B, where At ille sits inside the Matt. 16 quotation.

§4 · MIGNE'S REFERENCES — printed as printed, not corrected

Recorded, not acted on (refDisplay keeps what he prints; §10.2 of the brief forbids touching an antecedent a following Ibid. depends on — and both of these have one).

  • 0204A [n: (Gen. XVII)] on Ecce odor filii mei — the verse is Gen. 27:27. Reproduced verbatim.
  • 0211C [n: (Luc. I)] covers Benedictus Dominus Deus Israel (Luke 1:68) and, under the following [n: (ibid.)], et benedictum nomen majestatis ejus, which is Ps. 71:19. The ibid. chain is therefore anchored to a citation that is right for the first half of its run and wrong for the second. Untouched.
  • 0200D [n: (I Cor. II)] on scientia non sanare, sed inflare — the sentence is 1 Cor. 8:1. Untouched.

§5 · RANGE CONVENTIONS (offered to the merge, not settled unilaterally)

Words displayed as words: the Latin is translated, the italics are kept. Four fall in this range, all in the same etymological construction that §5 of the brief ruled on for candidatio:

  • 0207D Jesus, Latina lingua Salutaris dicitur, vel Salvator → "Saving, or Saviour". The argument runs Jesus → Saviour → ipse enim salvum faciet populum suum, and Latin left standing would break it.
  • 0209C Christus autem unctus dicitur → "anointed". The whole of Caput X runs anointed → oil → ipse unctus et ungens.
  • 0207D eleos autem Graece, Latine misericordia est → the Greek* word is kept (eleos; it is named as Greek and is the foreign term), the Latin gloss is Englished: "eleos in Greek is, in Latin, mercy*". Two italic runs in, two out.

This is the same call 11638 §2.3 made and I have made it the same way; it is worth a line in the merge because 11638's own §1 lists Eleos and misericordia among its surviving italics without saying whether they were Englished.

Pattern 17. The range is almost entirely third person. Every second-person form is inside a quotation and every one is singular in the Latin (ubera tua, tu erudieris, faciem tuam, nomen tuum, inclina coelos tuos, tu es Deus absconditus) — so thou throughout. The two plurals are Philip addressing his readers (Nunquid non vobis… videbatur 0198B; De quo legistis 0197C; ut legistis 0199D) and the Matt. 23 Vae vobis, all rendered you. No mixed-number sentence occurs in this range.

Ruled vocabulary held throughout (brief §5): misericordia = mercy (~40 instances, never "pity" where the noun is used) kept distinct from clementia (does not occur here); charitas = charity (0206D a charitate Christi; 0211D ejus charitas se diffudit) — never "love", which is reserved for amor/dilectio, both of which also occur (0205C inducit… amorem, 0210B illius dilectio); Sponsus = Bridegroom, Sponsa = Bride; unguentum = ointment (never "perfume"), species = spices, confectio = confection/compounding.

§6 · PATTERN 7 — printed readings rendered as printed, conjectures kept here

1. 0202C, Pecte igitur virgo ubera sponsi vino dicit meliora. [sic: Pecte] — carried untranslated in italics. Pecte is a real Latin word ("comb!", imperative of pecto) but cannot fill the adverb slot the sentence gives it, and the conjecture is certain: Recte, which is exactly how the parallel sentence opens the same argument at 0196C (Recte, inquit, adventum tuum… praeoptavi) and at 0199C (Recte ergo Jesus dicitur, 0207D). I judged this over the line Pattern 12 draws between "a real word merely wrong" (render it) and carried type: rendering "Comb" would put a considered-looking reading on the page that misrepresents the plate more than the carried run does. This is the boundary Pattern 12 itself flags as worth watching (the 11081 @0030B case); if the merge prefers the other side of it, the fix is one marker.

2. 0204D–0205A, coepit tuam statim turpitudinem abhorrere. Rendered as printed — "began at once to abhor thy foulness" — inside a paragraph that is otherwise wholly third person and reflexive: the next clause is suae merito foeditatis ipsa sibi vehementius displicere, and the one after suo ipsius odio. The conjecture is suam. Rendered literally, not repaired; a real word wrongly inflected takes no marker under Pattern 12.

3. 0203D, quae Deus, honorum semper amans, legitur odoratus. Rendered "ever loving honours". The conjecture is bonorum ("ever loving good things"), which the context — God smelling the odour of sacrifices — plainly wants. A real word, so rendered, not carried.

4. 0206C, unitus patientia, certam velut fiducialiter et humiliter jam praesumit. certam is a feminine accusative with no noun anywhere in the sentence to govern it. Rendered as closely as the words allow ("presumes upon a sure thing, as it were"); the likely loss is certam victoriam or certam salutem (the latter is what the parallel at 0207A supplies — quasi datam teneat jam salutem). Not supplied in the text.

5. 0206B, ejus labores et agones fingit gratia misericorditer in praecepto. fingit rendered "fashions"; figit is possible and would give "fixes… in a precept". Both construe; no repair made, no marker.

6. 0207B, non apud se, ad modum invidorum; clauso spiraculo retentare. Migne's semicolon falls inside the phrase, between invidorum and its participial clause. Preserved (Pattern 8), which leaves the English punctuated oddly at the same point.

7. 0202A, Gal. 2:14 ends with a full stop where the sense is a question (quomodo gentes cogis judaizare.) — 0006 @0199A. The Vulgate prints ?. Preserved as a statement per Pattern 8; not supplied.

Negation audit. Every non / nec / neque / nisi / nunquam / nullus / nihil in the six Latin chunks was matched against the English on a second pass, with particular attention to the dense clusters at 0196D (non sponsorum… non lactari), 0198D–0199A (Nolebat… non solum… quod fas non est), 0208D (noluit misereri… non avertit… non convertit), 0209D (non principio, non fine, non loco, non tempore) and 0210A–D (non prius… non reddiderit se immundum… non Judaeo tantum, non Graeco… nec est ab aliquibus… interclusum). No negation was dropped and none was supplied. The one place where carrying a negation makes the English read strangely is 0210C — remotiores quoque ab eadem exclusi gloria non habentur — and it is carried.

§7 · WHAT A LATER BLIND READ SHOULD LOOK AT FIRST

  1. 0207D's 110-word guillemet run. If any repair has hidden anywhere in this range it is there: Migne's quotation marks enclose Philip's own prose, which means the reader cannot tell quotation from commentary and neither could I. Read it against the Latin as one unit.
  2. The [var:] at 0199C–D (the Ps. 18/Ps. 44 fusion) is the marker in this range making the largest claim, and it asserts a conflation rather than a variant. If the merge decides a fusion under one note is not a Pattern 14 case, that marker is the one to withdraw.
  3. [sic: Pecte] at 0202C — §6.1, the one place I chose the less conventional side of a Pattern 12 boundary.

Philip of Harvengt, Commentaria in Cantica canticorum, PL 203. Range covering CAPUT XII–XVII: the exposition of Cant. 1:2–4 (Ideo adolescentulae dilexerunt te → Nigra sum, sed formosa). Six chunks, 6,782 Latin words.

Marker totals for this range: 15 [var:] · 1 [sic:] · 0 [ed:] · 0 [d:] · 0 [nt:] · 0 [f:]. verify-english.mjs clean on all six (one ratio warning, 0013 at 1.61 — inside the 1.35–1.63 band 11638 established for this author's rhymed synthetic prose). Column anchors, [n:] contents and guillemet counts all verified 1:1 against the Latin twins by diff, not by eye.

§1 · TYPOGRAPHY — this range crosses NO seam, and the reason matters

⭐ 11632 does not switch marks the way 11638 does. It prints both, side by side, throughout, and the division is by FUNCTION. Every chunk in my range carries both, and a count across the whole work confirms the pattern holds from chunk 0000 onward (guillemets and italics appear together in 0000, 0002, 0003 … 0029); there is no run of italic-only chunks followed by a run of guillemet-only ones.

The functional division, consistent in all six of my chunks:

  • Italics — the Song lemma under exposition, both when quoted as the chapter's head-text (Ideo adolescentulae dilexerunt te., Trahe me; post te curremus…, Introduxit me rex in cellaria sua., Nigra sum, sed formosa…) and when re-quoted piecemeal in the gloss (Curremus, … Trahe me. … Memores, … in te;). Also Migne's marginal source-edition page numbers (120–128 run through this range) and one printed locator (§4 below).
  • « » — every other scripture quotation, without exception in this range: 53 guillemeted spans, all of them non-Song scripture (or, at 0220A, the Song quoted from elsewhere in the book — Mel et lac sub lingua tua, Cant 4:11, which is not the lemma under exposition and therefore takes guillemets).

That last case is the proof. At 0220A Philip quotes the Song itself and Migne guillemets it, because it is a proof-text, not the lemma. The mark tracks the quotation's role, not its book. Do not "tidy" 11632 toward 11638's book-boundary model — the two works are marked on different principles, and a sweep that assumes a seam in 11632 will manufacture one.

Guillemet asymmetries: none in this range. All six chunks balance (7/7, 6/6, 4/4, 13/13, 13/13, 10/10) and every pair is reproduced 1:1 in the English. Pattern 5 inquit-interruptions are frequent here — Philip's habit is to drop inquit / ait / inquit Petrus / ait Isaias inside the quotation — and all of them stay inside the guillemets, untouched.

§2 · THE COLLATION — all 80 spans, every one accounted for

The lemma repeats (Trahe me, Curremus, Recti, Exsultabimus, etc.) are short re-quotations of the head-text already collated at its full occurrence and are not re-listed individually below; each was checked against the head-text and none re-quotes it with different words.

⭐ The two Psalm markers are one finding, not two. Ps 15:9 and Ps 65:17 sit sixteen lines apart at 0219D–0220A, and Migne's Ps 15:9 has acquired exactly the two features of Ps 65:17 — the sub lingua and the first-person verb — while Ps 65:17 has in exchange acquired Ps 15:9's verb exsultavi for the Vulgate's exaltavi. The two verses have contaminated each other, and Philip builds directly on the result: « Ad ipsum… exsultavi sub lingua mea. » Sub lingua, dicit in corde. His whole distinction between laetari (of the heart) and exsultare (of the work) — set out over a full column, then qualified by the observation that exultation is sometimes inward too — rests on a phrase that in the Vulgate belongs to the other psalm and to a different verb. Both markers are placed at their own quotation and neither elides the clause it reports.

§3 · TYPE DEFECTS

⭐ 0015 @0220A — Desalutari (Luke 1:47). The one [sic:] in the range. Migne prints « Exsultavit Spiritus meus in Desalutari meo ». Deo salutari has been run together and lost its o: Desalutari is not a Latin word at all, so Pattern 10 governs (run-together division is non-word type) and it is carried into the English untranslated in italics inside [sic: …], with the surrounding in … meo rendered around it. Intended reading, near-certain: Deo salutari, "in God my saviour", the Magnificat's own words. The English therefore reads "« My spirit hath exulted in my [sic: Desalutari] »", which is ugly and is meant to be: the alternative is silently repairing a compositor's fusion in the one verse in this chapter that every reader knows by heart. ⚠ Note that the verse is otherwise in full agreement with the Vulgate — this is a plate defect, not a divergent reading, and it takes no [var:].

⭐ 0016 @0222D — percincti against Migne's own praecincti at 0223B. Luke 12:35 is quoted twice in one chunk, eight lines apart, and Migne spells the participle two different ways: percincti at 0222D, praecincti at 0223B. The Vulgate has praecincti. No [sic:]: percingo is an attested (if rare) verb, so this is Pattern 12's "real word that is merely wrong" class — rendered as ordinary English ("girt about" against "girded" at the second occurrence) and marked [var:] against the Vulgate, not [sic:] against the plate. The self-correction inside a single chunk is what makes it evidential: whatever Philip wrote, Migne's compositor knew the right form and set it eight lines later.

0012 @0213D — a misplaced full stop, preserved (Pattern 8, and 11638 §3). Migne prints cum in me totum Deum, Verbum Patris. Dei Filium introspexi — a stop dropped into the middle of an appositional series, breaking Verbum Patris from Dei Filium. The English carries the stop where the plate sets it, and the resulting fragment stands. Intended reading, obvious: …Verbum Patris, Dei Filium introspexi, "the Word of the Father, the Son of God, I beheld within". Not normalized — English has an exponent for a stop in the wrong place, so Pattern 9's normalization licence does not reach it, and 11638 ruled explicitly that this construction stands.

§4 · A PRINTED LOCATOR INSIDE A QUOTATION — 0016 @0222B–C

Migne prints « Bonus Israel Deus his qui recto sunt corde (Psal. [0222C] LXIX). » — the citation set in italics, inside the guillemets, with a column anchor falling in the middle of it, and no [n:] wrapper. It is therefore not one of the chunk's twenty notes (the count is 20 without it, verified against the body), and it is reproduced exactly as printed, anchor and all, italics and all. This is 11638 §1's "italics survive by function" case: an italic run inside a guillemet quotation that is a locator, not scripture.

⚠ The locator is also wrong — Bonus Israel Deus his qui recto sunt corde is Ps 72:1, not Ps 69. Reproduced verbatim and not corrected; the citation is refDisplay matter and correcting it upstream would break any following anaphora (brief §10.2).

Migne's citation errors in this range, all reproduced verbatim, none patched: (Ose. II) for Hos 11:4 · (II Cor. IX) twice for 1 Cor 9:26 and 9:24 · (Psal. LXIX) for Ps 72:1 · (Isai. XXI) for Isa 11:1 · (Deut. XXXII) on wording that is Ps 91:16's. Five distinct works misnamed in six chunks is a rate worth carrying to the merge — see §5.

§5 · THREE THINGS THE MERGE SHOULD KNOW

1. The mechanical quotation list does not see bare [n:]-noted quotations, and one of my markers is on a span it never listed. Rom 8:10 at 0226B (spiritus autem vivit propter justitiam for the Vulgate's propter iustificationem) is set with neither guillemets nor italics — it sits naked in Philip's sentence with only its note — so it does not appear among the 80 spans I was handed. It is nevertheless a genuine, expounded divergence: Philip repeats vivit propter justitiam eight lines later as the phrase he is glossing, so the Vulgate's iustificationem would take the keyword out of the argument (the 7a″ mechanism exactly). Other ranges should read their chunks for [n:]-noted spans the list could not catch. I found this one only by reading the notes against the prose after finishing the listed collation; there may be more of the class in this work, and no script will surface them.

2. Migne's citation sigla are unusually unreliable in this stretch — five misnamed references in six chunks — and two of them are the SAME error twice. (II Cor. IX) is printed for 1 Cor 9:26 at 0216C and again for 1 Cor 9:24 seven lines later. A repeated wrong siglum on one column is evidence about the copy-text or the compositor's exemplar, not a slip, and it is worth the merge counting the class across all 21 ranges before anyone proposes a citation-corrections.json entry. Nothing was corrected here.

3. 11632's marking practice is functional, not sequential — the brief's open question, answered for this range. Italics = the Song lemma under exposition (plus marginal page numbers and printed locators); guillemets = every other quotation, including the Song itself when quoted as a proof-text from elsewhere in the book (Cant 4:11 at 0220A, Cant 5:11 at 0226A, Cant 2:14 at 0226C — all guilleted, while the lemma five lines away is italic). If the whole work holds to this, 11632 has no seam to find, and the 419/635 corpus counts in the brief reflect a two-channel system running in parallel from column one, not a switch. The merge should test this against the ranges at the Explicit/Incipit boundaries before concluding either way.

Philip of Harvengt, Commentaria in Cantica canticorum, PL 203. Range 4 of 21, covering CAPUT XVIII–XXIV: the exposition of Sicut tabernacula Cedar, sicut pellis Salomonis (Cant. 1:4) through Nolite me considerare (1:5), Filii matris meae pugnaverunt contra me and Posuerunt me custodem in vineis (1:5), to Indica mihi… ubi pascas, ubi cubes (1:6). Six chunks, 5,293 Latin words.

Marker totals for this range: 6 [var:] · 1 [sic:] · 0 [ed:] · 0 [d:] · 0 [nt:] · 0 [f:]. verify-english.mjs clean on all six — no errors, and no ratio warnings (the six sit inside the 1.35–1.63 band). Column anchors (49), [n:] markers (55) and guillemet pairs (37 « / 37 ») were verified 1:1 against the Latin twins mechanically, not by eye.

§1 · TYPOGRAPHY — no seam here either; §7 of the brief holds throughout

Both marks run side by side in every chunk of this range, divided by function exactly as wave 1 described. The proof case recurs and is worth naming, because it is the cleanest instance yet:

⭐ 0239C — Cant. 2:1 is GUILLEMETED while the running Song lemma two columns earlier is italic. Quorum primus et praecipuus ait: « Ego flos campi [n: (Cant. II)]. » The chapter's own lemma, Indica mihi ubi pascas, ubi cubes, is italic at 0237C, and the Song quoted as a proof-text from elsewhere in the book takes « ». Same chunk, same column band, both marks. 11632 is not marked by book, it is marked by role, and no seam should be hunted here.

Two printed locators sit inside guillemet runs with no [n:] wrapper, the 0016 @0222B phenomenon, and both are reproduced exactly:

  • 0232D « Non sunt, ait, recordati foederis fratrum (Amos I). » — italic locator, inside the quotation, not counted among the chunk's four notes (verified: III Reg. III, Ephes. III, Joan. X, Psal. LIV). Here the locator is correct (Amos 1:9), unlike the 0222C case.
  • 0236D (Osee XII) — an italic locator inside Philip's own prose (Hos 12:1, Ephraim pascit ventum), again with no [n:].

Guillemet asymmetries: none. All six chunks balance (6/6, 2/2, 3/3, 6/6, 3/3, 17/17). Pattern 5 inquit/ait/inquiunt interruptions are frequent and every one stays inside the marks.

The [n:] does not always sit inside the closing ». At 0235B (…filiis sceleratis! » [n: (Isa. I.)]) and 0239B (…manduces pascha? » [n: (Marc. XIV.)]) Migne prints the note after the closing guillemet, where elsewhere he prints it before. Mirrored in both places; not tidied.

Marginal source-edition page numbers 129–135 run through the range, one or two to a chunk, kept italic and in place.

Capitalization mirrored, per brief §7a. Virgo/virgo alternates within single paragraphs (0229D–0230A has virginem, virgo, virginis lower case in the middle of a chapter that is otherwise Virgo; 0231B virgo prudens; 0235D conversa virgo) and the English follows word by word — "the Virgin" / "the virgin", "the Bridegroom" / "the bridegroom" (0229D sponsi thalamus). ⭐ The sharpest case is 0238D, where John 3:29 is guilleted with lower-case sponsam sponsus inside a sentence whose surrounding prose has capital Sponsus three times. Rendered "he that hath the bride is the bridegroom" inside the marks, "the Bridegroom" outside.

§2 · THE COLLATION — all 80 listed spans, plus the [n:]-only sweep

Every span in data/quotations/11632/0018-0023.md was collated word by word against the Vulgate. Spans recorded as AGREES were checked and found to agree; the absence of a marker on them is a finding, not a silence. Short re-quotations of a head lemma already collated at its full occurrence are noted once and not re-listed.
