Nolite, / Nolite me considerare quod nigra sum, quia decoloravit me sol.Cant 1:5⚑⚑ [var:] FIRED — the most consequential divergence in the range. The Vulgate reads Nolite me considerare quod fusca sim, quia decoloravit me sol. Migne prints nigra sum: the colour word is changed and the mood with it. Brief §5 rules the colour triple strictly distinct (nigra = black, fusca = swarthy, and fusca is never "black") — so the Vulgate lemma at this verse is not a blackness lemma at all, and Migne's is. Philip then builds two entire chapters on nigredo: Quod nigra sum, quod moesta sum · Sic et ego nigra sum · me vult denigrari · eamdem nigredinem vult inesse · dignam consideratione meam nigredinem · objectu meae nigredinis. Conforming this lemma to fusca sim would leave four columns of exposition attached to a word not on the page — 7a″ in its purest form. The indicative for the subjunctive is part of the same divergence and is named in the marker.

§3 · PATTERN 7 / PATTERN 8 — printed readings rendered as printed

1. 0233D — a comma inside its own phrase, preserved. Migne prints non de bono ut aiunt, opere, sed de blasphemia persequuntur: the parenthetical ut aiunt has been dropped between the adjective and its noun, and the commas set around the wrong words. The English carries the interruption at exactly that point — "not for a good, as they say, work, but for blasphemy" — and reads as oddly as the Latin does. Pattern 8; not normalized, because English has an exponent for a comma in the wrong place.

2. 0238A — divisisque ab invicem turris, non consummatur magnitudinis infinitae. The ablative absolute divisisque ab invicem has no noun anywhere in the sentence to agree with (the sense requires the builders, or the tongues, neither of which is in the nominative or ablative here), and turris stands against a genitive magnitudinis infinitae. Rendered as closely as the printed words allow — "and, they being divided one from another, a tower of infinite greatness is not completed" — with "they" supplied only as English grammar's minimum. Conjecture: an ablative such as linguis or artificibus lost from the phrase. Not repaired, not marked — a real construction with a missing referent is not carried type.

3. 0238B — in qua filii Israel Deo non tibi, sed Moloch superstitione misera deferebant. As printed, the children of Israel paid honour to God, and then "not to thee, but to Moloch" — which contradicts itself inside six words, since the tu addressed throughout the chapter is God. Rendered literally, contradiction included: "wherein the children of Israel paid honour to God, not to thee, but to Moloch." Conjecture, near-certain: non Deo tibi, sed Moloch — "not to thee, their God, but to Moloch" — i.e. non has migrated one word to the right. Not repaired in the text (brief §9: never translate a word as something other than what it means to rescue a sentence), and no marker, because every word printed is a real Latin word correctly inflected.

4. 0235D — [sic: a beo], the one [sic:] in the range. Migne prints conversa virgo ad Sponsum vult a beo qui sint ejus plenius edoceri. A beo is not Latin: the space has migrated one letter to the right in ab eo, which is Pattern 10's split-type class (the defect is the division, so the whole run is carried, a included). Carried untranslated in italics inside [sic: …] with the sentence built around it — "wills to be more fully taught [sic: a beo] who are his." Intended reading, certain: ab eo, "by him", the Sponsum named four words earlier. Rendering "by him" and saying so in a crux was considered and rejected: it puts a considered-looking reading on the page where the plate has none.

Negation audit. Every non / nec / neque / nisi / ne / nunquam / nullus / nihil / nondum / necdum in the six Latin chunks was matched against the English on a second pass, with particular attention to the dense clusters at 0232D–0233A (non verentur… in nullo miserentur… noluerunt… non sorori exhibent, non denique homini), 0233B–C (nec dilexit… nec sensu mollitur… nec Scripturae testimoniis, nec naturae imperiis… nec Deum timent, nec hominem reverentur… nec virginem in conceptu, nec post partum virginem), 0236A–B (non verbo, non lingua, non solo strepitu… non in omnibus locis, non in cunctis pascuis… non habere… non senserit abhorrere) and the whole of 0237D–0238B, which is a chain of five successive non pascis denials. No negation was dropped and none supplied. The two places where carrying one makes the English read strangely are §3.3 above and 0236A quae vitalem succum noverit non habere / quae a vita non senserit abhorrere — a double negative Philip means positively; both are carried.

§5 · THE THREE THINGS THE MERGE SHOULD CARRY

1. ⭐⭐ Cant. 1:5 prints nigra sum for the Vulgate's fusca sim (0230D), and this is the range's most important datum. Brief §5 rules nigra = black and fusca = swarthy, strictly distinct, fusca never "black" — which means the Vulgate's Cant. 1:5 is not a blackness verse and Migne's is. Philip's CAPUT XIX–XX are four columns of nigredo built on it, and the whole nigra sed formosa architecture of Capp. XVII–XXI depends on the colour word being the same one as in v. 4. If another range meets Cant. 1:5, expect nigra sum and do not conform it — and if any range meets fusca, that is a fact worth reporting, because it would mean Migne is inconsistent with himself across the work.

2. All nineteen [n:]-only spans in this range were Philip's own prose, not quotations — and the class is still worth every minute it costs. Wave 1 found Rom 8:10 in this class and it was a genuine expounded divergence; I found none. That is the useful result to report, not a null one: it tells the merge that the class's hit rate is low but that the reading pass is cheap, and it means the range's six [var:] markers all sit on spans Migne himself marked. Two of the nineteen are nevertheless worth the index's attention because they are citation-practice data rather than variants: the Ps 40:10 + Ps 54:14 fusion at 0234B under a single (Psal. LIV) note, and the Ps 110:2 gloss at 0239B where Philip writes voluntates meas for the psalm's eius while glossing a different psalm.

3. 11632's two-channel typography holds through CAPUT XXIV, and 0239C is the cleanest proof in the work so far. Cant. 2:1 (Ego flos campi) is guilleted as a proof-text in the same chunk whose own Song lemma stands in italics — same chapter, same speaker, same book, different marks, because the roles differ. Three wave-1 agents converged on this and my six chunks add nothing against it. Two subsidiary facts for the merge's typographic sweep, both new here: Migne prints the [n:] outside the closing » at 0235B and 0239B (elsewhere always inside), and he prints two locators inside guillemet runs with no [n:] wrapper at all ((Amos I) 0232D, and (Osee XII) 0236D in bare prose). Neither is an asymmetry and neither was tidied, but a script counting notes by their position relative to guillemets will mis-bin them.

§6 · WHAT A LATER BLIND READ SHOULD LOOK AT FIRST

  1. 0238B Deo non tibi, sed Moloch (§3.3) — the one sentence in the range that says the opposite of what the argument needs, rendered literally and unrepaired. If any silent repair has hidden anywhere here, this is where the pressure to make one was greatest.
  2. The Mark 14:14–15 compression at 0239B — the span I judged a compression rather than a variant, and the closest call among the eighty.
  3. [var:] on Isa 5:7 Sabaoth (0235A) — the marker in this range making the smallest claim; if the merge decides a Hebraism substituted for its Latin equivalent is not a Pattern 14 case, that is the one to withdraw.

Philip of Harvengt, Commentaria in Cantica canticorum, PL 203. Six chunks, 6,853 Latin words.

No guillemet asymmetry anywhere in this range — every « has its », none stray, none unopened.

§1 · ⭐ THE BOOK BOUNDARY — I CROSS ONE, AND THERE IS NO TYPOGRAPHIC SEAM AT IT

This is the range brief §7 asks for. Chunk 0025 ends Book I and prints ## LIBER SECUNDUS. as its last head (col. 0246C), with an empty body; chunk 0026 opens ## CAPUT PRIMUM. under it. Migne even prints the transition in Philip's own voice — primo huic tandem libro terminum imponamus … curabo quiescentem calamum retorquere.

Nothing about the marking changes across it. Guillemets and italics are both in use on both sides, in the same functional division wave 1 established:

  • Book I side (0024–0025): italic lemma (Indica mihi…, Ne vagari incipiam…), italic marginal numbers 136–139, italic printed locator; guillemets on Gen. 49:9, Wisd. 9, Matt. 17:4, Cant. 6, Luke 12:32.
  • Book II side (0026–0029): italic lemma and its piecemeal re-quotations, italic marginal numbers 140–145; guillemets on twenty-nine quotations.

So the brief's ruling holds at the one place in the work where 11638's book-boundary model predicted a switch. 11632 has no seam. A later range that crosses the Book II/III boundary should test the same thing and say so; on this evidence the merge can stop looking.

1a. ⚑ But the FUNCTIONAL rule needs widening: guillemets are not scripture-only

Wave 1 stated the division as "« » carries scripture, italics carry everything else," and recorded that every guilleted span in cols 0181–0227 was scripture. That is no longer true from col. 0251D onward, and the counter-examples are not marginal — they are the argument of a whole chapter. In 0028 Migne guillemets:

  • « Scito, inquit, te ipsum, homo. » (0251D) and « Scito, ait, te ipsum, homo. » (0252B) — the Delphic oracle, twice, attributed by Philip to unum e septem Graeciae sapientibus or to Apollo. Not scripture, not italic.
  • « Dii, si qua est pietas coelo. » (0253A) — a line of classical verse (Aen. 2.536, si qua est caelo pietas), introduced sicut ille poeta.

The prologue's Horace and the two poets at 0198A / 0201A were italic. So classical verse takes italics in Book I and guillemets in Book II. The stable description is therefore not "scripture vs. everything else" but « » = a quotation adduced as an external AUTHORITY (whatever its source), italics = the lemma under exposition, printed locators, marginal numbers, and words displayed as words — with 0029's exception below.

1b. ⚑ And guillemets can carry a single word displayed AS a word

0254B prints « Meos » dicit … and dicit « tuos » — two bare pronouns, guilleted, each being discussed as the word of the lemma (pasce haedos tuos, against John 21's agnos meos). Rendered « my » and « thy ». Under wave 1's rule these would have been italic. Reproduced as printed; do not tidy in either direction, and note that 0029 therefore has 12 guillemet pairs where a reader counting quotations would expect 10.

1c. A printed locator inside the guillemets, again

0244C prints « Nolite timere, pusillus grex (Luc. [0244C] XII). » — italic locator inside the quotation, containing the column anchor, with no [n:] wrapper. Third instance of the class (cf. 0203A, 0222B–C). This is why 0025's noteCount is 2 and not 3. Reproduced exactly, anchor and italics and all.

1d. Marginal source-edition numbers

Each kept italic and verbatim at the exact word it interrupts — 137 falls between vobiscum and et laborat, 143 between tamen and virum, and the English clause was built round it rather than moving it.

§2 · THE COLLATION — all 70 listed spans, plus the unlisted [n:] weaves

Every span in data/quotations/11632/0024-0029.md was collated word by word against the Vulgate. Spans recorded as AGREES were collated and found to agree; the absence of a marker on them is a finding, not a silence. Lemma re-quotations (Egredere, et abi, Si ignoras, Equitatui meo, etc.) are short repetitions of a head-text collated at its full occurrence; each was checked against its head-text and none re-quotes it with different words.

2c. The [n:]-only class — read against the prose after the listed collation

All fourteen ⭐ spans on the list were traced back to their real left edge. Thirteen of the fourteen turn out to be Philip's own prose, written with scripture rather than quoting it (accusative-and-infinitive frames, third-person recastings, passive recastings). None takes a marker; a [var:] on unmarked prose would misrepresent it as a lemma. But two are worth the merge's attention:

  1. ⭐ 0240B, Luke 9:58 cited, Matt. 8:20 worded. Quia ergo vulpes foveas, nidos coeli volucres habere dignoscuntur [n: (Luc. IX)]. Luke 9:58 reads volucres caeli tabernacula ; nidos is Matthew's word. Philip's own syntax, so no marker — but the note names the gospel whose wording is not printed. Same class as cruces-0012's Deut. 32:4-cited / Ps. 91:16-worded case.
  2. ⭐⭐ 0245A, Ps. 90:5–6 fused, and Philip then expounds the fusion. He writes vel sagitta in tenebris, vel incursu meridiano [n: (Psal. XC)]. The Vulgate has a sagitta volante in die, a negotio perambulante in tenebris, ab incursu et daemonio meridiano — the arrow flies by day; what walks in darkness is the negotium. Migne's arrow flies in the dark, and the very next sentence glosses the fused form: Sagitta volans in tenebris, quae ferit graviter dum nescitur, occulta est suggestio. The whole hidden-suggestion / open-assault antithesis of Caput XXVI rests on it. No marker, because Migne marks it as neither quotation nor lemma** — it is Philip's prose with a bare note, exactly the class the extractor cannot see — but this is the single most consequential textual observation in my range and the merge should carry it. If a later range meets Ps. 90:6, expect the arrow in darkness.

The remaining twelve, listed so nobody re-opens them: 0240D 1 John 5:19 + Luke 1:35 woven; 0240D John 19:26 recast; 0241C John 13:23 ([n: (Cap. §3 · THE FOUR FINDINGS THE MERGE SHOULD CARRY

⭐⭐ 3.1 · Cant. 6:4 at 0244C — the dropped grex is the word the sentence exists to prove. Philip's point is that the faithful are called a grex singular and the false a greges plural: sciens quia convenientius nomen justis attribuitur singulare. He then adduces two proof-texts for the singular. Migne prints the first as « Capilli tui sicut caprarum » — with no noun at all where the Vulgate has sicut grex caprarum. The keyword has fallen out of the proof-text adduced for it, leaving a bare genitive and only the second half (dentes tui sicut grex ovium) carrying the argument. Rendered as printed, "Thy hair as of goats", with the [var:].

⭐ 3.2 · The head lemma of Book II Caput III prints pulchra where Caput I prints the Vulgate's superlative — and Philip's exposition follows the short form. At 0245D the lemma is o pulcherrima inter mulieres, the Vulgate's superlative. At 0250B, four columns later and heading the same verse's exposition, it is o pulchra inter mulieres, positive. And the gloss between them is unambiguously on the positive: O pulchra, inquit, inter mulieres (0247A), Quamvis quod pulchra inter mulieres dicitur (0247B), then o pulchra four more times at 0253A. So the divergence is not a one-off compositor's slip on a head line (the shape cruces-0006 found for ubera sua at 0196C): six of the seven printings of the phrase in this range read pulchra, and the Vulgate's superlative appears only once, at the head that opens the book. [var:] fired at 0250B only, since 0245D is the one that agrees. ⚑ Worth a count across the later ranges: if pulchra keeps winning, it is Philip's text and the 0245D superlative is the outlier, which reverses the usual expectation.

⭐ 3.3 · Luke 17:10 at 0252D — omnia bona, and the next sentence expounds it. Migne prints « Cum omnia bona feceritis, dicite, quia servi inutiles sumus » where the Vulgate has cum feceritis omnia quae praecepta sunt vobis. Philip's immediately following gloss is built on the substituted phrase: non omnia bona quivis facere comprobatur, si non istud dicere bonis caeteris apponatur; et bonorum congeriem… non colorat. Conforming the lemma to "all things commanded you" would leave four sentences arguing about good things from a verse that no longer mentions them — the 7a″ mechanism exactly. Rendered as printed.

⭐ 3.4 · Exod. 15:1 at 0255B — contamination from the verse quoted two lines later. Migne prints « Equum et ascensorem projecit in mare » (Vulg. deiecit), and then, in the same sentence, « Currus Pharaonis et exercitum ejus projecit in mare », which is Exod. 15:4 and where proiecit is correct. The first verse has taken the second's verb. The sense is not changed — both verbs mean "cast" — and I record explicitly that I fired the [var:] on the word, not on a sense-shift, because this is the same evidential class as cruces-0012's Ps. 15:9 / Ps. 65:17 mutual contamination: two adjacent quotations of the same song, one having borrowed from the other. ⚑ If the merge rules that a sense-neutral lexical swap does not earn a Pattern 14 marker, this is the one to withdraw — the finding survives in this file either way.

§4 · PATTERN 7 — printed readings rendered as printed, conjectures kept here

Two [sic:] fired. Neither carried run is ALSO translated in the running text (brief §8's named failure).

  1. 0241C [sic: lehari] — ne a gloria deprimamur, dum ad formam lehari stulte invadimus altiora. Read Icari, near-certain: the sentence's own frame is the Daedalus myth (Inter utrumque ergo non Dedalus, sed Pater spirituum doceat nos volare), and the antithesis is exactly Daedalus's counsel — too low into mud and dregs on one side, too high after Icarus's fashion on the other. lehari is not a Latin word, so Pattern 7 governs: carried untranslated in italics, and the English deliberately does not also say "Icarus".
  2. 0254D–0255A [sic: vidilicet] — ut vidilicet sequatur exemplo. Read videlicet, certain. ⚠ This one sits on a boundary and I record the choice rather than hide it: an e/i interchange in an unstressed syllable is the sort of thing Pattern 9 exempts as period orthography, and a case could be made for rendering it "namely" and marking nothing. I marked it because wave 1 marked exactly this shape — [sic: eumdum] for eumdem at 0191C — and a work that carries one and renders the other is incoherent on its own page. If the merge prefers Pattern 9 here, it should also revisit eumdum.

Rendered as printed, no marker (real words, merely wrong or merely odd):

  • ⛔ 0250B Nolens Sponsus gradatim ad profectus Virginem promovere, docet eam quomodo mereatur proficiendi gratiam obtinere. The printed Nolens contradicts its own sentence: the Bridegroom is said not to will to promote her, and in the same breath to teach her how to obtain the grace of promotion, which the whole of Caput III then does. The conjecture is Volens, and it is as near certain as the parallel constructions allow. Under brief §9 the negation is CARRIED — the English reads "The Bridegroom, not willing to promote the Virgin by degrees to advances, teaches her how she may deserve to obtain the grace of advancing." It is meant to look wrong. ⚠ This is the sentence in my range most likely to be silently repaired by a later reader, and the repair would be invisible: dropping one participle's negative gives a perfectly smooth chapter opening.
  • 0253A quod quidem difficile est, sed tamen 143 virum est. virum is accusative and fills the slot of a neuter predicate; the clause does not construe. The conjecture is verum ("but yet it is true"), which is what the argument requires — Philip has just said Si here is affirmative, not dubitative. virum is a real word, so Pattern 12 keeps it on the English side and it is rendered, not carried: "which indeed is difficult, but yet is a man". ⚠ Second place most likely to be tidied. Do not.
  • 0242D cum invitat justus secum patientiam ad laborem. The proof-text three lines above is Wisd. 9's ut mecum sit, et mecum laboret, of sapientia — so patientiam is almost certainly sapientiam. A real word that construes in its slot; rendered "invites patience along with himself to labour", no marker.
  • 0250B si, quae tam obtinuit, apud se… sic reponat. tam where the sense wants jam. Rendered "which she has so obtained".
  • 0247B de qua nasci voluit, sepe carnis novo genere non abrupta. sepe = saepe, ablative of saepes, "hedge" — attested medieval orthography, Pattern 9, deliberately unmarked. Rendered "the hedge of her flesh not being broken".
  • 0252C Et Adjunxit: « Pro hujusmodi gloriabor ». Migne capitalizes the verb mid-sentence. The English supplies the pronoun English requires ("And he added"), which relocates the capital and so cannot mirror it; logged here rather than forced. Not a Pattern 8 punctuation case and no mark was deleted.

Negation audit (brief §9), second pass, against the Latin. Every printed non / nec / neque / nisi / nunquam / nullus / nihil was matched, with particular attention to the dense clusters at 0242B (non nisi meridie cubare), 0243D (non nisi dies una non proficiens non deficiens dilucescit, cujus non fuscatur splendor, calor splendidus non tepescit), 0250C (vel non quati ariete, vel flatu quantumvis modico non moveri… nunquam animo consentire), 0250D (si non de his quae acceperat superbiret… Deo paria non sentiret), 0252D (quia non omnia bona quivis facere comprobatur, si non istud dicere… apponatur… qui eam vanitatis vitandae gratia non ignorat), 0255C (minasque Pharaonis non evadunt tali praesidio… equo aut rota volubili non transitur… sicut non navigium, sic nec vehiculum), and 0256A–B (non culpam tibi contrahis, non peccatum, non frangeris opprobriis, non iter deseris… Nec solum caput tuum non premit… sed nec rivus praeteriens). No negation was dropped and none was supplied.* The one place where carrying it makes the English contradict itself is 0250B's Nolens*, above, and that is the point.

§5 · CONVENTIONS SET OR HELD IN THIS RANGE

  1. ⚑ amica mea (Cant. 1:8) = "my FRIEND", not "my love", and the gloss forces it. Caput V opens by glossing the word — Amicam dicit, cujus animus auditui penitus concordat — and proves it from John 15:14, « Vos amici mei estis, si feceritis quae praecipio vobis ». Douay's "my love" would leave the chapter arguing from friends to a lemma that says love, and would also collide with amor and dilectio, both of which are in use in the same columns. This lemma recurs many times later in the Song (2:10, 2:13, 4:1, 4:7, 5:2, 6:3), and the merge should hold every range to one English form of it. Flagged as the range's one work-wide vocabulary decision.
  2. LIBER SECUNDUS. → "BOOK TWO.", after wave 1's LIBER PRIMUS. → "BOOK ONE." The head sits at the end of 0025 with an empty body and its Caput I opens the next chunk; nothing was moved.
  3. Migne's CAPUT PRIMUM in words, then CAPUT II–V in numerals, mirrored and not tidied — and note that Book II restarts the numbering while Book I ended at CAPUT XXVI. Preserved as printed.
  4. ⚑ Sponsus/sponsus, Virgo/virgo capitalization mirrored word by word (brief §7a). The live case in this range is 0243B–C, where Migne prints lower-case sponsum — sponsum tenere sinu, affectu, velut brachio circumplecti — inside a paragraph that has Sponsus capitalized four times before and after it. The English reads "bridegroom" there and "Bridegroom" everywhere else. Likewise 0252D quae nondum dat filius (lower case, rendered "the son") beside Sponsus capitalized in the same sentence. Mechanically checkable against the Latin; do not regularize.
  5. Pattern 17 does real work here. Caput I–V of Book II is the Bridegroom speaking to the Virgin, singular throughout — Tu, ait, quae majorem cunctis mulieribus gratiam jam adepta (0247D), attende diligentius quid tibi jam meo munere sit collatum, si… memoriter consideraveris te habere, assimilavi te, te addixi, te benedixi, tuas… maculas, te perduco, tibi contrahis, caput tuum, vera mater facta es — so thou without exception. Philip's own frame is plural and takes you: sicut nostis (0241C), cum vobis, fratres and the whole 0242C–0243A exhortation (castigatis, alligatis, relegatis, laboratis, manducatis, dicitis, aestuatis), Videtis Paulum (0252C), ut… noveritis (0252D). The one mixed-number sentence is 0255B's « Vos amici mei estis, si feceritis quae praecipio vobis » — plural, inside a chapter otherwise addressed to one woman, and the English shows it.
  6. Brief §5 vocabulary held: charitas = charity (0241D sua erga eos charitas) kept distinct from amor / dilectio = love (0241C amoris gratia, dilectionis floribus, where Philip's own doublet forces the repetition and it was not varied for elegance); misericordia = mercy (0255D in misericordia tua), clementia does not occur; fusca = swarthy — live at 0247B, matrem elegerit fuscam, luscam, and at 0243D, cujus non fuscatur splendor, both rendered "swarthy"/"made swarthy", never "black"; Sponsus = Bridegroom, Sponsa = Bride; equitatus = cavalry, quadriga = four-horse car, kept distinct from currus = chariot (0255C–D runs all three in two sentences).
  7. Migne's Si discussed as a word at 0253A is NOT italicized on the plate (Quod enim dicit Si, non dubitativa, sed affirmativa conjunctio est), unlike every other word-as-word in this work. The Latin word is kept in the English and no italics were supplied — adding a run the plate lacks would break italic parity to make a point the sentence already makes.

An entry defending an unusual rendering deserves more scrutiny than an unlogged passage, not less.

The safe form is "guillemets = a quotation adduced as an authority; italics = the lemma, locators, marginal numbers and words-as-words" — with 0254B's « Meos » / « tuos » standing as a genuine exception to the last clause.

§1 · THE TERM DECISION THE MERGE MUST RATIFY — muraenula stays Latin

⭐⭐ This is the most consequential thing in the range and it is work-wide, not range-local. Caput VIII (chunk 0032) expounds Cant. 1:10 Muraenulas aureas faciemus tibi, vermiculatas argento, and its entire argument is that the word names a fish:

Muraenula piscis est, qui nutritus in aquis… Cujusmodi piscem forte Sponsus promittere Virgini videtur… quod intellectum ad litteram nobis penitus interdicit, cum eumdem piscem aureum vel argenteum esse dicit.

Then the fish's shape carries the whole chapter — tail to mouth, a ring, meshes of a net, a chain, Moses' head-and-tail offering, ut integretur macula, fiat annulus, muraenula retundatur. Rendering the lemma "chains of gold" (the 10379 solution) makes seventeen paragraphs explain nothing: a chain that "is a fish" is not an argument, it is a non-sequitur.

So this range follows 10804's precedent, which translation-style.md names as correct for this very word: muraenula / muraenulae stays in italic Latin, in the lemma and in the prose alike (17 instances in 0032). This is the Song ruling's case 2 — the gloss IS the etymology, the stylus/epistylium and murenulae/ferculum class — and not a Pattern 12 carry-through, so no [sic:] and no crux-per-instance.

⚑ The lemma recurs later in the work and every later agent must render it the same way. Within a work: one voice (the style file's own boundary clause). If the merge prefers "little lampreys" or "chains", the change is mechanical, but it must be made everywhere or Caput VIII becomes incoherent on its own page.

The companion decision, and it went the other way: vermiculatas argento is translated, as "vermiculated with silver". The gloss chain here runs vermiculat → vermiculatio → vermilio → vermiculus → vermis (Ps. 21:7 Ego autem sum vermis), and English happens to carry the whole chain visibly — vermiculate / vermiculation / vermilion / little worm / worm. Nothing is lost, so nothing is left in Latin. Brief §5's candidatio rule governs: italic Latin is only for words with no clean English equivalent, and this one has one.

§3 · THE FIVE [var:], IN FULL

1. ⭐⭐ Ps. 11:7 at 0264C — eloquium SINGULAR, and it is [n:]-only. Migne prints Habetis quia eloquium Domini eloquium castum, argentum igne examinatum, probatum terrae, purgatum septuplum [n: (Psal. XI)]. The Vulgate reads the plural Eloquia Domini, eloquia casta. The singular is the word Philip goes on to expound, twice, within eight lines: Petri eloquium ignis non sonorum… Joannis vero eloquium non satis lucidum invenitur. His whole point is that one man's speech and another man's speech are each assayed like silver, and the plural would dissolve the comparison into a general predication about scripture.

⛔ This span is set in NEITHER guillemets NOR italics — it is the class the brief warns about at §8 and that cruces-0012 §5.1 found Rom. 8:10 in. The extractor listed it only because the note is attached; it could not know where it began, and the opening is eloquium, not Habetis.

2. Isa. 43:2 at 0264C — two words, and Philip's next clause uses both. Migne: « Si transieris, ait, per ignem, non combureris; et flamma non nocebit in te ». Vulg.: cum ambulaveris in igne, non combureris, et flamma non ardebit in te. (transieris has migrated from the preceding water clause, cum transieris per aquas.) The marker matters because the sentence Philip builds on it reads illaesum transiens, "passing through unharmed" — which picks up transieris and nocebit precisely, and neither of which is in the Vulgate's wording of the verse.

3. Lam. 3:65 at 0268A — tense, plus an added vocative. Migne: « Domine, ait, dedisti eis scutum cordis, laborem tuum ». Vulg.: Dabis eis scutum cordis, laborem tuum — future, no vocative. The tense is material in the place Philip puts it: the verse is the third of three proof-texts (utquid dereliquisti me · Laboravi sustinens · this) adduced to show that the incarnate life was non quietis haec habitatio, sed laboris — an accomplished labour, not a promised one. Same class as the 0193C Jer. 31:22 marker in wave 1.

4. Prov. 8:17 at 0273B — Ergo for Ego. Migne: « Ergo, inquit, diligentes me diligo ». Vulg.: Ego diligentes me diligo. Under Pattern 5 the interrupting inquit sits inside the quotation, so Ergo is the quotation's first word, not Philip's connective outside it. Rendered "Therefore" as printed; the marker records the emphatic pronoun the received text has and this printing does not. (This is the one marker in the range where the divergence is most likely a compositor's transposition rather than a copy-text reading — but Pattern 14 forbids speculating about why, so the note states both readings and nothing more.)

5. Luke 8:46 at 0273B — sensi for novi. Migne: « Tetigit me, inquit, aliquis: ego enim sensi virtutem de me exisse ». Vulg.: nam ego novi virtutem de me exiisse — "I know", not "I felt". Material here because the verse is adduced for a touch, and the paragraph around it is built on sensation: cum tangitur affectu placito diligentis… qui si tactu et amore digne credentium compungatur. The Vulgate's novi would put knowledge where Philip's argument needs feeling.

§4 · PATTERN 7 AND PATTERN 10 — four [sic:], and what was NOT marked

The four carried runs. None of the four is ALSO translated in the running text (brief §8's named failure).

  1. 0030 @0256C [sic: a vida] — et alter alterum non fastidit, sed fauce semper a vida satiatur. Pattern 10, split type: a vida is not a Latin phrase (vida is not a word), and the run is avida, agreeing with fauce — "with an ever-greedy throat". The whole broken run is carried, spacing included; the English reads "with a throat ever [sic: a vida] is satisfied" and does not also supply "greedy".
  2. 0031 @0260B [sic: munos] — Ipsa prior, ipsa felicior accipit grande munos. Read munus, certain (grande munus). Carried untranslated; the English does not also say "gift".
  3. 0032 @0263A [sic: cam] — nulla adversitas a proposito cam praevalet removere. Read eam, certain. The English reads "no adversity prevails to remove [sic: cam] from her purpose" and supplies no pronoun.
  4. 0035 @0273A [sic: idco] — idco forte divinus sermo vineas appellavit. Read ideo, certain. The English does not also say "therefore".

Rendered as printed, no marker (real words, merely wrong or merely odd) — conjectures live here and NOT in the text:

  • 0263C, fornax exstitit et incudo. The slot wants the nominative incus; incudo is a real word (1 sg. of incudo, "I forge on an anvil") and cannot fill it. Migne himself sets the correct form two columns later (tanquam in incude macula tunditur, 0265A). Rendered "anvil" as an inflectional error under Pattern 12's "real word merely wrong" clause; ⚑ if the merge judges incudo a non-word in this slot, the fix is one [sic:] and I flag it rather than defend it.
  • ⚠ 0265A, non viandi completio, non gaudium ei acceptio, sed promissio dat coronae. This clause does not construe as printed and it is the passage in the range most likely to be quietly repaired. gaudium is accusative in a list of nominatives, and coronae cannot be the object of dat. Rendered as closely as the printed words allow — "not the completing of the wayfaring, not joy, the receiving of it for her, but the promise gives of the crown" — which is meant to read wrong. Conjecture: non gaudii ei acceptio… sed promissio dat coronam. No emendation made, none smuggled into the English.
  • 0262C, Inquieta undarum profunditas… non sufficiunt admirari, quod festinant adversus Virginem… congregari. Rendered actively ("cannot wonder enough that they hasten…"), the waves personified — which is what obstupescunt attendentes eleven words later requires. A passive reading ("are not enough to be wondered at") is possible; logged, not adjudicated in the text.
  • 0266B, nec de utero altero concepisse. Rendered "nor had conceived of another womb". Odd as printed (de viro altero is the obvious sense); a real word, so rendered, not carried.
  • 0273B, temptationis oculis — see §2, 0035 table.
  • 0274A, in luctu fortior habeatur. Rendered "the stronger in the wrestling": luctus for lucta is attested medieval usage (Pattern 9, no marker), and the paragraph is unambiguous — athletam strenuum, cum recens accingitur in agone, with the wrestler's oil three lines above; the same chunk-neighbour uses lucta correctly (0270A, sopita lucta carnis).
  • 0273B, volverit aut valuerit perscrutari. Rendered "shall have turned it over or been able to search it out" — volvere "to turn over in the mind" is good Latin and construes with ipsum. The rhyme partner makes voluerit the likely intention; not read that way, logged here.
  • 0272B, Migne's misplaced full stop, PRESERVED with its lower case. He prints potius quam secunda, ut aiunt. qui viderunt, vini peroptimi tam fecunda. The English reads "…rather first than second, as they say. who have seen it, so fruitful of the very best wine…". Brief §5's ruling is explicit — lowercase after a misplaced stop STANDS, because English has an exponent for it — and 11638 §3 and cruces-0012 §3 both settled the construction. ⚠ Do not churn this.
  • 0272B, the second stop, likewise preserved: ut ejus gaudium excellentius caeteris liquido cognoscatur. Botrus, de quo sermo est… — a stop cutting a purpose clause from the main clause it depends on. Two sentences in the English, as printed.

Negation audit (brief §9). Every non / nec / neque / nisi / nullus / nihil / nunquam / haud in the six Latin chunks was matched against the English on a separate second pass. The dense clusters are 0256D (non laedit macula, non corruptio… non sordescit… non pallescit), 0257A–B (nullius meriti, nullius… alterum ultra nescit… nec sic alterum vult habere, nec in ligno viridi vult sedere), 0257D–0258A (non se tamen Christum, non esse Sponsum… eligit non mentiri… non se Sponsum asserit, sed amicum), 0258B (non potest non gaudere — a double negative carried as a double negative), 0258C (non germinat, non justo germine fecundatur, nisi Sponso largiente), 0262C (Impellunt, non expellunt; convellunt, non evellunt; concutiunt, non excutiunt), 0262D (Nullum quippe scrupulum, nullum offendiculum), 0264B (nec vermiculi nec argenti), 0265B (haud dubium quin et Spiritus sanctus — carried as "there is no doubt but that"), 0269C–0270A (non solum non eligant consentire… Neque enim possumus… non penitus relegare), 0272C (aliis varie diffidentibus non diffisa), 0272D (non consuetudo, non necessitas), 0273A (Engaddus vineas dicitur non habere), 0274B (nulli par esse creditur non secunda). No negation was dropped and none was supplied.

§5 · TYPOGRAPHY AND CAPITALIZATION — this range crosses no seam either

Brief §7 holds without exception across cols 0256C–0274C, and this range adds two more instances of the decisive proof. Guillemets carry every non-lemma scripture quotation (42 runs); italics carry the running Song lemma, printed locators and Migne's marginal page numbers 146–155. The Song quoted as a proof-text takes guillemets — « Cum esset, inquiens, Rex in accubitu suo [n: (Cant. I)] » at 0270B and « Tenui eum, nec dimittam [n: (Cant. III)] » at 0271A, both guilleted while the italic lemma sits a few lines away in the same column. That is now Cant. 4:11 @0220A, 5:11 @0226A, 2:14 @0226C, 1:12 @0270B and 3:4 @0271A — five instances, three ranges, one rule. 11632 has no seam and no one should go looking for one.

Guillemet asymmetries: none in this range. All six chunks balance and every pair is 1:1 with the Latin twin. Pattern 5 inquit / ait / inquiens / ait sacerdos interruptions are very dense in this stretch — Philip drops one into roughly every second quotation — and every one stays inside the marks, in the italic lemma runs (Cum esset, inquit, Rex in accubitu suo) exactly as in the guillemeted ones.

Two printed locators inside guillemet runs, neither wrapped in [n:]: (ibid) at 0260D and (Matth. [0267C] XVI) at 0267B — the latter with a column anchor inside it. Both reproduced exactly, italics and all; neither counts toward noteCount (verified against the body).

⚑ §7a mirroring — the drift point — held word by word. The range is full of mixed case inside single sentences and none of it was regularized: Virgini… virgo diligens hilarescit (0258A) · cum ea sponsus est (0258B, lower case in a chunk that capitalizes Sponsus eleven times) · in utero virginis Deus homo (0259C) · Patrem cum filio et sanctum aeque Spiritum (0265B) · Sponsae virgini loquens (0265B) · nardus virginis (0268A) beside Virginis throughout 0266 · Dilectum vero suum virgo (0270A) · amore sponsi (0269D) · Bonus iste Fasciculus (0270B, capital) · nostra virgo (0268D) and hujus virginis (0273D, 0274A) in a chapter that capitalizes Virgo nowhere after 0272A. The Cant. 1:13 lemma prints Dilectus capitalized once and lower case three times. All mirrored. This is mechanically checkable against the Latin twin and I would check it first in any review.

Pattern 17. Philip's own frame is plural throughout and takes you (accepistis 0259C, vobis videtur 0259D and 0263C, nostis 0261A and 0264A, Videtis 0258A, 0263C, 0269C, Habetis 0264C, Nostis 0269A, legistis 0270C, accepistis 0273A). Every second-person singular is inside a quotation and every one is singular in the Latin — vincula colli tui, captiva filia Sion; si transieris… non nocebit in te; dereliquisti me; dedisti eis… laborem tuum; consentiens adversario tuo, dum es in via; faciemus tibi — so thou throughout. The one plural inside a quotation is Matt. 11:29 Tollite jugum meum super vos, et discite, rendered you, sitting four lines from the singular Isa. 52:2 — the number distinction is visible on the page exactly as Pattern 17 intends.

Ruled vocabulary held (brief §5): charitas = charity throughout 0032, including the doublet dilectio sive charitas (0263B) which is split "love, or charity"; misericordia = mercy (0266D, 0273C); torcular = winepress (0263D, 0272B); species = spice (0269A, of myrrh); adolescentulae = maidens (0265C, 0274B); recti, cellaria, clementia, nigra/fusca/formosa do not occur. Sponsus = Bridegroom, Sponsa = Bride, unguentum = ointment, nardus = nard (and nardus pistica = spikenard at 0268C, where Migne's own Latin distinguishes them).

One new fixed equivalence this range had to set, offered to the merge: accubitus = "repose", with accubuit / accumbens / accubitui rendered "reposed" / "reposing" / "his repose" throughout Caput IX. The chapter turns on the single root — in accubitu suo → in meo utero Rex ille gratanter accubuit → cujusmodi accubitus accumbenti complacuit → Sponso accumbente in dextera divinae majestatis — so a Douay-style "at his repose" for the lemma and "reclined" for the verbs would have severed it. recumbenti (John 12, of Christ at table, 0268C) is kept distinct as "reclining", because Migne's Latin distinguishes it.

§6 · THINGS DELIBERATELY NOT REPORTED (brief §10, checked once)

  • Column-band arithmetic: no anchor in this range is followed by text broken mid-word or mid-construction. The bands run cleanly A–D. No [ed:], no patch, no plate check. §10.1.
  • noteCount matches the body [n:] count in all six chunks (5/5/19/17/10/7), verified by script — and note that the two printed locators (§5) are correctly outside that count.
  • Migne's sigla, all reproduced verbatim, none corrected (§10.2): (Rom. XIII) for Rom. 11:16 @0258C · (Matth. XXI) for Matt. 26:10 @0268D. Two in six chunks — notably lower than the five-in-six rate cruces-0012 §5.2 recorded for cols 0212–0227, which is itself a datum for the merge's count of that class.
  • Attested medieval spellings left alone, unmarked (Pattern 9): mirrha, muraenula (for murenula), tanquam, quodcunque, utquid, praetiosae beside pretiosi, Quodpropter, siquis, coelo, spiritalis, luctus for lucta, aethnicum/ethnicum.
  • No [f:]. 11632 is lemma-and-gloss, not a florilegium (§10.4).

§7 · WHAT A LATER BLIND READ SHOULD LOOK AT FIRST

  1. 0265A, non viandi completio, non gaudium ei acceptio, sed promissio dat coronae (§4). The English is deliberately unconstruable because the Latin is. This is the single most likely place in the range for a well-meaning repair.
  2. 0264C, the Ps. 11:7 [var:] (§3.1). It is on an [n:]-only span, which means nothing on the page marked it as a quotation and nothing mechanical would ever have found it. If it is wrong, it is wrong invisibly — check the left edge of the quotation, which I judged to begin at eloquium and not at Habetis.
  3. The Cum / Dum lemma of Cant. 1:12 (§2, 0033). Four printings, no marker fired. Either the merge rules it Philip's Bible (brief §6 shape) or it is a compositor's habit; the decision needs the other twenty ranges' evidence, not mine.
  4. §1's muraenula decision. It is the only term choice in this range that would be expensive to reverse late.

Philip of Harvengt, Commentaria in Cantica canticorum, PL 203. Range covering Book II, Capp. XIII–XXI: the exposition of Cant. 1:14–2:3 (Ecce tu pulchra es, amica mea → Ecce tu pulcher es, dilecte mi, et decorus → Lectulus noster floridus; tigna domorum nostrarum cedrina → Ego flos campi, et lilium convallium → Sicut lilium inter spinas → Sicut malus inter ligna silvarum). §1 · THE COLLATION — all 65 listed spans, every one accounted for

Every span in data/quotations/11632/0036-0041.md was collated word by word against the Vulgate. Spans recorded as AGREES were collated and found to agree; the absence of a marker on them is a finding, not a silence.

§2 · THE [n:]-ONLY CLASS — hit rate, and two logged candidates

⚑ Hit rate reported as brief §8a requires. The range carries 21 [n:]-only spans. Nineteen are Philip's own prose, itemized above. Two are genuine weaves whose wording diverges from the Vulgate in a way that matters — and per brief §8a both are logged with full evidence and NOT marked, because the plate marks neither with guillemets nor italics and we cannot establish the quotation's left edge without asserting a boundary Migne does not print.

That is 2 of 21 ≈ 10%, against wave 1's Rom. 8:10 (1 hit) and the 0018–0023 agent's null result (0 of 19). The separate second pass over the [n:] notes against the prose, which the brief mandates, is what produced both — neither was visible from the extractor's clause alone, because in both cases the printed clause the script hands you begins in the wrong place.

2.1 ⭐⭐ 0277B — Wisd. 7:26 + Heb. 1:3 fused, with imago veritatis for imago bonitatis

Migne prints, inside Philip's own quia-clause:

Pulcher, inquam, es, quia candor lucis aeternae, speculum sine macula divinae majestatis, paternae splendor gloriae, figura substantiae, imago veritatis [n: (Hebr. I)]

Three things at once:

  1. The note names Hebrews only, but the first two members are Wisdom 7:26 (candor est enim lucis aeternae, et speculum sine macula Dei maiestatis, et imago bonitatis illius), and only splendor gloriae, figura substantiae is Heb. 1:3. A two-book fusion under a one-book siglum.
  2. Wisdom's imago bonitatis is printed imago veritatis. The change is real and is not a truncation: bonitas and veritas are different predications of the Son.
  3. Wisdom's Dei maiestatis is printed divinae majestatis.

Not marked, and the reason is exactly brief §8a's: the run is set in neither guillemets nor italics, it is grammatically a string of appositives inside Philip's own sentence (the finite verb is his es), and the extractor's left edge — Pulcher, inquam, es — is his prose, not the quotation's. If the merge rules the class markable, this is the site in this range that takes the marker, and imago veritatis is the word to put in it. Nothing in the surrounding exposition picks the word up, which is why I do not think it rises to §3's level even if the class were opened.

2.2 ⭐ 0278D — Prov. 31:19, manum ad collum where the sense requires colum

Migne prints:

illa mulier cujus fortitudo praedicabilis commendatur, manum ad collum mittere, et fusum digitis apprehendere memoratur [n: (Prov. XXXI)]

The Vulgate of Prov. 31:19 reads Manum suam misit ad fortia, et digiti eius apprehenderunt fusum. Two separate observations:

  • ad collum, "to the neck", cannot be right beside fusum, "the spindle". The word wanted is colum, the distaff — a real Latin word one l away, and the reading behind the Hebrew and the Old Latin of this verse. Migne's doubled l makes it the neck.
  • Even colum would be a non-Vulgate reading, since the Vulgate has ad fortia here.

Rendered as printed — "to put her hand to the neck, and to take hold of the spindle with her fingers" — under Pattern 7. No [sic:]: collum is a real word merely wrong in its slot (Pattern 12's explicit exclusion, the fuges / munde class), and no [var:] because the span is [n:]-only. The conjecture colum lives here and not in the text. The tail of the same span, panem suum non comederit otiosa, is Prov. 31:27 (panem otiosa non comedit) recast into Philip's eo quod clause, with the negation carried.

§3 · THE FOUR [var:], IN FULL

1. ⭐ Luke 23:34 at 0284D — ignosce for dimitte, and quia for non enim. Migne: « Pater, inquit, ignosce illis, quia nesciunt quid faciunt ». Vulg.: Pater, dimitte illis: non enim sciunt quid faciunt. The main verb is a different word — ignoscere, "to pardon", against dimittere, "to remit" — and it is the Old Latin form of the most famous sentence in the Passion, which is precisely the 7a″ conformation hazard: the remembered English arrives before the printed Latin is read. The marker matters here because the sentence Philip builds round it reads cum manu misericordiae spinarum turpitudinem abradebat — a hand of pardon scraping the thorns, not a debt remitted. Rendered "pardon them" so that the divergence is visible in the English, per Pattern 7a's rule that a [var:] may not elide what it exists to report. The negation is intact on both sides (non enim sciunt / nesciunt) and is carried.

2. ⭐⭐ Isa. 35:1 at 0285A — germinabit for florebit, and Philip expounds the divergent verb twice. Migne: « Laetabitur, inquit, deserta et invia, et exsultabit solitudo; et germinabit quasi lilium ». Vulg.: et florebit quasi lilium. This is the range's clearest marker. Within nine lines Philip writes quia juncta lilio quasi lilium germinabit, and then spe fructus exsultabit habens primitias germinantes — the whole close of Caput XX runs on budding-into-fruit, not on blossoming, and florebit would put the argument's keyword back in a verse that no longer contains it. Everything else in the verse agrees word for word (deserta et invia, exsultabit solitudo), which is what makes the one substitution legible as a reading rather than a paraphrase.

3. Acts 10:26 at 0286D — an added clause, sicut et tu. Migne: « …Petrus autem levavit eum dicens: Surge, et ego ipse homo sum, sicut et tu ». The Vulgate ends the verse at et ego ipse homo sum; the comparative clause is in no edition. It is material in its place: Philip's whole point is that Peter refused adoration by asserting parity with Cornelius, and sicut et tu states the parity the argument needs. (Also in the same span: Migne supplies the subject Cornelius, which the Vulgate carries in the preceding verse, and prints levavit / autem for elevavit / vero — neither marked.) ⚑ Note the marker's content deliberately quotes the Vulgate's wording, not Migne's, so that it cannot collide with Pattern 14's mirror test against the Latin twin.

4. ⭐ Eph. 2:3 at 0288D — Sumus for eramus, present for imperfect. Migne: « Sumus, inquit, natura filii irae ». Vulg.: et eramus natura filii irae, sicut et ceteri — "we were". The tense is the point in the place Philip puts it: the sentence he is proving reads Nos autem miseros multo minores angelis culpa fecit… eo quod versum est vitium in naturam, an argument about our standing condition, not about a state Paul has left behind. The Vulgate's past tense would make the proof-text say the opposite of the sentence it is adduced for. ⚑ Cross-reference for the merge: cruces-0024 recorded Eph. 2:3 as an unmarked weave at 0030 (irae filius ex natura). This is the same verse returning as a guilleted proof-text with the tense changed — a second attestation, and worth counting.

§4 · MIGNE'S SIGLA — four misnamed references in six chunks (brief §8b)

All reproduced verbatim, none corrected. The count is the point.

  1. ⚠ (Psal. XCII) at 0275B for « Deus, Deus meus ». Ps. 92 is Dominus regnavit, decorem indutus est and contains no such words; the doubled vocative is Ps. 21:2 or Ps. 62:2. And the same siglum is CORRECT eleven columns later at 0281A, where it points at Ps. 92:5 domum tuam decet sanctitudo. One siglum, two uses, one right and one wrong, inside one range.
  2. ⚠ (Matth. XX) at 0274D for Matt. 22:40 — off by two chapters.
  3. ⭐ (Marc. XV) at 0283B for wording that is verbatim MATT. 27:54. Migne prints « Vere Filius Dei erat iste »; Mark 15:39 reads Vere hic homo Filius Dei erat, Matthew Vere Filius Dei erat iste. The decisive evidence is in the previous range: cruces-0030 records the same six words at 0267D under [n: (Matth. XXVII)]. So Philip quotes Matthew twice and Migne labels the second occurrence Mark. This is the cleanest instance of the class so far in this work — the control is internal, not editorial.
  4. ⚠ (Matth. XXV) at 0286C for fratres eos non confunditur vocare + cohaeredes, which are Heb. 2:11 and Rom. 8:17.

Also recorded as a form rather than an error: (cap. I) at 0281C, a bare chapter number with no book name, the book carried by Habacuc in the running prose. And the (ibid.) at 0286D resolves correctly to Acts X — do not propose a correction upstream of it (§10.2).

§5 · PATTERN 7 / 10 / 12 — one [sic:], and what was NOT marked

1. 0283A — [sic: ooopertus]. Migne prints Deus est in homine mundae carnis trabea ooopertus. Three o's: not a word in any Latin, and therefore Pattern 7's non-word class. Read coopertus, "covered", certain from the slot (trabea ablative of means) and from opertorium / occultavit five lines away. Carried untranslated in italics inside the marker, and the English does NOT also supply "covered" — the failure brief §8 names ("a [sic:] on a word that was ALSO translated passes"). The clause reads "is God in man, [sic: ooopertus] with the robe of clean flesh."

Rendered as printed, no marker (real words, merely wrong or merely odd) — conjectures live here and NOT in the text:

  • ⚠ 0287C, « Conservus tuus suum, et fratrum tuorum… ». The Apoc. 19:10 re-quotation has lost its only finite verb: suum stands where sum belongs, and Migne himself prints the correct conservus enim tuus sum nine lines above at 0287A, in the full quotation of the same verse. So the conjecture is certain and the plate refutes itself on the same page. Even so, suum is a real word, which puts it in Pattern 12's explicit exclusion (the fuges / munde class: "rendered as ordinary English under Pattern 7, because they can be rendered"), so no [sic:]. The English reads « Thy fellow-servant his own, and of thy brethren that have the testimony of Jesus, adore God. » — verbless and wrong, deliberately, with Migne's commas preserved. ⛔ This is the single most likely place in the range for a well-meaning repair. ⚑ If the merge judges suum a non-word in this slot (the incudo question cruces-0030 §4 left open), the fix is one [sic:] and I flag it rather than defend it — the two cases should be decided together.
  • 0283C, nonnullas videtur sentire functiones. functio has no sense here that construes cleanly against its rhyme-partner laesiones; medieval usage (onus, munus) would give "burdens". Rendered neutrally and literally as "workings", from fungi; conjectures concussiones / fluctuationes are possible and not supplied. Logged rather than adjudicated in the text.
  • 0275A, ut humilem spiritu reddat virginitatis flosculus clariorem, flore claram virgineo, spiritu humilis pulchriorem. A chiasmus with only one finite verb: virginitatis flosculus is the first subject, and the second is spiritu humilis — a nominative adjective, where spiritus humilis would be expected. Rendered as printed ("the little flower of virginity renders her that is humble in spirit the brighter, and one humble in spirit renders her that is bright with the virginal flower the fairer"), the second verb supplied by English zeugma only. Conjecture spiritus humilis, not supplied.
  • 0275B, nec videtur diligenti lectio haec justo amplius requisita. dilectio would be the obvious sense in a sentence whose subject two clauses earlier is dilectio; but lectio is a real word and construes with the Horatian tag that follows (juxta poetam decies repetita — A.P. 365, of a poem that will please though ten times re-read). Rendered "this reading." Logged, no emendation.
  • 0279B, quem tu manu gratiae, ego laboris et industriae serenavi.* The verb is first-person singular and governs a second-person subject as well (likewise adornavi* in the next clause). English "have made serene" / "have adorned" carries both persons; the Latin zeugma cannot be reproduced exactly. Logged so the smoothing is on the record.
  • 0288D, ut sancta confirmatio aeque vestigio permaneret. vestigio has no governing preposition. Rendered "should equally remain in its footing"; conjecture in vestigio, not supplied.
  • 0277D, auctorem mortis Zabulum triumphares. Zabulus for diabolus is attested patristic and medieval Latin (Pattern 9): translated normally as "the devil", no italics, no [sic:].
  • 0286B, copulantur nectura naturali. A rare verbal noun from necto; rendered "by a natural binding". Not marked.
  • 0287A, nostri plenitudine temporis deopertum.* Likewise rare, and transparent (de- + operio*); rendered "uncovered". Not marked.

Negation audit (brief §9). Every non / nec / neque / nisi / ne / haud / nunquam / nullus / nihil / nil / nescit / necdum / nondum in the six Latin chunks was matched against the English on a separate second pass. The dense clusters are 0274C (non prior, non posterior ulla), 0275D (quibus haec naturae dona non omnibus omnia conferuntur — the double restriction carried as "not all of them bestowed upon all"), 0276A (non capitis lumen occiduum), 0276C (te non nisi deformem, non nisi hominem intuetur), 0276D (unum tamen, et non alterum), 0277A (nullius conceptio, nullius caruit vitio), 0277B (non possum non amare — a double negative carried as a double negative, "I cannot not love thee"), 0278B–D (nescit amor… non tam laborare… panem suum non comederit otiosa), 0280D (enodes… nunquam recalcitrat; scrupulus non habetur), 0281B (quid habet quod ab alio veraciter asserat non habere? — the negation is inside the indirect statement and stays there), 0281C (ne vel nesciri possem, vel a sciente non facilius apprehendi), 0281D (non nisi operi manuum respondet), 0282C (nec nisi super humilem), 0283C (nullas sustinet laesiones), 0284C (Nunquid non lilium… diffundebat? — both particles carried in the English interrogative), 0284D (Quis nesciat), 0286A (non est salus, non est vita, non indeficiens), 0287B (Non vult Christo angelus… non ligno fructuoso), 0287D (non tamen multum minor), 0289A (vident nec invident), 0289B (non fruges, non aries, non vitulus, non denique homo vel angelus; nec erat nomen aliud). No negation was dropped and none was supplied.

§6 · TYPOGRAPHY AND CAPITALIZATION

Brief §7 holds without exception across cols 0274D–0289C. Guillemets carry every non-lemma quotation adduced as authority (24 runs, all scripture in this range — no classical or oracular material occurs here); italics carry the running Song lemma with its piecemeal re-quotations, and Migne's marginal source-edition numbers 156–164. No seam, no exception, nothing tidied.

Guillemet asymmetries: none. All six chunks balance and every pair is 1:1 with the Latin twin (3/2/0/4/3/12 pairs). ⚑ Chunk 0038 carries zero guillemets across 1,004 words — an entire chapter and a half of exposition in Christ's own voice with not one adduced proof-text, which is worth noting only because a parity check that assumes at least one pair per chunk would misfire.

Pattern 5 interruptions (ait, inquit, inquam, inquiens, ait David) are as dense here as in the preceding range and every one stays inside the marks, in the italic lemma runs (Ecce, inquam, tu es pulchra,) exactly as in the guilleted ones (« Minuisti eum paulo minus ab angelis, ait David »).

[n:] placement varies and is reproduced as printed, per brief §7: usually inside the closing », but at 0283A it falls six words OUTSIDE, after Philip's sicut certum est Scripturam perhibere. At 0286C the column anchor precedes the note (amare cohaeredes [0286C] [n: (Matth. XXV)]). At 0283B and 0287D column anchors fall inside guillemet runs, splitting rex … Israel and servum… jura.

⚑ §7a mirroring — the drift point — held word by word. Mixed case inside single sentences, none of it regularized: pulchram virginem bis dixisse beside Virgo mirabiliter perseverat (0274D–0275A) · mater Sponsi, Sponsa filii (0277A — Sponsi and Sponsa capital, filii lower, in one four-word phrase) · hominem de homine genitum sine Patre… Dei Filium sine matre (0284B — capital Patre, lowercase matre, one sentence) · natus unicus fuit Patris… de virgine, unicus item Matris (0286C) · Cui flori et lilio virgo studet (0284A) and inter istos… virgo non frangitur (0284B) in a chapter whose lemma-word Sponsa is capitalized four lines away · Dilectus Sponsae praeeminet (0287C, capital) beside dilectus meus in the lemma. All mirrored.

⚑ Two mirrorings I want the merge to see, because both look like errors and are not:

  • Migne capitalizes Cedri / Cedrus / Cypressus as common nouns at 0280B–0280D and then writes ad cedri et cypressi similitudinem lowercase at 0281A. Mirrored — "beams of Cedar… because Cedars, as they say" — which reads oddly in English and is meant to.
  • 0288A, sed ille Spiritus immortalis, of the ANGELIC nature, not the Holy Spirit. Mirrored as "that immortal Spirit". I flag it because a reader may take it for the third Person and a sweep may "fix" it; the Latin capitalizes it and the referent is settled by angeli natura six words earlier.

Pattern 3. ⭐ Fires twice on bare forms, exactly as the brief warns. 0282C, inclinantque aurem Scripturarum monitis → "the admonitions of the Scriptures"; 0287B, angeli nonnunquam in Scripturis filii nominantur → "in the Scriptures" — the identical bare form cruces-0030 found at 0260A and that 11638's sweep missed. A third, singular, at 0287D: si quod Scriptura perhibet → "what Scripture declares". A later sweep of 11632 must match bare Scriptura and Scripturae as well as divina and sacra. Also at 0283A, sicut certum est Scripturam perhibere → "Scripture".

Pattern 17. Philip's frame is plural throughout and takes you (Videtis 0275C and 0286D, audistis 0275C and 0283C, noveritis 0283C, legistis 0288A, potestis — none in this range). Every second-person singular is inside the Bride's or the Bridegroom's address to the other, or inside a quotation, and every one is singular in the Latin (tu pulchra es · accendisti · descendisti · es constitutus · processisti · quem tu manu gratiae · Vide ne feceris · conservus tuus · Tu ergo non angelum, sed Deum adora · Minuisti eum) — so thou throughout. No plural second person occurs inside any quotation in this range, so the Dorotheus effect does not show here.

§7 · RULED VOCABULARY (brief §5) — held, plus three new fixed equivalences

Held: amica mea = "my friend" (0274C, 0283C, 0285C — the Cant. 2:2 occurrence the brief predicts) · misericordia = mercy (0279B, 0282B ×2, 0284C) kept distinct from clementia (does not occur) · charitas (does not occur) · Pattern 3 as above · Sponsus = Bridegroom, Sponsa = Bride, Virgo = Virgin, Deitas / deitas = Godhead. muraenula, vermiculatas, nigra / fusca / formosa, cellaria, recti, adolescentulae, torcular, candidatio, tomus do not occur in this range. Cant. 1:12 does not recur here, so this range contributes no evidence to brief §8c's Cum / Dum count.

Three new fixed equivalences this range had to set, offered to the merge:

  1. ⭐ lectulus = "little bed", lectus = "bed", never interchanged. Forced by 0279B: non tamen Virgo lectum, sed magis lectulum nominavit; quo nomine legem illam… adimplevit, qua tam verbo quam opere humilia tenere consuevit. The diminutive is the humility argument. Fourteen instances across 0037–0038. The lemma is Cant. 1:15 and will recur.
  2. laquearia = "panelled ceilings" (not "rafters", Douay's word), because Caput XVII glosses them as laid beneath the beams and stretched wall to wall as a binding — a rafter is the tignum, which is the other half of the same lemma and must stay "beam".
  3. malus = "the apple tree" throughout Caput XXI, including where Migne writes neuter malum (0287B) — the chapter's three-term proof (umbra, fructus, odor) is about the tree, not the fruit, and poma is separately "apples" at 0286A.

Also fixed within the range for consistency: accubitum = "repose" (0278C), following cruces-0030's ruling · solitudo = "solitude" throughout 0285A–B, because Isa. 35:1's solitudo and Philip's nostra… solitudo are the same word and the gloss depends on it · scrupulus / scrupulosa = "scruple" / "scrupulous" (0280D), keeping the pun between the cypress's knotless wood and scrupulous obedience · convalles = "deep valleys" against valles = "valleys", which Migne's own Valles, imo convalles distinguishes.

§8 · THINGS DELIBERATELY NOT REPORTED (brief §10, checked once)

  • Column-band arithmetic: no anchor in this range is followed by text broken mid-word or mid-construction; the bands run cleanly A–D and every chunk's colFirst / colLast matches its body. No [ed:], no patch, no plate check. §10.1.
  • noteCount matches the body [n:] count in all six chunks (8/6/3/7/4/13), verified by script — and note that [CAP. II.] at 0281B is correctly outside that count.
  • Attested medieval spellings left alone, unmarked (Pattern 9): tanquam, quodcunque, quidquid, coelum / coelestis, spiritalis, nunquam, Zabulus, Hierusalem, mirrha-class orthography, utcunque, nonnunquam, Absalon, Maecenas as a common noun, haereditario, praelatio.
  • No [f:]. 11632 is lemma-and-gloss, not a florilegium (§10.4).
  • No [nt:]. All 41 notes in the range are bare citation sigla.
  • Migne's own ( sic ) does not occur in this range.

§9 · WHAT A LATER BLIND READ SHOULD LOOK AT FIRST

  1. 0287C, « Conservus tuus suum… » (§5). The English is verbless because the Latin is, and Migne prints the correct sum nine lines above — which makes this both the most obviously repairable spot in the range and the one where a repair would be least visible. Decide it together with cruces-0030's incudo.
  2. 0284D and 0285A, the two Luke/Isaiah [var:] (§3.1, §3.2). Isa. 35:1 is the confident one — Philip uses germinabit twice — and Luke 23:34 is the judgment call, because ignosce / dimitte are near-synonyms and the marker rests on the argument round it rather than on the lexicon.
  3. 0277B, the Wisd. 7:26 / Heb. 1:3 fusion with imago veritatis (§2.1). [n:]-only, so unmarked under brief §8a — but if the merge opens that class this is where the marker goes in this range. Check the left edge, which I judged to begin at candor and not at Pulcher.
  4. 0283A, « Deus autem ignis est » (§1, 0039 table). Guilleted, abridged, and deliberately unmarked. The closest call in the range.
  5. The four sigla of §4, and particularly (Marc. XV) at 0283B, which the previous range's (Matth. XXVII) at 0267D turns from a suspicion into a demonstration. That pair is the strongest single piece of §8b evidence the work has produced so far and the merge should count it.

Philip of Harvengt, Commentaria in Cantica canticorum, PL 203. Range covering Book II Caput XXII–XXVI (Cant. 2:3–7: Sub umbra illius quem desideraveram, sedi → Introduxit me rex in cellariam vinariam → Fulcite me floribus → Laeva ejus sub capite meo → Adjuvo vos, filiae Hierusalem), then the explicit-less transition to LIBER TERTIUS. and Book III Caput I–II on Cant. 2:8 Vox dilecti mei. Six chunks, 6,343 Latin words.

Marker totals for this range: 7 [var:] · 1 [sic:] · 0 [ed:] · 0 [d:] · 0 [nt:] · 0 [f:]. verify-english.mjs reports no errors on any of the six; four ratio warnings (0044 1.62, 0045 1.65, 0046 1.68, 0047 1.61), all inside the 1.35–1.68 band this work has already shipped (0004 1.64, 0005 1.68, 0026 1.66, 0035 1.65). Column anchors (13/10/8/9/13/4), [n:] strings (16/7/5/5/4/4, each matching its frontmatter noteCount) and guillemet counts were diffed 1:1 against the Latin twins by script, not by eye: anchors byte-identical in order and place, [n:] contents byte-identical in order. Every italic run in the English is accounted for against the Latin's own runs plus the seven [var:] and the one [sic:].

§1 · ⭐⭐ THE THREE FINDINGS THE MERGE SHOULD CARRY

1.1 · Lam. 4:20 at 0291B — an expounded quotation Migne marks with NOTHING AT ALL, and the extractor could not see it

This is the range's principal find and it came from the §8a second pass, not from the list. After the guilleted half-verse « In umbra, inquiunt, ejus vivemus in gentibus » [n: (Thren. IV)], Philip turns back to the first half of the same verse and writes:

Ideo praemittunt: Spiritus ante faciem nostram Christus Dominus.

The Vulgate reads spiritus oris nostri christus dominus — "the breath of our mouth". Migne prints ante faciem nostram, which is the Old Latin / LXX reading (πνεῦμα προσώπου ἡμῶν, spiritus faciei nostrae). And the divergent phrase is the one Philip expounds — it is the subject of his next two sentences, three times over:

Christus Dominus ante faciem nostram spiritus tunc habetur, cum eum nostra fides jam non secundum carnem, sed secundum spiritum intuetur… Ideo Paulus… Deum et ea quae sunt ejus, ante faciem proponenda.

Conform the lemma to oris nostri and the whole ante faciem / posteriora Christi architecture of the chapter — Peter putting Christ's hinder parts first, Paul setting God before the face — collapses.

⛔ Migne marks this span with NEITHER guillemets, NOR italics, NOR a note. It is not in data/quotations/11632/0042-0047.md in any class, because the extractor keys the [n:]-only class on the note and there is no note. No [var:] fired, per brief §8a: where the plate marks the words as neither quotation nor lemma we cannot establish the quotation's left edge, so marking it would assert a boundary the plate does not print. Logged in full so the merge can rule the class with this candidate in front of it. It is the exact shape of Ps. 90:5–6 at 0245A (cruces-0024 §2c.2) and of Rom. 8:10 at 0226B, and it is the third instance of the class in three ranges — which is itself the argument that the class is real.

⚑ A methodological consequence worth stating. Two of this work's three [n:]-only-class finds were attached to a note; this one was not. A range that reads only the extractor's ⭐ list will miss this shape entirely. The pass that found it was: read every scripture-sounding clause in the prose, note or no note.

1.2 · ⭐⭐ Cant. 2:7 at 0299D — the head lemma prints Adjuvo for Adjuro, and the correct form stands seven words earlier

The head lemma of Caput XXVI is printed:

**Adjuvo vos, filiae Hierusalem, ne suscitetis, neque evigilare faciatis dilectam, quoadusque ipsa velit.

Adjuvo means "I help". The verse is Adiuro vos — "I adjure you" — and the entire chapter is about the adjuration: humano more obtestatur durius et adjurat · astringit eas durius et interserit juramentum · Sponsi monita, quibus adjurat filias Hierusalem · filiae Hierusalem adjurantur (twice) · Mandatum vero sic adjurantis · si, per quod adjuratur… and the verse returns in full at 0302A as « Adjuro vos, inquit, filiae Jerusalem, per capreas, cervosque camporum. »

⚑ The decisive detail: Migne prints the right form immediately before the wrong one. The last words of chunk 0045 (col. 0299C) are the lemma tag Adjuro, etc. — so within seven words of printed text the plate has Adjuro and then Adjuvo.

Rendered as printed ("I help you"), which is meant to look wrong, with a [var:] naming the received reading. Not a [sic:]: adjuvo is a real word and Pattern 12's "real word merely wrong" clause keeps it on the English side. ⚠ This is the sentence in the range most likely to be silently repaired by a later reader, and the repair would be invisible — one letter restores a perfectly smooth chapter opening.

The head lemma also omits per capreas cervosque camporum (truncation, not a variant; the words return at 0302A) — which is itself notable, because the whole back half of the chapter is an exposition of the roes and harts.

1.3 · ⭐ Cant. 2:4 at 0292D — rex added, and cellariam for cellam

**Introduxit me rex in cellariam vinariam: ordinavit in me charitatem.

The Vulgate has introduxit me in cellam vinariam, with no rex.

  • rex is Philip's text, not a slip. His first sentence glosses it: Quem et quare nominet regem, supra recolo me dixisse — he takes the lemma to name the king and refers back to his own exposition of Cant. 1:3. Conforming would strand the gloss.
  • cellariam is the harder call, and it matters because brief §5 rules cellaria = storerooms against cella vinaria = wine cellar, and this lemma fuses them. Philip's own prose immediately separates them again: cum in regis cellaria introductam Virgo meminit se fuisse; quae… non tamen esse vinaria memorantur. Nunc vero in cellam vinariam Virgo se perhibet introduci — and thereafter tota cella vinaria (0293A), sed cella redundans; domus vinaria (0293A), Hoc in cella vinaria Christus beneficium operatur (0295B). Six printings of the prose form against one of the lemma form.

Rendered so the distinction survives on the page: the lemma reads "the wine storeroom", the retrospect reads "the king's storerooms", and every prose occurrence reads "the wine cellar" — three English forms for Migne's three Latin forms. [var:] fired on the lemma for both divergences.

§2 · THE COLLATION — all 72 listed spans, every one accounted for

Every span in data/quotations/11632/0042-0047.md was collated word by word against the Vulgate. Spans recorded as AGREES were collated and found to agree; the absence of a marker on them is a finding, not a silence. Lemma re-quotations (Sub umbra, Et fructus, Ordinavit, Fulcite me, Dextera, Adjuro vos, etc.) are short repetitions of a head-text collated at its full occurrence; each was checked against its head-text and none re-quotes it with different words — with the single, decisive exception of Adjuvo / Adjuro (§1.2), which runs the other way: the re-quotation is right and the head is wrong.

Transposition, no marker · Heb. 3:14 « Si tamen, inquit, initium substantiae ejus usque ad finem firmum retineamus » — agrees exactly · Matt. 7:21 « Domine, Domine » — agrees · 1 Thess. 2:12 « Ut ambuletis, inquit, digne Deo » — Vulg. ambularetis, imperfect subjunctive in a past-sequence indirect command; Migne's present is the same construction in primary sequence, and nothing is asserted that the Vulgate does not assert. Every one of the twenty is Philip's own prose, written with scripture rather than quoting it: accusative-and-infinitive frames, third-person and first-person recastings, his own rhymed clause-endings. None takes a marker; a [var:] on unmarked prose would misrepresent it as a lemma.

Reported per brief §8a even though it is a null result, and it is a real datum about the class: 0/20 here, against 1/14 for the 0024–0029 range and 0/19 for 0018–0023.

§3 · TYPOGRAPHY — the Book II/III boundary is crossed, and there is NO SEAM

⭐ This range answers the question cruces-0024 §1 left for a later agent. Chunk 0047 opens ## LIBER TERTIUS. at col. 0303A (empty body, exactly as LIBER SECUNDUS. sat at 0246C), and ## CAPUT PRIMUM. follows under it. Migne prints the transition in Philip's own voice at 0302D — stylus meus ad prosequendum caetera non festinet, sed dormiente Sponsa, iste paululum se reclinet — and names the division himself: cujus ab osculo primus liber sumpsit exordium, in somno finem accipiat hic secundus.

Nothing about the marking changes across it. Both marks run in the same functional division on both sides: Book II side (0046) has the italic lemma, the italic marginal numbers 171–172, and a guillemeted Ps. 100:5; Book III side (0047) has the italic lemma twice, the italic marginal 173, and a guillemeted Isa. 52:6. So 11632 crosses two book boundaries with no seam at either, and 11638's book-boundary model is now falsified twice over on this work. The merge can stop looking.

LIBER TERTIUS. → "BOOK THREE.", after LIBER PRIMUS. → "BOOK ONE." and LIBER SECUNDUS. → "BOOK TWO." CAPUT PRIMUM spelled in words then CAPUT II in numerals, in the same chunk, preserved as printed (brief §7a) — and note that Book III restarts the numbering while Book II ended at CAPUT XXVI.

3a · ⚠ The guillemet asymmetry at 0295C — a NESTED unclosed «

0044 prints 4 « against 3 », and the extra opening is inside an existing quotation run:

« Factum est, inquit, ut sororem Absalon Thamar adamaret Ammon filius David… Dixitque Ammon: « Thamar sororem Absalon amo [n: (II Reg. XIII)]. »

Migne opens a run at Factum est, and then, at the point where the narrative gives Ammon his own direct speech, opens a second « without ever closing the first. The single » at the end closes the inner one. Reproduced exactly as printed, unbalanced (Pattern 5 corollary), and logged here rather than repaired. It is the first guillemet asymmetry recorded in this work since wave 1.

3b · Four guillemet runs carved out of ONE verse — John 5:3 at 0298A

Migne dismantles the verse and reassembles it around Philip's own questions, guillemeting each fragment separately:

« In his, » ait, porticibus « jacebat multitudo magna. » Quare jacebat, exponit: « Languentium. » Quare in porticibus, adjungit: « Exspectantium aquae motum [n: (Joan. V)]. »

porticibus — Philip's word, pulled up from John 5:2 — sits outside the marks, between them. This is why 0045 has seven guillemet pairs where a reader counting quotations would expect four. Reproduced 1:1; the English keeps the same four fragments and the same interleaved prose, at the cost of some awkward word order ("« In these, » he says, porches, « there lay a great multitude. »"). Same class as 0254B's « Meos » / « tuos » (cruces-0024 §1b): the mark is doing grammatical work, not quotation work.

sic fides sine opere legitur et intelligitur otiosa (Jacob II). Italic, inside the running prose, with no [n:] wrapper, and correctly not counted in 0044's noteCount of 5 (verified against the body). Fourth or fifth instance of the class in this work (cf. 0203A, 0222B–C, 0244C, 0260D, 0267B). Reproduced exactly, italics and all.
