3e · ⚑ §7a mirroring — the drift point — held word by word

Mixed case inside single sentences, none of it regularized:

  • 0291D virgo Mater — lower-case virgo, capital Mater, in a work that capitalizes Virgo almost everywhere. Rendered "the virgin Mother".
  • 0294A, 0294B, 0295C Virgo mater — the same pair the other way up. Rendered "the Virgin mother" all three times.
  • 0292D non modicam virgo fiduciam sibi sumit and 0293A cujus meriti virginem aestimamus — lower case in chapters that capitalize Virgo eleven times. Rendered "the virgin".
  • 0290A nonnullos miserans spiritus, vehemens terret — lower case, the Acts 2:2 spiritus vehemens. Rendered "the vehement spirit", against capital Spiritus at 0291B, 0292A, 0293A, 0293D, 0294D, 0295A, 0298C.
  • 0293D vera Mater and 0295A in Matre diligente — capital, rendered "Mother".
  • Sponsus / Sponsa / Sponsi / Sponsae are capitalized everywhere in this range (thirty-odd instances, no lower-case exception), which is itself worth recording against 0243B–C where Migne dropped the capital.

This is mechanically checkable against the Latin twin and I would check it first in any review.

3f · Pattern 17

Both frames in this range are plural and take you: the Virgin addressing the adolescentulae (vos interim… convenite, fulcite, removete, refovete, floreatis, proferatis, vos ire gaudentes, digni habiti estis, 0296B–0297B) and the Bridegroom addressing the filiae Hierusalem (ne suscitetis, neque evigilare faciatis, revocetis, vobis, volo ergo vos, adjuro vos, 0299D–0302C). Philip's own frame to his brethren is plural too (ut audistis, ne putetis, vobis profero, ut legistis, sicut recolitis vos legisse, de quo legistis).

Every second-person singular in the range is inside a quotation and every one is singular in the Latin — Ne tradas regnum tuum · Absit a te · non sapis · Ex toto corde tuo… ex omnibus viribus tuis · ut intres sub tectum meum · in dextera tua · Quare sic attenuaris macie · Tu es ipse Deus meus — so thou throughout. The one plural inside a quotation is 1 Thess. 2:12 Ut ambuletis digne Deo, rendered you, sitting four lines from the singular Matt. 16 pair. The number distinction is visible on the page exactly as Pattern 17 intends.

§4 · PATTERN 7 — one [sic:], and the readings rendered as printed

One carried run, and it is NOT also translated in the running text (brief §8's named failure):

  1. 0294C [sic: reete] — Hunc itaque proximum reete Virgo diligit ut seipsam. Read recte, certain: Philip uses recte correctly at 0290A, 0290C, 0292B, 0297A, 0299D and 0303A. reete is not a Latin word, so Pattern 7 governs: carried untranslated in italics, and the English deliberately does not also say "rightly" — it reads "This neighbour therefore the Virgin [sic: reete] loves as herself." The plate sets the broken word between proximum and Virgo; English word order puts it one word later, immediately before the verb it modifies.

Rendered as printed, no marker (real words, merely wrong or merely odd) — conjectures live here and NOT in the text:

  • ⛔ 0290D, quia fides mortua, etsi non diligens, operatur. As printed this says that a dead faith, though it does not love, does work — which is the reverse of the Jas. 2:20 maxim Philip quotes correctly at 0297A (fides sine opere… otiosa) and sits awkwardly against his own next sentence, Dilectio quippe vita est fidei. Rendered exactly as printed ("since a dead faith, even though it does not love, does work"). Conjectures: quia fides mortua est, si non diligens, operatur, or quia fides mortua, etsi non diligens, non operatur. Neither supplied. ⚠ This is the single most likely place in the range for a well-meaning repair, and under brief §9 the printed negation count is exactly what stands: one non, on diligens, and no other.
  • 0290C, Tu es ipse Deus meus. A four-word sentence standing outside the Ps. 115:1 guillemets, with no mark of any kind, in a paragraph otherwise in the third person. It reads as the continuation of the psalm-verse in the psalmist's voice (cf. Ps. 30:15 Deus meus es tu, Ps. 117:28), but Migne marks it as nothing. Rendered as printed ("Thou art thyself my God"), no marker, no quotation supplied.
  • 0290A, insolubilis vi necturae. nectura is not classical, but it is Philip's own word — he uses it again at 0294B, natura, naturalique nectura proximum suum esse. Pattern 9: attested usage of this author, unmarked. Rendered "the unloosable force of her binding".
  • 0298B, the doubled comma. Migne prints Quae ideo laeva satis congrue nominantur,, quia in hac praesenti vita…. A doubled comma has no English exponent (Pattern 9's test) and reproducing it would read as our own build defect; one comma is set and the doubling is logged here. ⚑ If the merge prefers Pattern 8's "never delete a mark", the fix is one character at 0298B.
  • 0292C, nondum ad ventrem pervenit, quo perfecta satietas, invenitur. Migne sets a comma between subject and verb. Not reproduced (English cannot carry it without reading as a typo of ours); logged.
  • 0291A, fides optatae praesentia non est rei. The genitive rei is split from praesentia by non est, which is Philip's rhyme-driven word order, not a defect. Rendered "faith is not the presence of the thing wished for".
  • 0299D, timorem incutiat sacramentum. sacramentum here means the sworn oath (juramentum two words earlier), not the sacrament. Rendered "sacrament", the word Migne prints, because English carries the same ambiguity and glossing it would be an emendation. Logged.
  • 0301A, Verum in hoc dramate. drama for the Song's dialogue. Rendered "in this play"; not italicized, because English has the word.
  • 0295A, carne mundum et Spiritu Deo cunctis inaccessum genere counitum. The word order is very hard; cunctis inaccessum is taken with Deo, and genere with counitum, giving "clean in flesh and by the Spirit united in kind to God who is inaccessible to all". An alternative construal takes cunctis inaccessum with the child. Logged, not adjudicated in the text.
  • 0296C, malagma sive oleum, sive ligatura reputabitur aegrotanti. Rendered "a poultice, or oil, or a binding"; malagma is a real English-available word (emollient plaster) and is not carried in Latin.

Negation audit (brief §9), second pass, against the Latin. Every printed non / nec / neque / nisi / nunquam / nullus / nihil / nil / nondum / necdum / ne was matched against the English. The dense clusters are 0290C (Sine hac fide Deo quispiam non placebit, nec est digna conscientia, cujus Deum scientia non tenebit… qui nescitur, a nesciente non potest acceptari… qui non crediderit, nec dici debet esse; qui autem non est, consequenter nec in umbra est… his qui non sunt… Non esse recte dicitur, qui Deum esse nescit), 0290D (Etiam non justus erit in fide, sed nonnisi justus vivet in fide — carried as "Even one that is not just will be in faith, but none save the just shall live in faith"), 0291C (non fiet istud, non morieris… non sapis quae Dei sunt), *0293B–C (non perturbat… non confundit… non obscurat, non aufert scientiam, sed infundit; malum non cogitat, non agit perperam… iram non suscitat, non infert odium — six in one sentence), 0294A (non jubetur modus aliquis, non mensura… non scriptor aliquis docuit, non Scriptura… videtur non quantum, sed ex quanto), 0294C (non amplexum pertulit, non juncturam… nullum sensit dolorem corporis, non laesuram… nec omnino potuit… nec erat quis tam felix), 0295A (ut seipsam illi non solum non praeferat, sed nec etiam conferat in amore — a triple, carried as a triple), 0297A–B (non habentibus, sed facientibus… Non possumus quae audivimus et vidimus non loqui… non capitis injuria, non membrorum paralysi… non febris angustia, non corporis quavis molestia… nihil ardentius, nihil vehementius… videtur nec tenetur… nec potest inveniri), 0300C–D (non audimus, vel magis audientes… nullatenus obedimus… non dominari clero… non curis exterioribus, non negotiis saecularibus… non causis forensium, non saecularium contentionibus… necessitas eos referat, non voluptas), and 0302C (ut non solum non suscitem nec evigilare faciam quoslibet dormientes, nec* mandati reus inveniar — carried whole). No negation was dropped and none was supplied.

§5 · CONVENTIONS SET OR HELD IN THIS RANGE

  1. ⭐ amica Sponsi = "the friend of the Bridegroom" (0303C). Brief §5's ruling on amica mea is honoured in its other grammatical form: Philip recasts John 3:29's amicus sponsi into the feminine and the first person, Ego igitur amica Sponsi sto et gaudeo propter vocem Sponsi. "Friend", never "beloved" or "love" — the whole point of the sentence is that the Bride, who is about to hear the Bridegroom's voice, is standing in the Baptist's place. This is the same lemma-word the merge must hold across the work.
  2. New fixed equivalences this range had to set, offered to the merge: - langueo / languor / languens = "languish / languor" throughout (Caput XXIV–XXV turn on the single root: quia amore langueo → amoris incendio Virgo dixerat se languere → ne amor durius langueat, languor moram sufferat duriorem → nihil undique languidum relinquetur). Kept strictly distinct from aegrotare = "to sicken" and deficere = "to fail", because the Ammon paragraph at 0295C runs all three of them in two sentences and the argument is the contrast between the sick lover and the languishing one. - fulcire = "to stay up" · stipare = "to compass about", fixed at the lemma and held through fulta vel stipata (0296D) and se stipari (0296C). - otium = "leisure" against negotium = "business" — Caput XXVI's whole argument is the pair (otio vel negotio spiritali, spiritali otio quamdam velut injuriam, vestra debere negotia… sua vero otia), and any variation would dissolve it. - laeva = "left hand" · dextera = "right hand", nouns not adjectives, after the lemma; sinistra (0299B, 0299C) likewise "the left".
  3. Pattern 3 fires on a bare Scriptura at 0294A — quantum diligatur Deus, non scriptor aliquis docuit, non Scriptura. Neither divina nor sacra is present. Rendered "Holy Scripture", per brief §5's ⚑ and the 0260A precedent (cruces-0030 §2). This is the second attested bare-form instance in this work; a later sweep must match bare Scriptura(e) too.
  4. Brief §5 vocabulary held: charitas = charity throughout (0293C ordinat charitatem, ordo charitatis; 0295A–B charitatem praecipuam ordinavit, excellentia charitatis; 0296D, 0302A affectus charitatis), kept distinct from dilectio / amor = love (0290D Dilectio quippe vita est fidei; 0293C in caeteris pluribus dilectio sit diffusa; 0301D geminae dilectionis mandatum) — and note 0294A, where dilectione and diligatur and diligendi run in three consecutive clauses beside charitas, which is exactly the doublet pressure the rule exists to resist · candidatur (0293B) is translated ("is made white"), per the candidatio rule · cellaria = storerooms, cella vinaria = wine cellar (§1.3) · adolescentulae = maidens (0296A, 0296C, 0296D, 0299D) · Sponsus = Bridegroom, Sponsa = Bride. nigra / fusca / formosa, clementia, misericordia, recti, torcular, muraenula, moralitas do not occur in this range.
  5. ## CAPUT XXII.–XXVI. → "CHAPTER XXII."–"XXVI."; CAPUT PRIMUM. → "CHAPTER THE FIRST." — the numeral/word distinction preserved as printed inside chunk 0047, which carries both forms.
  6. 0303A's frontmatter incipit begins ## CAPUT PRIMUM. — i.e. the chunker captured a head into the incipit field. Copied verbatim into the English frontmatter, unaltered, per the brief's frontmatter rule. Not a defect of ours and not to be tidied.

Checked: no anchor in any of the six chunks is followed by text broken mid-word or mid-construction. The bands run cleanly A–D throughout 0289–0303. No [ed:], no patch, no plate check.

§7 · OPEN — for the merge or a blind read

  1. ⛔ The blind polarity read has not been done and cannot be done by me. The three passages most likely to be wrongly "repaired" are, in order: (a) Adjuvo at 0299D (§1.2) — one letter makes a smooth chapter opening, and the correct form stands seven words earlier on the plate, which makes the repair feel authorized; (b) quia fides mortua, etsi non diligens, operatur at 0290D (§4) — the English is meant to read against the Jas. 2:20 maxim, because the Latin does; (c) the carried reete at 0294C.
  2. ⚑ §1.1's Lam. 4:20 is this range's candidate for the class brief §8a left open, and if the merge rules that an expounded unmarked weave earns a [var:], the marker goes at 0291B on Spiritus ante faciem nostram Christus Dominus. ⚠ Note that it is a harder case than Ps. 90:5–6, because it carries no [n:] at all — so a rule framed as "an expounded [n:]-only weave" would not reach it. The class the merge needs to name is "an expounded weave Migne leaves unmarked", note or no note.
  3. ⚑ The cited-X-worded-Y count is now at least five across four ranges (0240B Luke/Matthew · 0290D Habakkuk/Hebrews · 0291C Matthew/Mark · plus cruces-0012's Deuteronomy/Psalms). Two of this range's three are inside guillemets, which is new. Worth a work-wide tally before anyone proposes anything, per §8b.
  4. ⚑ §3's no-seam result at the Book II/III boundary should be recorded in the merge as closing the question, together with cruces-0024 §1's result at Book I/II. Two boundaries, two negatives; brief §7's ruling is now confirmed rather than assumed.
  5. The doubled comma at 0298B (§4) is a one-character judgment I made against Pattern 8's letter and in favour of Pattern 9's test. If the merge disagrees, it is a one-character fix and I flag it rather than defend it.

Philip of Harvengt, Commentaria in Cantica canticorum, PL 203. Range covering Book III(?) Caput III–IX — the exposition of Cant. 2:8b–13: Ecce iste venit saliens in montibus, transiliens colles → Similis est dilectus meus capreae hinnuloque cervorum → En ipse stat post parietem nostrum → Et dilectus meus loquitur mihi → Surge, propera, amica mea → Jam enim hiems transiit → Vox turturis audita est in terra nostra. Six chunks, 6,351 Latin words.

⚑ No book head falls in this range; the chunks carry only CAPUT heads, and the numeration runs III → IX continuously across the six, so no division boundary is crossed here.

Marker totals for this range: 2 [var:] · 3 [sic:] · 0 [ed:] · 0 [d:] · 0 [nt:] · 0 [f:]. verify-english.mjs reports no errors on any of the six; one ratio warning, 0052 at 1.61, inside the band this work has already shipped (0004 1.64, 0005 1.68, 0035 1.65, 0046 1.68). Ratios: 1.52 / 1.53 / 1.51 / 1.49 / 1.61 / 1.56.

Column anchors (13/13/11/6/11/6), [n:] strings (16/16/10/8/9/10 — each matching its frontmatter noteCount) and guillemet counts (13/2/7/2/2/11 pairs) were diffed 1:1 against the Latin twins by script, not by eye: identical in content, order and position in all six chunks. No guillemet asymmetry anywhere in this range — every « has its », none stray, none unopened. Every italic run in the English is accounted for against the Latin's own runs plus the three [sic:] and the two [var:] (asterisk counts: 8→12, 4→6, 10→10, 16→16, 12→12, 6→12, the deltas being exactly the marker contents).

§1 · THE COLLATION — all 90 listed spans, every one accounted for

Every span in data/quotations/11632/0048-0053.md was collated word by word against the Vulgate. Spans recorded as AGREES were collated and found to agree; the absence of a marker on them is a finding, not a silence.

Migne supplies the subject Jesus where the Vulgate has none, drops the seven-demons clause, and moves autem to the second sentence. [var:] deliberately NOT fired: supplying an implicit subject asserts nothing the Vulgate does not assert (cruces-0030's John 5:19 reasoning), and the omission is abridgment. Recorded so the absence is a decision.
« Pax vobis, inquit, ego sum [n: (Luc. XXIV)]. »Luke 24:36AGREES; truncated before nolite timere.
« Non audietur in plateis vox ejus [n: (Isa. XLII)]. »Isa. 42:2⭐⭐ [var:] FIRED — see §2.2. This is the range's principal find.

Marginal number: 182 (0318D).

The [n:]-only class — hit rate in this range

34 spans listed, plus four further weaves found on the second pass that the extractor never listed (Surge, quia hora est jam te de somno surgere and et veni, quia ego tecum sum, dicit Dominus at 0314C; quam non homo percipit animalis = 1 Cor. 2:14 and debitorem ut sapientibus, sic et stultis = Rom. 1:14 at 0317D–0318A). All 38 are Philip's own prose. Hit rate: zero.

That is a null result and it is real information: 0018–0023 reported 19/19 prose, this range reports 38/38, against wave 1's single Rom. 8:10 and cruces-0030's Ps. 11:7. The mechanism is consistent across every one of the 38 — Philip absorbs the scriptural words into his own rhymed clause endings (the -it / -it, -issit / -essit, -avit / -avit pairs that end nearly every colon in this work), which forces a change of person, tense, or voice. Where the wording survives untouched it is because it happens to fit the rhyme (scientia destruetur, frigus erat), not because he is quoting.

⚑ The two 0314C tails are the class's real warning, and they are the reason the second pass is not optional: quia hora est jam te de somno surgere and quia ego tecum sum, dicit Dominus are near-verbatim Rom. 13:11 and Jer. 1:8, carry no note at all, and were therefore invisible to the extractor in both directions. A [n:]-only sweep that trusts the note list will miss them.

§2 · THE TWO [var:], IN FULL

1. ⭐ Eph. 2:3 at 0307C — sumus for eramus, and the tense is the argument. Migne prints « Natura, » inquiens, « filii sumus irae ». The Vulgate reads et eramus natura filii irae, sicut et ceteri — imperfect, not present. The marker is fired because the tense is precisely what Philip is arguing:

Quod enim primo parenti primitus delinquenti solo accidit vitio non natura, nobis posterioribus longe miserioribus inest, tam vitio quam natura… et Paulus nimis verax est.

His whole point is that what was accidental in Adam is still, now, constitutive in us — and the proof-text is adduced as a present-tense predication about the speaker and his hearers. The Vulgate's eramus places it in the pre-baptismal past, which is the opposite of the claim; and Philip's very next sentence apostrophizes Paul as though the Apostle had just said something he wishes were untrue (Utinam esses, Paule, vir non habens spiritum), which only works if Paul has spoken in the present. Rendered "we are children of wrath"; [var:] records the received reading.

2. ⭐⭐ Isa. 42:2 at 0318D — in plateis, which is MATTHEW's word, in a chapter built on the street. Migne prints « Non audietur in plateis vox ejus » under [n: (Isa. XLII)]. Isaiah 42:2 reads non clamabit… nec audietur vox eius foris — "abroad", "outside". The phrase in plateis is Matt. 12:19's rendering of the same prophecy (neque audiet aliquis in plateis vocem eius).

This is fired, and the reason is 7a″ exactly: platea is the keyword of the whole chapter. Caput IX turns on the turtledove's voice being secret rather than public, and Philip states it with that noun three times around the quotation:

nuntiabat, non turbis in platea, sed apostolis in secreto (0318B) · quem prorsus turbis absconditum foro gaudentibus vel platea (0318C) · vox secreta, quam non capit turba fremens, fori litibus et tumultibus assueta (0318C)

— and then adduces the prophecy as proof, De qua voce scriptum est. Conforming the lemma to Isaiah's foris would leave three sentences arguing about the street from a proof-text that no longer mentions one.

The marker states both readings and names the second witness; it does not speculate about why they differ (Pattern 14). It is worth the merge's notice that this is the third attested instance in 11632 of the class cruces-0024 named at 0240B — a note citing one book while the words printed are another book's (Luke 9 cited / Matthew 8 worded; Deut. 32 cited / Ps. 91 worded; now Isa. 42 cited / Matt. 12 worded). Here, unlike the other two, the span is guilleted, so a marker is available and was used.

§3 · PATTERN 7 AND PATTERN 10 — three [sic:], and what was NOT marked

None of the three carried runs is ALSO translated in the running text (brief §8's named failure — checked word by word on a separate pass).

  1. 0304A [sic: signa] — cujus amor amantes conciliat, et consensum eis ingerit spiritalem, ut signa prius ardeat, habere non timeat aemulam non rivalem. Pattern 10, run-together type. signa is a real word but cannot fill this slot: it is neuter plural and ardeat is third singular, and ardere signa governs nothing. The run is si qua, "if any woman burn first" — which is exactly what the sentence before it says (Neque enim movetur invidia si et aliis copia hujus detur) and what the clause after it needs (aemulam non rivalem, a fellow-lover and not a competitor). Carried whole per Pattern 10; the English reads "so that [sic: signa] may burn the sooner" and does not also supply "if any". ⚠ I record this as a judgment rather than defend it. Pattern 12 exempts "a real word that is merely wrong", and signa is a real word; Pattern 10 overrides that exemption for word-division defects and names sedet for sed et — itself a real word — as the governing precedent. If the merge reads it as Pattern 12 instead, the fix is to delete the marker and render "so that the signs may burn first", which construes no better; I judged the division defect the likelier account and the marker the honester one.
  2. 0306C [sic: vul] — et hic iste in montibus, hoc est, in praecelsis vul muneribus praesentari. A non-word, and it is one translation-style.md Pattern 7 names by name (vul for vult). Carried untranslated in italics; the English does not also supply "wills". ⚑ Note that vult does not construe here either — the sentence already has its infinitive governed by leguntur/praesentari — so the crux carries the conjecture without asserting it.
  3. 0318D [sic: torrae] — Quae nimirum vox, postquam torrae insonuit et a discipulis est audita, terra sinus laetos aperuit. Read terrae, certain: Migne prints the correct terra six words later in the same sentence, and insonuit wants the dative. Carried untranslated; the English reads "after it sounded to the [sic: torrae]" and does not also say "earth" in that slot.

Rendered as printed, no marker (real words, merely wrong or merely odd) — conjectures live here and NOT in the text:

  • ⛔ 0306B, Hujusmodi montes iste veniens et saliens virgini auferre voluit et conferre. auferre + dative means "to take away FROM", which contradicts conferre in the same breath and the whole exchange the sentence describes (he gives the mountains, she renders them back). Conjecture afferre, near-certain. Rendered as printed — "willed to take away from the virgin and to bestow" — so that it reads wrong. ⚠ This is the sentence in my range most likely to be silently repaired, and the repair would be invisible: one letter gives a smooth clause.
  • 0306C, ut sine his non inveniatur aliquoties apud aliquos coena duci. This clause does not construe as printed: coena is nominative and duci passive infinitive, giving "that a supper be led", with no obvious sense in a sentence about beauty, birth and learning not being necessary to salvation. Rendered as closely as the printed words allow ("that without them it is not sometimes found among some that the supper is led"), which is meant to read wrong. Conjectures considered and not supplied: coenam duci (led to the supper, i.e. the marriage supper of Matt. 22) or coena dari. Logged, not adjudicated in the text.
  • 0308A, tardum et retrogradum pigra boni similis aegritudo. The slot wants bovis: the sentence's own antithesis is asinina… hebetudo / this, and eleven lines later Philip writes qui asini hebetudinem, pigritiam bovis nescit, pairing the same two beasts with the same two nouns. boni is a real word and construes as a genitive, so Pattern 12 keeps it on the English side: rendered "a sluggish sickness like a good man's". ⚑ If the merge prefers to treat it as carried type the marker would go here, but I judged it the fuges/sugas class, not the bonorem class.
  • 0316C, Maxime vero multus imber, multa eum munditia suffocavit. The subject munditia ("cleanness") suffocating a man in a paragraph about the flood of the passions is the reverse of the argument; the conjecture is immunditia, and the surrounding sentence (omnes denique tulit aqua, laesit diluvium, culpa mersit) requires it. A real word, so rendered, not carried: the English reads "a great rain, a great cleanness suffocated him." ⚠ Second most likely place in the range for a silent repair.
  • 0311A, tendens semper ad occasum — paries temporivus.* Not a classical form (tempestivus means something else); read as a medieval formation on tempus*. Rendered "belongs to time", Pattern 9, unmarked.
  • 0317C, cum tenera eorum dilectio, spes dilato desiderio lacessita, inter se disputant. Two nominatives left hanging before a plural verb whose subject is discipuli. An anacoluthon, not a defect; rendered with dashes so the broken construction survives into the English rather than being smoothed into an ablative absolute.

Punctuation — Pattern 8, two live cases, both preserved

  • ⭐ 0311A, a full stop MISSING where English and Latin both need one. Migne prints exaudiendis precibus [0311A] praesto esse Et signanter non ait Virgo — no terminal mark at all, and the next word capitalized. Nothing supplied; the English reads "…to be at hand for prayers to be heard And notably the Virgin says not…". This is the mirror image of the lowercase-after-a-misplaced-stop case that brief §5 rules must stand, and the same reasoning governs: English has an exponent for it, so Pattern 8 holds and no mark is invented.
  • 0317B, Migne's misplaced full stop with its lower case, PRESERVED. cum vernat viror novus. flores in terra varii se ostentant. The English reads "when a new greenness springs. flowers of many kinds show themselves in the earth." Brief §5 is explicit and cruces-0030 §4 settled it. ⚠ Do not churn this.
  • 0306A, the missing stop after « Quia amore langueo [n: (ibid.)] » — see the 0048 table. Not supplied.

Negation audit (brief §9)

Every printed non / nec / neque / nisi / haud / nunquam / nullus / nihil / nil / ne in the six Latin chunks was matched against the English on a separate second pass, after the prose was drafted. The dense clusters are 0304A (videns nec invidens… non haberi… Neque enim… non timeat aemulam non rivalem), 0304C (nunquam, nusquam credit fides sanior non adesse — a triple, carried as a triple: "believes never, nowhere not to be at hand"), 0306D (non despexit… non aspexit… non inhaesit… non tenetur… non habetur), 0308A (non nisi semper bonum impossibilitas non retundit — rendered "whose willing — never anything but good — no impossibility beats back", both particles carried), 0308C (non spatio, non obstaculo… non seducit… non abducit), 0309D–0310A (absentatur non deserens, non tanquam poenam inferens… nullis praesentibus refoveri… praeter ipsum nil haberi… non sustinet), 0310D–0311A (nemo… non admittit… non permittit… nemo carnem gerens… nemo vidit unquam… non ait Virgo… non aurora consurgens, non sol), 0312C (non solum non inhaeret praesentibus, non attendit — the "not only … not" carried whole), 0313A (vidensque et non visus, ut tamen valeat non nesciri), 0315A (aquae diluvii non repressae imperio non obstaculo repelluntur), 0316B (ut nec verum posset loqui… ne juvaret magistrum), 0316D (caeteris per gratiam evadentibus Judas perditus non emersit), 0318C–D (quam non capit turba… quam nesciunt nisi pauci… oculus pertinacia non caligat… Non audietur in plateis).

No negation was dropped and none was supplied. The one place where carrying the printed reading makes the English contradict itself is 0306B's auferre (above), which is a verb, not a negation, and it is carried for the same reason.

§4 · CONVENTIONS SET OR HELD IN THIS RANGE

  1. ⭐ amica mea = "my friend" — HELD, and this range is where the merge's ruling first pays. Cant. 2:10 is the first of the six recurrences brief §5 predicts, and it arrives with its own confirmation: Philip immediately glosses the word from friendship, not love — Quod quia vis cum volo, et cum nolo non vis, meam recte dixerim te amicam, attendens cunctis voluntatibus mihi displicentibus inimicam — and then adduces Sallust's definition of friendship (Idem velle et idem nolle, ea demum firma amicitia est) as his proof. "My love" would leave a paragraph proving friendship from a lemma that says love, with amor, dilectio and amicitia all live in the same twelve lines. Rendered "my friend" at 0313C and again in the 0314B re-quotation.
  2. ⚑ cancelli = "lattice(s)", ONE English word for the lemma AND the architectural sense — offered to the merge. Caput V turns on the shape of the cancelli (round, like an eye) and then makes the identification explicit: partem hujus illam quam digniorem meritis intellexit, in rotundum aedificans cancellum voluit nominare, in quo poni significantius Sanctum sanctorum voluit et altare (0312D). English "chancel" descends from this very word and is the natural term for the church-part — but using it here would sever the identity the sentence exists to assert, because the lemma cannot be "looking through the chancels". So "lattice" carries both, and the reader sees Philip name the round part of the church by the lemma's own word. This is the Song ruling's case 2 (stylus/epistylium, murenulae/ferculum) applied to an English pair rather than a Latin one. If the merge prefers "chancel" at 0312D it must accept that the argument goes silent there; I flag it rather than decide it unilaterally.
  3. caprea = "roe" · hinnulus (cervorum) = "the fawn (of harts)" · cervus = "hart", fixed for Caput IV. The chapter's entire structure is the roe's sight against the fawn's speed, with the hart as the slower third term (caprea, etsi cervo tardior, acutius tamen cernit), so the three must stay distinct. "Young hart" for hinnulus (Douay) would collapse two of the three.
  4. humor = "humour", kept as one word through Caput IV. The chapter runs the roe's eye-salve → the Spirit → the water of Siloe → the anointing of our inward eyes on the single noun (humorem quemdam habere perhibetur… interni hujus unctio dat humoris… Humor est Christi Spiritus… humorem illum sui spiritus nostris interioribus oculis superfundit). "Moisture" and "humour" alternating would break it.
  5. incolatus = "sojourning" (Ps. 119:5, printed twice in this range at 0312B and 0317C, and glossed at 0317C by suum in terra incolatum dure queritur prolongari). One English word both times.
  6. Brief §5 vocabulary held: charitas = charity (0313D, ad curam proximorum ejus excitat et suscitat charitatem), kept distinct from amor / dilectio = love, which run beside it throughout 0304A and 0310A; misericordia = mercy (0311D, 0315C, 0316B); adolescentulae = maidens (0313C); Sponsus = Bridegroom, Sponsa = Bride, Virgo = Virgin. clementia, torcular, cellaria, recti, moralitas, muraenula, nigra/fusca/formosa as a triple do not occur — but formosa mea (Cant. 2:10) = "my comely one", holding the formosa = comely rule even where the colour triple is absent.
  7. ⭐ Pattern 3 fires on a bare Scripturae at 0307D. Sumens quippe psalmum et Scripturae tam novae quam veteris harmoniam — no divina, no sacra, and a genitive singular, which is a form neither 11638's sweep pattern nor cruces-0030's bare-in Scripturis case would match. Rendered "the harmony of Holy Scripture, the new as well as the old". ⚑ A later sweep of 11632 must match bare Scriptura in every case, not only the ablative plural.
  8. Pattern 17. Philip's own frame is plural and takes you — ut legistis (0306D), Meministis (0316B), nunquid non videntur vobis (0316B), Si meministis (0317C), si eumdem Dominum vultis (0318B), ne vos diu lateat (0313C), ut nostis (0313D). Every second-person singular in the range is inside the Bridegroom's address to the Virgin in Caput VII and every one is singular in the Latin — Tu, ait, quae… delitescis… hilarescis; surge… intermitte… admitte… vis… nolis… te amicam… aspiras… suspiras… te exponis… non postponis… non dimittis… praepolles… tibi contrahis… te exhibes… accingere… obedi… ne te inveniat… te confortans… nec te… derelinquam… invenies te propinquam — so thou without exception. The quoted 1 Reg. 3:9 audit servus tuus is likewise singular; there is no plural inside any quotation in this range.

XVIII→XVII, Luc. XXII→XXIII, Luc. X→XI). That is a different profile from (II Paral. III)'s thirty-two and (I Cor. II)'s three wrong verses, and it looks mechanical.

⭐ And two sigla the brief's §8b watch-list names are CORRECT here, which the merge needs as much as the misses: [n: (I Cor. II)] is right twice — at 0305C for 1 Cor. 2:6+8 and at 0318A for 1 Cor. 2:7 — and [n: (II Cor. IX)] is right at 0314C for 2 Cor. 9:7. So neither siglum is systematically wrong; they are wrong sometimes, which is a weaker and more useful finding than the accumulating count alone suggests.

The [n: (ibid.)] chains (0305B on Luke 1, 0306A on Cant. 2, 0317D on Luke 24) all resolve correctly against their printed antecedents and none was touched. ⚠ [n:] position varies and is reproduced, not normalized: it falls inside the closing guillemet everywhere in this range except at 0305A, where Migne prints salutis? [n: (Hebr. I.)] » — the note between the question mark and the closing guillemet — and at 0305C, tibi? [n: (III Reg. XXII.)] ». Both mirrored.

§6 · TYPOGRAPHY — brief §7 holds, with one counter-instance worth counting

Guillemets carry the adduced authority; italics carry the lemma, printed locators and marginal numbers, across all six chunks. 37 guilleted runs, and every one is scripture adduced as proof. Italics carry: the running Cant. 2:8–13 lemma and its piecemeal re-quotations, the counterfactual lemma at 0311A (En ipse stat intra parietem), the printed locator (Luc. [0317D] XXIV.) at 0317C, and the marginal source-edition numbers 174–182, continuous with cruces-0030's 146–155.

⚑ The counter-instance, and it cuts against the functional rule rather than for it: at 0314A Philip adduces Sallust (Cat. 20.4) explicitly as an external authority — non solum praesens veritas Canticorum, sed et verax sententia digne concinit ethnicorum — and Migne prints Idem, inquit, velle et idem nolle, ea demum firma amicitia est in neither guillemets nor italics. Under the widened rule cruces-0024 §1a proposed ("« » = a quotation adduced as an authority, whatever its source") this should have been guilleted, as the Delphic oracle and Virgil are at 0251D–0253A. It is not. Nothing was supplied. The merge should weigh this beside cruces-0030's Ovid case (also unmarked): the widened rule may need to be stated as permissive rather than predictive — Migne guillemets non-scriptural authorities sometimes, and never italicizes them in prose.

⭐ A guillemet pair Migne himself splits. 0307C prints « Natura, » inquiens, « filii sumus irae ». This is the construction Pattern 5 forbids us to introduce, and here the plate has it. Reproduced 1:1 — two pairs for one quotation — which is why 0049's guillemet count is 2 pairs for what a reader would call one citation. Do not merge them.

⚑ §7a mirroring — the drift point — held word by word. Migne's mixed case runs through this range and none of it was regularized: Ideo et hic virgo dilecti non abscondit praesentiam (0304A, lower case in a chunk that capitalizes Virgo nine times) · Hujusmodi montes iste veniens et saliens virgini auferre voluit immediately followed by conferenti Virgo eosdem referre studuit — both cases inside one sentence (0306B) · Spiritus sanctus superveniet in te (0305B, lower-case sanctus) · recte ad promovendam fidem sollicitudo virginis accersitur (0317D, in a chunk with no capital Virgo at all) · Sponsus / Sponsa capitalized throughout 0310–0314 without exception. Mechanically checkable against the Latin twin; do not regularize.

Heads mirrored as printed, not tidied: CAPUT III. through CAPUT VII. carry a full stop; CAPUT VIII and CAPUT IX (chunks 0052, 0053) do not. The English heads reproduce the presence and absence of the stop exactly. Same discipline as brief §7a's CAPUT PRIMUM / CAPUT II rule.

§7 · THINGS DELIBERATELY NOT REPORTED (brief §10, checked once each)

  • Column-band arithmetic: checked, and no anchor in this range is followed by text broken mid-word or mid-construction. 0049 opens with the anchor glued to the following word ([0307B]Plerique) exactly as the Latin prints it, and 0051 opens with no anchor at all (colFirst 0313B, first anchor mid-paragraph) — both normal. No [ed:], no patch, no plate check. §10.1.
  • noteCount matches the body [n:] count in all six chunks (16/16/10/8/9/10), verified by script; and note that the printed locator (Luc. XXIV.) at 0317C is correctly outside that count.
  • Attested medieval spellings left alone, unmarked (Pattern 9): tanquam, coelum/coelesti, unquam, nunquam, quemdam, eumdem, Hierusalem, lacrymae, Sabbati, charitas, spiritalis/spiritalem, aethnicum/ ethnicum, axilla, reumate, Debbora, Dydimo, philomena, cophinus, sindone, mirrha-class forms.
  • No [f:]. 11632 is lemma-and-gloss, not a florilegium (§10.4).
  • No [d:], no [nt:]: no dittography anywhere in the range, and all 69 notes are bare citations, none editorial prose.
  • Cant. 1:12's Cum/Dum (brief §8c) does not occur in this range — the lemma has moved to Cant. 2. Recorded as a null so the merge's count is complete.

§8 · WHAT A LATER BLIND READ SHOULD LOOK AT FIRST

  1. 0306B, virgini auferre voluit et conferre (§3). The English is deliberately self-contradictory because the Latin is. One letter (afferre) makes it smooth, which is precisely why it must not be changed.
  2. 0316C, multa eum munditia suffocavit (§3). Second most repairable sentence in the range; the conjecture immunditia is in the crux and must stay there.
  3. 0318D, the Isa. 42:2 [var:] (§2.2). If it is wrong it is wrong on the most consequential span in the range. The check is whether in plateis really is absent from every edition of Isa. 42:2 and present in Matt. 12:19 — it is, but it is the claim to test.
  4. 0304A, [sic: signa] (§3.1). The only marker in the range whose class is arguable (Pattern 10 vs Pattern 12). I have stated the case both ways.
  5. §4.2, the cancelli = "lattice" decision. It is the one term choice here that would be expensive to reverse late, and it is the only place in the range where a natural English word (chancel) was declined on purpose.

Philip of Harvengt, Commentaria in Cantica canticorum, PL 203. Range covering Book III Caput X–XV, the exposition of Cant. 2:13b–15: Vox turturis audita est in terra nostra (continued from the previous range) → Surge, amica mea, Sponsa mea, et veni, columba mea, in foraminibus petrae, in cavernis maceriae → Ostende mihi faciem tuam, sonet vox tua in auribus meis → Capite nobis vulpes parvulas quae demoliuntur vineas (twice) → Nam vinea nostra floruit. Six chunks, 6,368 Latin words.

⚑ No book head falls in this range. The chunks carry only CAPUT heads and the numeration runs X → XV continuously across the six, so no division boundary is crossed. Every head in this range prints its full stop (CAPUT X. … CAPUT XV.) — unlike 0052–0053, whose CAPUT VIII/CAPUT IX print none. The English heads reproduce the stop in all six.

Marker totals for this range: 4 [var:] · 3 [sic:] · 0 [ed:] · 0 [d:] · 0 [nt:] · 0 [f:]. verify-english.mjs reports no errors on any of the six; two ratio warnings (0055 at 1.63, 0059 at 1.62), both inside the 1.35–1.68 band this work has already shipped (0004 1.64, 0005 1.68, 0035 1.65, 0046 1.68). Ratios: 1.54 / 1.63 / 1.56 / 1.54 / 1.55 / 1.61.

Column anchors (19/10/8/8/13/4), [n:] strings (11/3/2/5/12/7 — each matching its frontmatter noteCount) and guillemet counts (9/3/1/4/9/2 pairs) were diffed 1:1 against the Latin twins by script, not by eye: byte-identical in content, order and position in all six chunks. No guillemet asymmetry anywhere in this range — every « has its », none stray, none unopened. Asterisk counts la→en are 8→12, 14→20, 12→12, 6→6, 6→8, 4→6; every delta is exactly the content of a [sic:] or [var:] and nothing else.

§1 · ⭐⭐ THE FOUR FINDINGS THE MERGE SHOULD CARRY

1.1 · ⭐⭐ Cant. 2:13 at 0323C — the lemma prints Sponsa mea for the Vulgate's speciosa mea, and Philip's next sentence proves it is his copy-text

The head lemma of Caput XI is printed:

Surge, inquit, amica mea, Sponsa mea, et veni, columba mea, in foraminibus petrae, in cavernis maceriae.

The Vulgate reads surge amica mea speciosa mea et veni columba mea. Migne's Sponsa mea is not a slip, and the proof is internal and needs nothing outside the work — the whole chapter exists to explain the substituted word, and Philip states the substitution himself, in the second sentence, as an observation about the text in front of him:

Quam igitur amicam, columbam, formosam, cum primo Surge diceret, nominavit, iterum surge dicens, amicam et columbam nihilominus nominavit; Sponsae nomen interserens, quod nusquam eum supra recolo nominasse (0323D)

He is collating his own two printings of the invitation: at Cant. 2:10 the three epithets were amica mea, columba mea, formosa mea; here, he says, two of the three return and the name of Bride is inserted in the third slot — the slot the Vulgate fills with speciosa. He then notes that the name is new to the book (nusquam eum supra recolo nominasse), and the remaining four columns are an exposition of why the Bridegroom reaches for the bride-name at the moment he asks her to leave contemplation for public work:

hoc illi nomen objicit quo eam novit ad obedientiam plus teneri (0323D) · Cum igitur audit Virgo sponsam diligentius se vocari… intelligit non se Sponso debere vel in modico refragari (0324A) · Sponsam, inquit, volo nonnunquam adolescentulis demonstrari (0324B)

Conform the lemma to speciosa mea and Caput XI has no subject. [var:] fired, naming the Vulgate reading only; it does not quote Migne's own words, per Pattern 14's mirror test.

⚑ This is §6-shaped evidence (Zech. 4:14, Gen. 3:19): a divergence the author knows is there and builds on. It is the strongest such instance so far in a lemma rather than a proof-text.

1.2 · ⭐ Cant. 2:14 at 0323C — in cavernis maceriae, PLURAL, and the plural is what is expounded

The same lemma prints in cavernis maceriae against the Vulgate's in caverna maceriae, singular. The plural is not incidental: every one of Philip's six later handlings is plural, and the argument turns on there being many hollows, one per angelic office —

Cujus cavernae et internae velut mansiunculae vel recessus, quos patentes invenit quisquis… (0324D) · Digne ergo eidem Virgini cavernae maceriae non clauduntur, sed recessu patulo ad capiendum eam latius diffunduntur (0325C) · ab antiquo in hac maceria cavernae patuerunt, ex quo inde angeli lapsu perdito corruerunt (0325D) · omnesque suos aditus, omnes illi exerit aperturas (0325D)

The last of these is the decisive one: the hollows are the gaps left by the fallen angels, which are necessarily many, and which men enter one by one. A singular caverna makes the whole angelology unstatable. [var:] fired.

1.3 · ⭐ Isa. 56:10 at 0328C printed under [n: (Isa. LI)] — and the same siglum is CORRECT eleven columns later

Migne prints « canes muti [n: (Isa. LI)], » — the words are Isa. 56:10 (speculatores eius caeci omnes… canes muti non valentes latrare), and the sentence continues, outside the guillemets, dormientes et amantes somnia, which is the same verse (videntes vana, dormientes et amantes somnia).

⭐ And [n: (Isa. LI)] is used again at 0332D–0333A, where it is right: « animae meae: Incurvare, ut transeamus » is Isa. 51:23. So within one range, one siglum, one chapter number: wrong once, right once — the exact shape the brief's §8b names for (Psal. XCII) at 0275B/0281A. Reproduced verbatim in both places, corrected in neither.

⚠ The guillemets here wrap only canes muti, though the rest of the verse runs on unmarked immediately after. Reproduced exactly; no marks supplied.

1.4 · ⭐ Migne prints the Vulgate reading in his OWN apparatus at 0321B — and that is why no [var:] fired there

2 Pet. 1:19 is printed:

« Habemus firmiorem propheticum sermonem, cui benefacitis attendentes quasi lucernae lucenti in obscuro [ alias caliginoso] loco [n: (II Petr. I)]. »

The Vulgate reads in caliginoso loco. Migne's text has obscuro, and his own bracketed variant supplies caliginoso — i.e. the divergence is already adjudicated on the page, by the editor, in the printed apparatus. A [var:] would tell the reader a second time and blur whose observation it is; this is the ( sic ) reasoning of brief §10.5 and the Nicetas note-(c) precedent applied to a variant bracket. Logged, no marker. The [ alias caliginoso] is reproduced verbatim and untranslated, per the register rule on [ al., …].

⚑ Worth the merge's eye as a class: this is the first place in 11632 where Migne's own apparatus, rather than our collation, is the witness to a Vulgate divergence. If more [ alias …] brackets turn up in later ranges the merge should rule the class once — my reading is that they never take a [var:].

§2 · THE COLLATION — all 57 listed spans, every one accounted for

Every span in data/quotations/11632/0054-0059.md was collated word by word against the Vulgate. Spans recorded as AGREES were collated and found to agree; the absence of a marker on them is a finding, not a silence.

§3 · THE FOUR [var:], IN FULL

1. Matt. 6:9 at 0319A — qui est for qui es, and Philip repeats the third person in his own gloss. Migne prints « Pater noster qui est in coelis ». The Vulgate has qui es in caelis — a vocative address, not a predication. The marker is fired for two reasons and neither is that the sense is destroyed (it is not):

  1. Philip carries the divergent form into his own next clause — Si Patrem, inquam, qui est in coelis non meum proprie, sed communiter nostrum dico — which is §6-shaped evidence about his copy of the text rather than a compositor's slip in one setting.
  2. ⛔ This is the single most conformable verse in the Latin Bible. An unmarked English "who is in heaven" reads to any reader as our slip against the Our Father, not as Migne's reading — which is precisely the situation Pattern 11 invented [d:] for. The marker says whose the reading is.

⚠ I record this as a threshold judgment, not a certainty. cruces-0048's practice on sense-neutral divergences (Heb. 1:14 capiunt/capient) was "logged, no marker", and a merge that applies that threshold strictly should demote this one. The evidence is all above; the English ("who is in heaven") is faithful either way and does not change if the marker goes.

2. Isa. 51:23 at 0332D — animae meae for animae tuae, which moves the addressee. Migne prints « animae meae: Incurvare, ut transeamus ». Isaiah reads qui dixerunt animae tuae: incurvare ut transeamus — the tormentors speak to Jerusalem's soul, in the prophet's second person. Migne's first person makes the prophet himself the one bowed over. The marker is fired because this is Pattern 7a's fifth mechanism exactly — reference or agency mis-bound — the class no negation-aware check can ever see, and the class where an English reader has no way to recover the printed Latin's referent from a smooth sentence. Nothing in Philip's application turns on it (he generalizes at once: Quis dabit ut in nobis ultra Belial non adjiciat pertransire), so the marker records rather than argues. Also dicunt for dixerunt — present for perfect, unmarked.

3. Cant. 2:13 Sponsa mea at 0323C — §1.1.

4. Cant. 2:14 cavernis at 0323C — §1.2.

3.3 · ⭐ Isa. 5:7 at 0333C — Domini Sabaoth for Domini exercituum: logged, and deliberately NOT marked

Migne prints « Vinea Domini Sabaoth domus Israel est » where the Vulgate translates the divine title: vinea enim Domini exercituum domus Israhel est. Sabaoth is the untranslated Hebrew form — an Old Latin / liturgical reading, and the same class of witness as brief §6's olei splendoris.

Philip repeats it in his own next sentence — Recte vinea Domini Sabaoth miros flores proferens… domus Israel appellatur — so it is his copy-text, not a setting error.

No [var:], and the reason is brief §8c's own ruling: Sabaoth and exercituum name the same title and the sense is untouched, which is Pattern 14's threshold; the Cum/Dum precedent decided exactly this shape the same way. But like Cum/Dum it is copy-text evidence, so it is recorded here for the merge's count. If Isa. 5:7 recurs in a later range, record which form Migne prints.

§4 · CONVENTIONS SET OR HELD IN THIS RANGE

  1. ⭐ grossus — the fig word and the adjective are ONE word in Latin and the chapter is a pun on it; English keeps the pun with "gross". Caput X runs grossos suos (the fig, "green figs", fixed by chunk 0053 and the Cant. 2:13 lemma) straight into grossi hujusmodi homines appellantur, qui grosso magis sensu quam corpore… aspernantur, then obscuratum grossitudine habentes intellectum, then de quorum lateribus videbatur grossa nimis arvina dependere, and finally meritorum copia grossiores. The fruit stays "green figs" (0053's word, and the lemma's); every adjectival use is rendered "gross / grossness / grosser", which is the one English word that carries thick-witted, fat-bodied and coarse at once. The pun survives at the join ("such men are called green figs, who by a sense grosser than their body…") only because the two Englishes are adjacent; a reader who wants the identity has this note. ⚑ The lemma recurs; later ranges should keep "green figs" for the fruit.
  2. ⭐ maceria = "dry-stone wall", distinct from murus = "wall" (0058) and paries = "wall" (0050's lemma). Philip defines the word himself, and the definition is the argument: Maceria vero simplex lapidum congeries appellatur, quae instar sepis extensa caemento medio non ligatur — a wall with no mortar, which is why the angels who compose it ad persistendum firmius non indiget legis, non Evangelii ligatura (0324D). The mortarless binding is the whole point: plain "wall" would leave the sentence about binding-agents with nothing to bind. ⚑ The lemma recurs whenever Cant. 2:14 returns; later ranges must match.
  3. vulpes parvulae = "little foxes" and vulpecula = "little fox" — deliberately COLLAPSED, and logged as a collapse. Both run through 0057–0059 and Philip uses them interchangeably (Hujusmodi ergo vulpeculas at 0329A picks up vulpes parvulas of the lemma without a change of referent). No argument in the range turns on the diminutive, unlike lectulus/lectus at 0279B, so the lectulus rule is not engaged. Recorded so a later range that DOES find an argument on it can reverse this on the evidence.
  4. sodales Sponsi = "the Bridegroom's companions", fixed through 0057–0059 (Philip's fourth dramatic persona, identified with the angels at 0329C). adolescentulae = "maidens" per brief §5, held throughout — and note that 0057 identifies the maidens with the apostles, so "maidens" is applied to men in Philip's own voice. Not tidied.
  5. odor = "scent" throughout Caput X, one English word for the whole chain (odorem suum daret → fugit culpa → odor et fetor → odorem suum dare / venundare), against fetor = "stench". The chapter's last movement turns on the three ways of giving a scent, so elegant variation would break it.
  6. ⭐ Pattern 3 fires on a bare nominative singular Scriptura at 0331B — sicut enim Scriptura meminit — rendered "as Holy Scripture recalls". No divina, no sacra, and a nominative singular, which is a third form after cruces-0030's bare ablative plural in Scripturis (0260A) and cruces-0048's bare genitive singular Scripturae (0307D). ⚑ The sweep pattern for 11632 must match bare Scriptura in every case; three forms have now been attested in three ranges and the sweep that misses one will miss the others. No other occurrence in this range.
  7. Brief §5 vocabulary held: misericordia = mercy (0323B, ampliorem dignabitur misericordiam impertire; 0330C, Magistri miserentis); adolescentulae = maidens; Sponsus = Bridegroom, Sponsa = Bride, Virgo = Virgin, case mirrored (§6). charitas, clementia, muraenula, lectulus, cancelli, cellaria, torcular, recti, moralitas, and the nigra / fusca / formosa triple do not occur in this range — but formosam at 0323D (Philip's retrospect on the Cant. 2:10 epithets) is rendered "comely one", holding the formosa = comely rule.
  8. Pattern 17. The second person in this range is entirely determined by the Latin and there is no drift. Plural → "you": Philip's own address to his hearers (ut legistis 0320C, ne putetis 0320C, si diligens lector putat 0320D, si tamen auditum memoriae vestra diligentia commendavit 0329B, sicut nostis 0329C and 0331D, Videtis 0332D) and the Bridegroom's address to the angels in Caput XIV (Vos, inquit, angeli… volo sedulos vos adesse, Vos, ait, qui potestis… capite nobis vulpes). *Singular → "thou": the Bridegroom's address to the Virgin at 0325A (Tu, ait, cujus… surge et propera, nec timor aliquis te retardet… non est tamen cur timeas) and throughout Caput XII (tibi datum est… volo… te habere… ut mihi non formides… tuam conscientiam exhibere… tuum merito jam non claudis… Etsi, ait, faciem videre volentibus non ostendis). Inside quotations: Matt. 25:25 talentum tuum and Luke 22:32 fides tua are singular → thou; Luke 22:31 expetivit vos is plural → "you", in the same sentence as the singular pro te* — reproduced, and it is the Dorotheus/Phil. 4:7 case exactly: the reader can see Satan ask for all the apostles and Christ pray for one man, with no apparatus.
  9. Hierusalem (0332B) kept as printed, not normalized to Jerusalem — but rendered "Jerusalem" in English, as at 0299D. Pattern 9; the Latin column carries the spelling.

4.1 · The Sir. 15:9 weave at 0327C, and why the substituted word is worth the merge's minute

quia et in ore peccatoris non est laus, sicut legitur, pretiosa. The Vulgate reads Non est speciosa laus in ore peccatoris.

⚑ The substituted word is the one the chapter cannot spare. The clause immediately before it is si non antecesserit vocem facies speciosa — and speciosa is the chapter's own predicate of the Virgin's face (decoris sui merito concupitam, amator legitur speciei, tantae placet merito speciei). Had speciosa stayed in the quotation, Philip would have used one word for the sinner's praise and the Virgin's face in adjacent clauses; pretiosa keeps them apart.

Whether that is Philip's deliberate choice, his copy-text, or a compositor is exactly the research question Pattern 14 forbids a marker to answer. Logged, no marker — and the frame sicut legitur is his own, so §8a's left-edge argument applies as well.

§6 · TYPOGRAPHY — brief §7 holds, and the range adds a THIRD unmarked pagan authority

Guillemets carry the quotation adduced as an authority; italics carry the lemma, its re-quotations, words discussed as words, and the marginal numbers. 28 guilleted runs across the six chunks, and every one is scripture adduced as proof. Italics carry: the running Cant. 2:12–15 lemma and its piecemeal re-quotations; Philip's two collated invitations Surge / surge at 0323D (words discussed as words, the brief §7 category, and the case is clean — they are cited to be compared with each other); Migne's variant keyword alias at 0321B; and the marginal source-edition numbers 183–190, continuous with cruces-0048's 174–182.

⭐ The counter-instance, and it is the third of its kind in three ranges. At 0328D Philip adduces Ovid (Rem. Am. 81) explicitly as an authority — mala morbi semina, dum nova sunt, juxta poetam, opprimere — and Migne prints it in neither guillemets nor italics. At 0330C he adduces Virgil (Aen. VII.338, mille nocendi artes) explicitly — et juxta quemdam ethnicum, mille artes et eo amplius sunt nocendi — and again prints nothing.

⛔ The Virgil case is the sharpest evidence yet that the widened rule is permissive and not predictive, because it is the SAME AUTHOR Migne guillemets at 0251D. « Dii, si qua est pietas coelo » is guilleted there; mille artes… nocendi is bare here. Nothing was supplied in either place. Together with cruces-0048's Sallust at 0314A and cruces-0030's Ovid at 0259, that is four unmarked classical authorities against two marked ones, and the merge should weigh the ratio: for non-scriptural authorities in this work, bare looks like the norm and the 0251D–0253A cluster like the exception.

⚑ §7a mirroring — the drift point — held word by word, and this range is one of the richer ones for it. Migne's mixed case runs through 0054 in particular and none of it was regularized: sed quod sponsae est, sponsus sibi satis vindicat opportune and recte sponsa terram quoque non tuam (0319A, both lower case) stand thirty words from recte Sponsa invitatur (0321D) and Vult Sponsus (0321D), capitalized. Likewise praebeat aurem sponsa, dictis oltemperet (0324A) and audit Virgo sponsam diligentius se vocari (0324A), lower case, inside a chunk that capitalizes Sponsa and Sponsus elsewhere throughout; and ut libere virgo introeat (0325D) in a chunk with capital Virgo nine times. All mirrored. Mechanically checkable against the Latin twin; do not regularize.

Migne's parentheses at 0333C are content, not apparatus, and are reproduced: Qui paulo ante (vineas) consequenter (vineam) nominat singularem… Et dicunt se (populum)… et (oves) se appellant. Philip is discussing the two nouns as words, and Migne marks them with round brackets rather than italics — a fifth marking device in this work, used once. Kept exactly.

§7 · PATTERN 7, 8 AND 10 — three [sic:], and what was NOT marked

None of the three carried runs is ALSO translated in the running text (brief §8's named failure — checked word by word on a separate pass).

  1. 0322B [sic: hila rescat] — Pattern 10, split type. ut ad ejus primitias intuentis digne oculus hila rescat. Read hilarescat, certain: the verb is Philip's own and he prints it correctly at 0326A (velut jugi convivio facies hilarescat) four columns later, in the same construction. Carried whole per Pattern 10 — including the space — and the English does not also say "grow cheerful" in that slot; it reads "the beholder's eye worthily [sic: hila rescat]".
  2. 0324A [sic: oltemperet] — a non-word. praebeat aurem sponsa, dictis oltemperet, amet imperium et subscribat. Read obtemperet, near-certain: dictis obtemperare is the standard idiom and the clause sits in a list of three obedience-verbs. l for b is a plausible plate defect. Carried untranslated in italics; the English does not also supply "obey". ⚑ Note the cost is visible: the English clause has no verb, which is exactly what the plate leaves.
  3. 0334A [sic: tempere] — a non-word in this slot. In hoc ergo tempere vulpes non immerito parvulae perhibentur. Read tempore, certain: hoc is masculine/neuter ablative singular and demands it, and Philip prints cum finis temporum venerit eight words later. ⚠ I record the one argument against the marker: temperi (also tempori) is an attested adverb meaning "in season", so a reader might take tempere for a variant of it and invoke Pattern 9. It cannot be: an adverb cannot take in hoc. Marked.

Rendered as printed, no marker (real words, merely odd) — conjectures live here and NOT in the text:

  • ⛔ 0324D, ipse qui invitat vitae foramina et cavernas maceriae pollicetur. The clefts are the rock's everywhere else in the chapter (petrae foraminibus five times in two columns, twice in the lemma itself), and the conjecture petrae is near-certain. But vitae is a real word and construes ("the clefts of life"), so Pattern 12 keeps it on the English side: rendered "the clefts of life". ⚠ This is the sentence in my range most likely to be silently repaired, and the repair would be invisible — one word restores a chapter that is otherwise perfectly consistent.
  • 0325A, ut columba tali freta praesidio, fiducialibus expleat quod jubetur. A bare ablative/dative plural adjective with no noun anywhere in the sentence to govern it; fiducialiter would be the expected adverb. Rendered "may with confidence fulfil what is commanded", which is as close as the printed words allow — but the reader should know that the printed form is a plural adjective and that English cannot express a plural adjective standing alone. Logged, not adjudicated in the text.
  • 0330C, seducunt Judam Iscariot avarum pecuniae magis quam salutis; et ne magistrum diligat; dolo multiplici dissuadent. Migne's semicolon falls inside the ne-clause, cutting it from the verb that governs it. Preserved** (Pattern 8): the English reads "and lest he love his master; they dissuade him with manifold guile". Not repunctuated.
  • 0332D–0333A, Qui dicunt ait Isaias, « animae meae… — Migne prints no comma after dicunt, so the parenthetical ait Isaias is unclosed on its left. Nothing supplied (Pattern 8): the English reads "Who say says Isaias, « to my soul: … »". It reads wrong because it is printed wrong.
  • 0328D, qui venari pigritantes somno suam negligentiam configurant. configurant + accusative + dative ("shape their negligence to sleep") is an unusual government but attested medieval usage; Pattern 9, unmarked.
  • 0327B, nullius facies tanta conspicuat gratia vel decore. conspicuo as an active intransitive is not classical; a medieval formation on conspicuus. Rendered "shines with", Pattern 9, unmarked.
  • 0333D, cum Ananiam et Saphyram… adhuc male teneros occulta fuerint avaritia demolitae.* male teneros* is odd (the pair are the foxes' victims, not the tender vines), but both words are real and construe. Rendered "as yet ill and tender". Logged.

Punctuation — Pattern 8, the live case, PRESERVED

⭐ 0320C, Migne's misplaced full stop with its lower case. ne putetis de eodem populo deinceps nullos esse, qui audire velint Christum. et eum audientibus interesse. The stop breaks a qui-clause in half and the next word is lower-case. Preserved exactly: the English reads "…who would hear Christ. and be present among his hearers". Brief §5 is explicit that Migne's lower case after a misplaced stop stands, and cruces-0030 §4 and cruces-0048 §3 both settled it. ⚠ Do not churn this.

Negation audit (brief §9)

Every printed non / nec / neque / nisi / haud / nunquam / nullus / nihil / nil / nemo / ne in the six Latin chunks (161 tokens: 66/24/25/11/27/9 non plus 34 others) was matched against the English on a separate second pass, after the prose was drafted. The dense clusters are 0319A (nil deinceps habere dicendi sunt non commune, a nil + non pair carried as "nothing… that is not common"), 0319B (si terra tua tantum, et non nostra… non vox turturis audiretur… non proferret, eisque non prolatis, non fructus alios… subinferret — four, carried as four), 0319D (et non cedunt loco… non solum non defluit… pares in gratia non habentur… aequari non merentur… dignus mensae nisi regiae non inferri — the nisi/non pair rendered "worthy to be set on no table unless a king's", both particles present), 0321A (non prece, non pretio, non minarum impetu repelluntur, a triple carried as neither/nor/nor), 0321B (veterem, non obscurat; non praejudicat… non adversatur), 0321C (nullus ordo, non apostolo… non prior, non posterior), 0325B (nonnisi terrae dediti ad petram solidam non venerunt — carried as "given over to nothing but the earth, came not to the solid rock"), 0326D (nihil nisi Sponso fiducialiter se ostendit — "shows itself in nothing save to the Bridegroom"), 0330B (non caro hominibus, non culpa malis spiritibus pares fecit… superbia vel inobedientia non projecit), 0331B (adversus justos penitus nil valere — "of no strength at all against the just"), 0332B (nequando inimici exsultent), 0334A (eos nolunt nec sufferunt… praemonent et adjuvant illarum fraudibus non subesse — the double negative of "help them not to lie under" carried whole).

No negation was dropped and none was supplied. There is no place in this range where carrying the printed reading makes the English contradict itself — unlike cruces-0048's auferre at 0306B.

§8 · THE [n:]-ONLY CLASS — hit rate in this range

12 spans listed by the extractor, plus five further weaves found on the second pass that it never listed (Ps. 21:17 and 2 Cor. 5:16 at 0325B–C; Eph. 4:5 at 0333C; and at 0321D–0322A the fused Mic. 4:4 / Matt. 8:20 weave sub vite sua, sub ficu sua caput valeant reclinare, which carries no note and which is striking because chunk 0058 later guillemets the other half of Matt. 8:20, Vulpes foveas habent, as a proof-text). All 17 are Philip's own prose. Hit rate: zero.

Running total across the ranges that have reported: 0018–0023 19/19 prose · 0048–0053 38/38 prose · this range 17/17 prose, against wave 1's single Rom. 8:10 and cruces-0030's Ps. 11:7. The mechanism cruces-0048 identified holds here without exception — Philip absorbs the scriptural words into his own rhymed colon-endings, which forces a change of person, number, tense or voice: parvulos tuos → parvulos nostros, animam aggravat → cauterium hoc impressit, cor unum erat → ut cor esset, partes vulpium erunt → vulpium partes esse.

⛔ But two of this range's four most quotation-like weaves carried NO note at all — Ps. 21:17 (foderunt manus et pedes) at 0325B and Eph. 4:5 (unus Dominus, fides una) at 0333C — and were therefore invisible to the extractor in both directions, exactly as cruces-0048's two 0314C tails were. A [n:]-only sweep that trusts the note list will miss them. They are also the two least altered spans in the range, which is the uncomfortable part: the more verbatim the weave, the less likely it is to carry a note.

⚑ The closest call, recorded so a later reader can reverse it on the evidence: Prov. 1:17 at 0331B (§2, chunk 0058). It has a note, a frame naming Scripture, and near-verbatim Vulgate wording; it lacks guillemets, italics, and any attachment of the note to the words rather than to the frame. I judged it prose. If the merge judges otherwise, the divergences are autem dropped and rete jacitur for iacitur rete — both sense-neutral — so the ruling changes the class, not the English.

§1 · ⭐⭐ THE THREE FINDINGS THE MERGE SHOULD CARRY

1.1 · ⭐⭐⭐ Cant. 2:17 at 0338D — Migne prints Bethel where the Vulgate has Bether, and the whole back half of the chapter is an etymology of the divergent word

The head lemma of Caput XVIII is printed:

Revertere, dilecte mi: similis esto capreae hinnuloque cervorum, super montes Bethel.

The Vulgate reads revertere; similis esto, dilecte mi, capreae hinnuloque cervorum super montes Bether. Two divergences, and they are of completely different weight:

  1. The vocative is transposed — Revertere, dilecte mi: similis esto for Vulg. revertere: similis esto, dilecte mi. Sense-neutral, and the re-quotation at 0340A (« Similis, inquit, esto capreae, hinnuloque cervorum ») drops dilecte mi altogether while Philip's own re-quotations at 0339A and 0339C print Revertere, dilecte mi as a unit. Migne's own text is internally consistent; the Vulgate's is not being followed.
  2. ⭐⭐ Bethel for Bether — and this is the range's principal find, because Philip does not merely quote the word, he construes it, at length, as the name of the Virgin's conscience:

Ut aiunt qui notitiam Hebraeorum nominum aestimant se habere… Beth, domus; el vero Deus interpretatur; et Bethel domus Dei Latino eloquio nominatur. Domus autem Dei non incongrue interna Virginis conscientia judicatur, thalamus scilicet spiritalis, qui Deo Dei Filio praeparatur… (0341A–B)

and the identification then governs the remaining twenty lines of the chapter: Quae nimirum domus vel inhabitatio, jure dicitur montuosa · qui super montes Virginis. Conform the lemma to Bether and the entire etymology, and with it the chapter's conclusion, ceases to have anything to stand on. Hebrew Bether ("division", "cleft") yields nothing remotely like domus Dei.

[var:] fired at the head lemma, stating both readings and naming the witness; it does not speculate about whether this is Philip's copy-text, an Old Latin reading, or a compositor's letter (Pattern 14). ⚠ The re-quotation at 0341A also prints Bethel (Super montes, inquit, Bethel), so the reading is attested twice in the chunk, which puts it in the evidential shape of brief §6's Zech. 4:14 and Gen. 3:19 — a copy-text reading, not a slip. This is the strongest §6-class candidate the work has produced since those two, and the merge should treat it as one.

1.2 · ⭐⭐ Matt. 7:8 at 0345B — Migne prints « Incipit et invenit » where the argument requires accipit, and the correct form stands twice within twenty words

Caput XX's whole close is an argument about the tenses and the verbs Matthew prints. Philip has just quoted Matt. 7:7 (future throughout) and Matt. 7:8 (present, then future), and he says so explicitly:

Hoc de praesenti tempore. Non enim dicit, accipiet et inveniet, sed « Incipit et invenit. » … Non enim ait, « pulsanti » aperitur, sed « aperietur, »

Incipit means "he begins". The antithesis Philip is drawing is accipiet (future, which the text does not say) against accipit (present, which it does), and the whole point collapses on the word printed.

⚑ The decisive detail is internal. Migne prints the correct accipit twice inside the same paragraph — « Omnis qui petit accipit, et qui quaerit invenit » at 0345A and « Omnis enim qui petit accipit, et qui quaerit invenit » at 0345B, the latter five words before the defective printing — and accipiet three words before it. So within one column the plate has accipit, accipiet and Incipit, and only the third is impossible.

Rendered as printed ("He beginneth and findeth"), which is meant to read wrong, with a [var:] naming the received reading. Not a [sic:]: incipit is a real word and Pattern 12's "real word merely wrong" clause keeps it on the English side — the same call cruces-0042 made for Adjuvo/Adjuro at 0299D, and this is the same shape one column later in the work. ⚠ This is the sentence in the range most likely to be silently repaired, and the repair would be invisible: one letter restores a perfectly cogent argument.

1.3 · ⭐ Matt. 7:7 at 0345B — et accipietis for the Vulgate's et dabitur vobis, in the one place where the verb is the argument

« Petite, ait, et accipietis, quaerite et invenietis; pulsate et aperietur vobis [n: (ibid.)]. »

Vulg. Matt. 7:7 (and Luke 11:9) read Petite, et dabitur vobis. Et accipietis is the wording of John 16:24 (petite et accipietis).

Ordinarily this would be logged and left unmarked — both readings are future, and nothing is asserted that the Vulgate does not assert. It is marked because of what Philip does with it four lines later: Non enim dicit, accipiet et inveniet, sed « Incipit [i.e. accipit] et invenit ». His antithesis is between the future accipietis of v. 7 and the present accipit of v. 8 — one verb in two tenses. With the Vulgate's dabitur vobis the pairing is between two different verbs and the argument is materially weaker. This is 7a″'s test exactly: the exposition rests on a word, so the word is marked where it diverges.

⚠ I record this as a judgment rather than defend it. If the merge reads accipietis/dabitur as below Pattern 14's threshold, the fix is to delete one [var:]; §1.2's marker is independent of it and stands either way.

§2 · THE COLLATION — all 65 listed spans, every one accounted for

Every span in data/quotations/11632/0060-0065.md was collated word by word against the Vulgate. Spans recorded as AGREES were collated and found to agree; the absence of a marker on them is a finding, not a silence.

2c · The [n:]-only class — hit rate 1 of 12 on the listed spans, and the one hit needs no marker

All twelve ⭐ spans were traced back to their real left edge. Eleven are Philip's own prose, written with scripture rather than quoting it — accusative-and-infinitive frames, changes of person and tense forced by his rhymed clause-endings, his own added adjectives. None of the eleven takes a marker; a [var:] on unmarked prose would misrepresent it as a lemma.

The eleven, listed so nobody re-opens them: 0060 — 0336A Gen. 29–30 (Si patriarchae olim quos constat post invicem uno patre… non omnes genitos una matre — Philip's own conditional; the note points at two whole chapters, not at quoted words) · 0336C Gen. 48:15 + Matt. 14:21 (Qui olim patriarcham Jacob a juventute sua pavit, qui multo recentius de quinque panibus quinque millia hominum satiavit — two relative clauses of his own; note that Gen. 48:15, the source of the first half, carries no siglum at all while Matthew does). 0062 — 0339B Prov. 8:17 (tu Scripturae testimonio diligentem diligere te dixisti — the Vulgate's first-person Ego diligentes me diligo recast as a second-person apostrophe under his own dixisti) · 0339B 1 John 4:10/19 (nonnullos… antequam diligerent, dilexisti, with his own parenthesis ut experti praedicant) · 0339D 1 Cor. 13:12 (Promisisti quippe finito vitae cursu, facie ad faciem te videri — only the three-word tag is Paul's, inside his own accusative-and-infinitive; and vidi per speculum imperfecte four lines later is the same verse recast again, unnoted) · 0340D Eccles. 9:1 (Nesciens enim utrum odio digna sit an amore — his own participle, and the Vulgate's amore an odio reversed, exactly as cruces-0042 records at 0291D and cruces-0048 at

  1. Third printing of the same reversal in the work; it is Philip's habit, not a variant). 0064 — 0343B Gen. 34:1 (Nec imitabor Dinam — the note names the person; ad videndum foras mulieres non exibo in the next clause is the pericope recast in his own first-person future) · 0343B Ps. 133:2 (ad dicendum bene extollam in noctibus manus meas — the Vulgate's plural imperative extollite manus vestras turned first-person singular future, and benedicite split into his own ad dicendum bene, which is a pun, not a quotation) · 0345A John 2:10 (etsi forte omnis homo vinum bonum ei quod est deterius anteponat — subjunctive inside his own etsi clause, with vinum bonum for Vulg. bonum vinum and anteponat for ponit) · 0345C Gen. 29 (Sic Jacob petenti et quaerenti non Liam in conjugium, sed Rachelem — narrative prose; the note points at the chapter). 0065 — 0347D Matt. 18:10 (cujus refecti adipe omnem prorsus molestiam ignoratis — see §2d.1: the note is correctly named but wrongly placed, and the Matthew matter is twelve lines earlier).

⭐ The one hit — 0336C, Matt. 4:2, and it diverges only in its connective.

Denique cum jejunasset quadraginta diebus et quadraginta noctibus, postea esuriit [n: (Matth. IV)].

Vulg. Matt. 4:2: Et cum ieiunasset quadraginta diebus et quadraginta noctibus, postea esuriit. Every word after the connective is verbatim Vulgate, and Migne marks the span with neither guillemets nor italics** — it sits naked inside Philip's sentence, carrying only its note. It is a genuine member of the class brief §8a names, and it is the only one of the twelve.

No marker, on two independent grounds: (a) §8a's ruling — where the plate marks the words as neither quotation nor lemma we cannot establish the quotation's left edge, which is precisely the question Denique raises; and (b) even if the edge were certain, Denique for Et is Philip's own discourse connective taking over, which is below Pattern 14's threshold and is the same call cruces-0048 made for 2 Cor. 9:7's dropped enim at 0314C. Logged in full so the merge can rule the class with a near-verbatim specimen in front of it — this is a different specimen from the three the class has so far (Rom. 8:10, Ps. 90:5–6, Lam. 4:20), because it is the case where the words are right.

Reported per brief §8a even where it is a null result. 1/12 here, against 0/20 for 0042–0047, 0/38 for 0048–0053, 0/19 for 0018–0023 and 1/14 for 0024–0029.

2c′ · ⭐ Weaves the extractor could NOT list, found on the mandatory second pass

Five spans in this range carry no guillemets, no italics AND no [n:], and therefore appear in the extraction in no class whatever. All five are Philip's own prose and none takes a marker; they are recorded because the class is the one brief §8a exists for.

  1. ⭐ 0337B — Excursus ejus a patre, ait Ambrosius, recursus ejus ad patrem. Not scripture, and the most interesting of the five: Philip adduces Ambrose by name as an authority, and Migne prints the sentence in neither guillemets nor italics. See §3a — this is a third counter-instance to brief §7's functional rule, after the Sallust at 0314A and the Ovid at
  2. ⚠ Note also the lower-case patre / patrem inside it, against capital Patre two columns later at 0337D; mirrored.
  3. 0337A–B — Cant. 2:1, Ipse etenim florem campi, et lilium convallium se fatetur. Verbatim Vulgate nouns (Ego flos campi, et lilium convallium) turned accusative under his own se fatetur. Philip's prose. No marker — and worth the merge's eye because it is the Song quoting itself unmarked, the mirror image of brief §7's "the Song takes guillemets when quoted as a proof-text".
  4. 0343D — Eph. 2:19, qui intra septa Ecclesiae cives sanctorum et Dei domesticos se fatentur. Vulg. cives sanctorum, et domestici Dei — verbatim but for case, turned accusative under the same verb se fatentur he used at 0337A. The construction is his signature. No marker.
  5. 0345B — 2 Pet. 1:19, donec dies illucescat et oriatur sol potius quam lucifer. Vulg. donec dies elucescat, et lucifer oriatur in cordibus vestris. ⭐ This is where Caput XX's whole architecture comes from — the entire chapter is built on the lucifer / sol antithesis (twelve occurrences of lucifer in two columns), and the verse that supplies it is quoted unmarked and unnoted, with the two nouns' roles reversed from the Vulgate's (Peter's day-star rises; Philip's sun rises rather than the day-star). Philip's prose, no marker — but a reader who does not know 2 Pet. 1:19 is standing behind the chapter will not learn it from Migne's page.
  6. 0347D — Ps. 83:11, in atriis illius Domini vobis datur plena refectio, dies una. Vulg. melior est dies una in atriis tuis super millia. Both phrases verbatim, split across his own clause and recombined in the reverse order; and dies una has already been used in his own voice at 0338A (dies occasum nesciens, dies una) with no scriptural intent at all. Philip's prose. No marker.

⚑ A methodological note for the merge's running count. A tally of failures alone would have made this range look like an absence of evidence. It is not: twenty-four checked-and-correct sigla in six chunks is a positive datum, and it is the strongest available support for §8b's revised claim that no siglum in this work is systematically wrong. The bad ranges and the good ranges are both real and they alternate.
