§7 · WHAT A LATER BLIND READ SHOULD LOOK AT FIRST

  1. ⛔⛔ 0407A, the lemma's fovum (§1.2). The single most repairable place in the range, and the one a reader will silently fix without noticing. Confirm the [sic:] is still there, that the English does not also say "honeycomb" in that sentence, and that favum still stands correctly six times in the two columns after it.
  2. ⛔ 0405A, the non… placent / evanescunt scope (§4, negation audit). The one place a faithful negation was nearly put outside its own clause. A count cannot see it; only the pair can.
  3. ⭐⭐ §1.1's displayed-verse rule. The claim to test is arithmetical and cheap: ten intra-paragraph line breaks in 126 chunks, nine italic quotations and one bare block that is Philip's own poem. If a single displayed classical quotation anywhere in the work is bare, the rule is wrong and cruces-0084 §3b's narrower statement should stand instead. I did not verify the identifications of the 0006, 0007 and 0110 verses against an edition — only their marking — so treat the poet-attributions in that table as provisional and the marking as scripted.
  4. ⭐⭐ 0412C, the (ibid.) → Ps. 118 on Ps. 31:8 (§1.3). Two things to test separately: that Ps. 118 contains no such clause (certain), and that Ps. 31:8 is the right verse (verbatim). ⛔ And confirm that nothing has been "corrected" — §10.2 is the reason.
  5. ⚠ 0412D, the Eph. 3:10 [var:] (§2g). The divergence is certain (principibus ‖ principatibus); the judgment that it clears Pattern 14 is mine, and rests on Philip's principibus et angelicis potestatibus two lines later. If the marker is wrong it is wrong on materiality, not on fact.
  6. ⚠ 0401D, the Cant. 4:16 [var:] (§2f). Same test, and note the deliberate asymmetry with ut comedat at 0403D. Reversing either one should reverse it in the direction §2f names.
  7. §3b's Trinity capitalization at 0402D–0403A — the mirroring decision in this range most likely to read as an error to someone who has not seen the plate.
  8. ⚠ §3a's CAPUT PRIMUM drift — 2 files say "CHAPTER ONE.", 2 say "CHAPTER THE FIRST.", and mine makes it 3–2. A merge sweep, not a range fix.

Philip of Harvengt, Commentaria in Cantica canticorum, PL 203. Six chunks, 6,457 Latin words, covering Caput VII–XVI of Book V — the exposition of Cant. 5:2–5:9: Aperi mihi, soror mea, amica mea → Exspoliavi me tunica mea → Dilectus meus misit manum suam per foramen → Surrexi ut aperirem dilecto meo → Manus meae distillaverunt myrrham → Pessulum ostii mei aperui dilecto meo → Anima mea liquefacta est → Invenerunt me vigiles → Adjuro vos, filiae Hierusalem → Qualis est dilectus tuus ex dilecto.

⚑ Book label, corrected for the merge. LIBER QUINTUS. stands in chunk 0091 (col. 0403B); LIBER QUARTUS. in 0068, LIBER SEXTUS. in 0107. So this range is Book V, and cruces-0084 (chunks 0084–0089, cols 0386D–0400C) is Book IV, not Book V as its header states. A label slip only; nothing in that file's findings depends on it.

⚑ No book head falls in this range. The chunks carry only CAPUT heads, VII → XVI continuously, and every one carries the full stop (CAPUT VII. … CAPUT XVI.); the English heads reproduce it. Numerals throughout — no CAPUT PRIMUM-style spelling.

Marker totals for this range: 3 [var:] · 3 [sic:] · 0 [ed:] · 0 [d:] · 0 [nt:] · 0 [f:]. verify-english.mjs reports no errors on any of the six (the run's VERIFY FAILED is the not-yet-translated chunks after 0101). Four ratio warnings — 0096 1.61, 0097 1.67, 0099 1.64, 0100 1.68 — all inside the 1.35–1.68 band this work has shipped. Ratios: 1.61 / 1.67 / 1.57 / 1.64 / 1.67 / 1.58.

Column anchors (12/12/8/11/8/11), [n:] strings (14/3/0/1/1/1 — each matching its frontmatter noteCount) and guillemet counts were diffed 1:1 against the Latin twins by script: anchors byte-identical in order and place, [n:] contents byte-identical in order. Every [sic:] content was machine-checked as a verbatim substring of its Latin twin; every [var:] was machine-checked NOT to be one. Marginal source-edition numbers 240–249 verified in place.

Guillemets: 1 « against 1 » in the whole range, at 0416D, balanced. That single pair is the last guillemet in the work — see §1.1, which is this range's headline finding.

§1 · ⭐⭐ THE FINDINGS THE MERGE SHOULD CARRY

1.1 · ⭐⭐⭐ THE GUILLEMETS STOP — the last « » in all 126 chunks stands at col. 0416D, and the change of practice falls inside this range

Brief §7 asks each range to report "a genuine change of practice at an Explicit/Incipit… as an exception with the column named," and warns that no single range can see a work-wide pattern. I ran the ⭐ whole-work grep. Counting « in the body of every one of the 126 Latin chunks:

chunkscols«
0000–00890181A–0400C420
00900400D–0403A1
0091–00950403B–0415C0
00960415D–0418C1 ← the last one in the work
0097–01250418D–0490B0

422 guillemets across the first ninety-seven chunks; then not one in the remaining twenty-nine — 29 chunks, ~72 columns, the back half of Book V and the whole of Book VI. Chunk 0089 alone (four columns) carries ten.

⛔ It is a change of MARK, not a fall-off in quotation. My five post-0416D chunks carry at least eight quotations adduced as authorities with an attribution verb and a correct [n:] — Isa. 53:1 @0421A, 1 Cor. 13:1 @0421A, 3 Kings 8:24 @0421B, Ps. 62:7 @0424D, Eph. 5:29 @0430D, plus the Cant. lemmata — and every one of them is set in italics. The quotations did not stop; the guillemet did.

⭐⭐ And the controlled comparison sits inside this one range, five columns apart, on the same prophet.

« Plenus sum, inquit [n: (Isa. I)]. Et iterum: Laboravi sustinens (ibid). » (0416D — guilleted) Domine, ait, quis credidit auditui nostro [n: (Isa. LXIII)]? (0421A — italic)

Same author, named in Philip's frame both times (Unde per Isaiam Deus / Unde Isaias), same inquit/ait attribution shape, same [n:] apparatus, one guilleted and one not.

⭐⭐ And there is a stronger control still, on the SAME VERSE, which I record here because the merge will want the best specimen. Isa. 53:7 is printed twice in the work, forty-one columns apart, with the identical siglum:

« Oblatus est enim quia ipse voluit [n: (Isa. LIII)]; » (0399C, chunk 0089) Oblatus est, ait, quia [0440B] ipse voluit [n: (Isa. LIII)]. (0440A–B, chunk 0106)

Same verse, same words, same note, same ait-shaped attribution, adduced as proof both times — guilleted before col. 0416D, italic after. (Verified by me in the Latin twins at the coordinator's prompt; the neighbouring John 10:18 at 0440A is italic too.) Nothing about the function has changed between the two printings; only the mark has. This is §8b's shape of evidence applied to typography — the same shape as the brief's Virgil control (guilleted 0251D, bare 0385A), but with a date attached: the mark is available at 0416D and gone by 0421A.

⚠ Where exactly. The transition is inside chunk 0096, between 0416D and 0417A: eight lines after the guilleted Isaiah, John 10:33 (De bono, inquiunt, opere non lapidamus te… [n: (Joan. X)]) is already italic, and so is everything thereafter. I do not claim a clean switch-point, because narrative speech and proof-text are not the same function and 0090–0095 (another agent's) is already unguilleted; what I claim is the countable fact and its last instance.

⚑ This does not contradict brief §7 — it dates it. §7's functional division (« = a quotation adduced as an authority · italics = everything else) is an accurate description of chunks 0000–0096. From col. 0418D onward there is no division to describe: italics carry every class. The brief's two book boundaries (0246C, 0303A) genuinely carry no seam, as it says; this is not at a book boundary either — LIBER SEXTUS. is thirty-nine columns later, at 0442C. It is a change of compositor's practice that happens mid-book.

⚑ The consequence for reading, and it is the practical half. Brief §7's closing warning — "an italic run in this work is NOT evidence of a pre-seam regime; it is probably just a lemma" — is sound advice through chunk 0089 and misleading after it. From 0097 the italics carry the lemma and every adduced quotation, so the mark cannot sort them and only function can: the lemma is the verse under exposition (it opens a Caput and is re-quoted in fragments as the gloss advances); a quotation is adduced as proof and normally carries an attribution verb and an [n:]. ✅ My chunks 0097–0101 were collated on that basis — every italic run was treated as a candidate quotation and collated against the Vulgate, not assumed to be a lemma — which is how §1.6 (Isa. 53:1 Domine), §2b's 3 Kings 8:24 (Ore fronted, tuo dropped), Ps. 62:7 (agrees, siglum correct) and §4's Eph. 5:29 unquam were all found. Nothing in those five chunks was passed over as "just a lemma."

⛔ What the merge should do with it. Nothing to any chunk: every range has reproduced what is printed, which is the rule, and mine reproduces one « and one ». But §7 should be given its scope — "« » carries an adduced authority in the first 97 chunks; the work abandons the mark entirely at col. 0416D" — so that the four remaining agents (0102–0125) are not left hunting for a mark that is not there, and do not read its absence as their own error. The table above is the whole evidence and it is reproducible in one grep.

1.2 · ⭐⭐⭐ Cant. 5:9 at 0429B — Migne prints ex dilecto ONCE where the Vulgate prints it twice, and Philip collates the variant himself, in the text, and reports his manuscripts

Qualis est dilectus tuus ex dilecto, o pulcherrima mulierum: qualis est dilectus tuus, quia sic adjurasti nos? (0429B, head lemma of Caput XVI)

Vulg. Cant. 5:9: Qualis est dilectus tuus ex dilecto, o pulcherrima mulierum? qualis est dilectus tuus ex dilecto, quia sic adiurasti nos? The phrase stands in both questions. Migne's second question has lost it.

⭐⭐⭐ And the omission is not merely expounded — it is adjudicated. Philip builds his whole Christological reading of the doubled question on the asymmetry (0430B–C):

Prima enim inquisitio cum dixisset: Dilectus statim ex dilecto supponit, secunda, dilectus repetens ex dilecto juxta quosdam codices non apponit: per hoc dans intelligi Deum dignum diligi ex Patre esse nihilominus diligendo, hominem vero etsi diligi, tamen dignum esse ex homine non aequaliter amplectendo… quarum prima posuit ex dilecto, secunda voluit reticere.

— and then, extraordinarily, he reports the collation against himself:

Quod si dixerit quispiam quia illud et prima posuit, et secunda non tacuit, nolo nimis contendere, pertinaciter reluctari, quia multos inveni codices huic testimonio suffragari. Nam, etsi non omnes, quos invenire potui codices, plerique tamen ex eis, sicut in prima inquisitione, sic et secunda habent dilectus ex dilecto; neque satis compertum habeo utrum ex dilecto repetitum fuerit ab auctore, an potius scriptum vitio vel errore. (0430C)

This is a twelfth-century commentator doing textual criticism on his own Bible, naming the two readings, conceding that MOST of the codices he could find carry the phrase twice, and declining to decide whether the repetition is the author's or a scribe's error. Migne's lemma prints the minority reading — the one Philip's doctrine of the two substances requires — and the four columns of Caput XVI stand on its absence.

[var:] fired at the head lemma, naming the Vulgate's repetition and pointing at 0430B–C. It does not speculate about origin (Pattern 14) — Philip's own two sentences do that better than any note could.

⚑ For the merge, this is a member of brief §6's class with an internal witness, which none of the other four members has. Zech. 4:14, Gen. 3:19, Bethel and Eccles. 9:1 are all inferred from recurrence; here the author states the variant. ⚠ It is also the one instance in this work where a merge might reasonably demote the marker on §10.7's logic ("Migne's own [alias] bracket… the divergence is already adjudicated on the page"). I fired it anyway, and the reason is that §10.7 concerns MIGNE'S apparatus. This adjudication is Philip's, inside the body text, in the twelfth century, in Latin, sixty lines below the lemma — it is not apparatus and a reader meeting the lemma has no signal at all. Flagged so the merge can rule the class once.

⚑ The phrase recurs at 0448A (chunk 0108) — Supra enim dixerant: Qualis est dilectus ex dilecto — where the daughters recall the question. Printed once there too (and with tuus dropped). So Migne is internally consistent: two printings, both single. That is the copy-text shape.

1.3 · ⭐⭐ Cant. 5:7 at 0427A — Migne prints vigiles for the Vulgate's custodes, and Philip's cross-reference note proves it is copy-text, not a slip

Invenerunt me vigiles qui circumeunt civitatem: percusserunt me, et vulnerarunt me, tulerunt pallium meum custodes murorum. (0427A)

Vulg. Cant. 5:7: Invenerunt me custodes qui circumeunt civitatem; percusserunt me, et vulneraverunt me; tulerunt pallium meum mihi custodes murorum.

Two divergences, and the first is material:

  1. ⭐⭐ vigiles for custodes. In the Vulgate the verse uses one word twice — custodes find her, custodes murorum take her cloak. In Migne it uses two, and Philip's Caput XIV is built on the distinction. He keeps the two parties apart for two columns (vigiles five times, custodes murorum → the apostles → the walls), and closes the chapter by subordinating one to the other:

civitatem ambiunt ad custodiam fortiter expediti, si tamen a vigilibus digne fuerint custoditi. (0428B)

The keepers of the walls are themselves kept by the watchmen. On the Vulgate's text, where both are custodes, that sentence cannot be written.

  1. The Vulgate's mihi is gone — a deletion, named inside the same [var:] so it cannot be elided. Nothing turns on it (Philip supplies the dative himself at 0427D, gaudet Virgo pallium sibi tolli), but it is recorded as a deletion because §8a's John 19:39 case is exactly the shape that leaves nothing on the page to notice.

⭐⭐⭐ The proof that vigiles is copy-text and not a compositor's reach is inside the work, and Migne prints the pointer. The very next words carry [n: (sup. l. III, c. 22)] — Migne's only note in the chunk, an internal cross-reference — and Philip writes Longe retro eamdem Virginem dicti sunt vigiles invenisse. I resolved it: Book III, Caput XXII is chunk 0065, col. 0346A, and its head lemma is Cant. 3:3 — Invenerunt me vigiles qui custodiunt civitatem. vigiles is the Vulgate's own word at 3:3.

So Philip identifies the finders of Cant. 5:7 with the finders of Cant. 3:3, and the identification works because his text uses the same noun in both places. On the Vulgate they are different nouns and the cross-reference is a looser gesture. Migne's Cant. 5:7 has been conformed to Cant. 3:3 — and the exposition that follows requires exactly that conformation.

⚑ Two by-products worth the merge's ledger:

  • (sup. l. III, c. 22) is CORRECT, resolving exactly (§8b wants the right ones logged as much as the wrong). It is also the only internal cross- reference siglum this range met; it is a locator, so it stays [n:], not [nt:].
  • The lemma prints syncopated vulnerarunt while the re-quotation eleven lines later at 0427A–B prints full vulneraverunt. Migne differs from himself inside one column. No sense change; logged, no marker.

1.4 · ⭐⭐ 0418B — Jer. 6:7 quoted with only an [n:], and it IS a quotation: the range's one [n:]-only hit

Sicut enim perhibente propheta frigidam cisterna facit aquam [n: (Jer. VI)]; sic frigidam fecit malitiam suam. (0418B)

Vulg. Jer. 6:7: Sicut frigidam fecit cisterna aquam suam, sic frigidam fecit malitiam suam.

No guillemets, no italics — only the note. And unlike every other [n:]-only span this range met, this one is not Philip's prose: the whole verse is there, both limbs, and the second limb (sic frigidam fecit malitiam suam) is word for word the Vulgate and stands entirely OUTSIDE the note, unmarked in any way. Migne's note falls at the semicolon, so the extraction could only ever see the first half.

Divergences in the first limb: present facit for the Vulgate's perfect fecit, and suam dropped, with the word order rebuilt (frigidam cisterna facit aquam for frigidam fecit cisterna aquam suam). The tense-break is the interesting one — the Vulgate's parallelism is perfect/perfect, and Migne's is present/perfect, so the simile becomes a general truth rather than a matched act.

Ruling applied: logged in full, [var:] NOT fired (brief §8a — where Migne marks the words as neither quotation nor lemma we cannot establish the quotation's boundary, and here the boundary problem is visible on both edges: the left edge runs into Philip's Sicut enim perhibente propheta, and the right edge runs past the note into unmarked verbatim Vulgate). The English renders what is printed: "For as, the prophet bearing witness, a cistern maketh water cold; so hath she made her malice cold."

⭐ Reported as a hit, and it is the class's third in the whole run. The running rate before this range was 2 of 109 (see §2c). Mine is 1 of 5.

1.5 · ⭐⭐ 0416D — 1 Cor. 11:3 quoted with an explicit Paulo teste and printed bare, and it is the chapter's controlling text

Caput Christi, Paulo teste, Deus est. (0416D)

Vulg. 1 Cor. 11:3: caput vero Christi, Deus. Every printed word is Paul's (the connective vero falls away where Philip's own frame takes over, and est is supplied from the Vulgate's ellipsis). Philip names his authority — Paul bearing witness — and Migne prints the words in neither guillemets nor italics, with no [n:] of their own.

⭐ And it carries the chapter. The lemma under exposition is quia caput meum plenum est rore; the identification caput Christi = Deus is what turns the dew into the Jews' refusal of Christ's divinity, and the next four sentences are entirely about that refusal (dum Christum hominem Deum esse, Dei Filium non intelligunt), proved from John 10:33 and John 5:18. Remove the Pauline sentence and Caput VII has no hinge.

Ruling applied: logged, no marker (brief §8a). This is the class the brief describes exactly — an expounded quotation Migne leaves unmarked — and, like the Virgil at 0385A, it is adduced as an authority with an attribution formula and printed bare, which is the shape §7's counter-instances take.

⚠ On the siglum, and I record it as CORRECT rather than wrong. The nearest note is [n: (I Cor. II)], one sentence later, at the end of …friget iniquitas Judaeorum. It is tempting to read it as a corrupted XI (a lost X would give exactly II) misplaced from Paulo teste — but 1 Cor. 2:8 (quam nemo principum huius saeculi cognovit: si enim cognovissent, nunquam Dominum gloriae crucifixissent) is a genuinely apt imagery pointer for the iniquity of the Jews, which is the clause it actually stands on. I therefore record (I Cor. II) as a correct pointer and 1 Cor. 11:3 as simply unnoted, and log the numeral hypothesis here only so the merge has it. Brief §8b's warning about manufactured patterns cuts directly against counting this as an error, and (I Cor. II) is the very siglum §8b says has been vindicated twice already (0305C, 0318A).

1.6 · ⭐ 0421A — (Isa. LXIII) for Isa. 53:1, and Migne prints (Isa. LIII) correctly five times elsewhere in this same work

Domine, ait, quis credidit auditui nostro [n: (Isa. LXIII)]? (0421A)

The words are Isa. 53:1. The note says Isaiah 63.

⭐ The control is internal and needs no appeal outside the work, which is the shape brief §8b asks for:

  • (Isa. LIII) is printed and correct at 0206B (0008), 0227D (0017), 0398B (0089) and 0439D–0442B (0106) — the work knows the numeral.
  • (Isa. LXIII) is printed and correct at 0264A (0032), where it stands on Ipsius quidem pro nobis, Isaia perhibente, rubuit indumentum, et velut calcantium in torculari sorduit vestimentum — Isa. 63:2 exactly.

So Migne prints both numerals correctly elsewhere and gets this one wrong. The shape is one extra I in the numeral (LIII → LXIII) — neither of brief §8b's two attested profiles ("off by exactly one chapter"; "note cites one book, the words are another book's"). It is a third shape, and a mechanical one. Reproduced verbatim; §10.2 forbids correcting it, and a following (ibid.) does not depend on it (there is none).

⚠ Also divergent in the same span, and marked: Domine is not in Isaiah. Vulg. Isa. 53:1 reads Quis credidit auditui nostro? with no vocative; the vocative belongs to the New Testament citations of the verse (Rom. 10:16, John 12:38). Philip introduces it as Isaiah's twice over (Unde Isaias … non fidem adhibent Isaiae), so a reader sent to Isaiah 53 will not find the word. [var:] fired, naming both witnesses.

⛔ This is the one marker in my range I would most expect a merge to demote, and I say so plainly: under a strict reading of Pattern 14 ("in a way that changes the sense") an added vocative is arguably below threshold, and by that reading it should have gone in §2b with distillaverunt and annuntietis. I fired it because it is a whole word added inside a marked (italicised) quotation — so the boundary is established and the marker is safe — and because the added word is the tell that Migne's text here is the NT citation form rather than Isaiah's, which is transmission evidence of the same kind as §6's class. Reversible; the crux carries everything the marker does.

0098 (cols 0421D–0423C). ⭐⭐ Cant. 5:5b head lemma Manus meae distillaverunt myrrham, et digiti mei pleni myrrha probatissima — Vulg. manus meae stillaverunt myrrham…. Migne prints the compound; the Vulgate prints the simple verb, and it prints it in both body occurrences (the head lemma, and the re-quotation Manus, inquit, meae distillaverunt myrrham at 0421D). Logged, NO marker, and the reason is an internal control that runs against firing:

Manus ergo virginis myrrhae amaritudinem stillaverunt, cum omnes actus ejus disciplinae regulam tenuerunt… (0422A)

Philip's own gloss of the lemma, eight lines below it, uses the SIMPLE verb — the Vulgate's. So the compound is not his and nothing in the argument rests on the prefix: his contrast is tenere / habere against distillare ("not to hold but to drop"), which the simple verb serves equally, and he glosses the sending- out with derivare ad exteros, not with the prefix. ⚑ The likeliest source of the compound is inside the work: Cant. 4:11's lemma at 0391A is Favus distillans labia tua, where distillans is the Vulgate's own word, thirty columns earlier and still in the same commentary. Under Pattern 14 the sense is untouched, which is §8c's threshold exactly. ⛔ But two printings is copy-text shape, so it is logged here with all its evidence for the merge to weigh against §6's other members. The English preserves the difference visibly: distillaverunt = "dropped down", stillaverunt = "dropped", stillicidium = "a dropping" · the rest of the lemma, digiti mei pleni myrrha probatissima, agrees word for word (printed twice more: 0422C Digiti, ait, mei pleni myrrha probatissima, and the frontmatter incipit). ⚠ Both re-quotations break the italics before the possessive (Manus, inquit, meae… · Digiti, ait, mei…), giving "Hands, saith she, mine dropped down myrrh"; kept, Pattern 5, on the cruces-0084/0066 precedent.

LXII)] — agrees word for word. Siglum correct, and logged as such per brief §8b's instruction to record the right ones: (Psal. …) is a siglum this work has been seen to get wrong ((Psal. Philip introduces it as illud propheticum quod in Psalmi versiculo breviter continetur — an authority formula, and it is italic, not guilleted (§1.1).

V)] — Vulg. Nemo enim unquam carnem suam odio habuit. unquam is deleted. Nothing turns on it; logged, no marker. 2c′ · ⭐ Weaves the extractor could NOT list — 33 found on the mandatory prose pass

These carry no guillemets, no italics and no [n:], so they appear in the extraction in no class whatever. None takes a marker. The first three are the ones the merge should see.

  1. ⭐⭐ 0416D — 1 Cor. 11:3, and it is §1.5. The range's Paulo teste find. Not repeated here.
  2. ⭐⭐ 0430A — the NICENE CREED, printed bare, and it is not scripture at all.

Ille quidem ex Deo Deus, lumen de lumine, et ex carne caro est, homo de virgine. (0430A)

lumen de lumine is the Creed's own clause, verbatim, and ex Deo Deus is its Deum de Deo recast into Philip's nominative frame. It is doing creedal work: the daughters are asking how God man may be firmly believed and loved, and Philip answers with the Creed's own formula, extended by a matching pair of his own (ex carne caro… homo de virgine) — which is why the Creed's rhythm has to be audible for the extension to land. No guillemets, no italics, no [n:]. ⚠ This is the range's Virgil. Brief §8a's warning is that a prose pass scanning for scriptural cadence walks past the next unmarked authority; here the unmarked authority is a creed, which no scripture-shaped search of any kind can reach. Logged, no marker (§8a: the boundary is not printed). ⭐ For the merge: the class of unmarked adduced authorities in this work now holds Virgil (0385A), Sallust (0314A), Ovid (0259), Ambrose (0337B), Paul (0416D) and the Nicene Creed (0430A) — a poet, a historian, a poet, a Father, an apostle and a conciliar formula. There is no genre that predicts it.

  1. ⭐ 0422A — a natural-history authority reported with dicitur. Myrrha enim molles et fluxas carnes dicitur confirmare, et ne lege naturali subjaceant putredini, conservare — the standard myrrh lemma (Isidore, Etym. XVII.viii, ultimately Pliny), which Philip flags as reported speech and Migne leaves bare. Recorded as a weak member of the class: there is no verbatim source-phrase to collate, only an attributed commonplace. Same shape as cruces-0084 §2c.4's Fons a fundendo.

3c · Pattern 17

Decided by morphology throughout, never by who is addressed.

  • Singular → thou. The whole of Caput VII is the Bridegroom to the Virgin and is singular from first word to last: Aperi mihi · Tu, ait, quae… obfirmasti… confirmasti · laxa fores… sepone… evigila… audi… excute · Cum te vacare patior · ne quod prius vel amplius haurire valuisti, videaris… invidere · sicut igitur claudis… detrahe… excute · quae amica facta es… diceris et columba · ut jam macula non sit in te · Tu igitur, quae… insigniris… experiris; vocem pulsantis audi, aperi fores clausas… vide causas — some forty tokens, all thou. Likewise John 10:33 (non lapidamus te… tu homo cum sis, facis teipsum Deum), 3 Kings 8:24 (locutus es… perfecisti), Ps. 62:7 (memor fui tui… meditabor in te), and the whole of the daughters' speech to the Virgin at 0429B–0430B (Tu, aiunt, quae… novisti… videris… teneris… Dic igitur… adjurasti… quia Patrem diligis… affectas… defectas… tibi autem… dic nobis… a te volumus edoceri… cum audis… intelligas… Moveat ergo te… ut non differas… dic qualis tuus ille dilectus), ~25 tokens.
  • Plural → you. Isaiah's complaint at 0416D–0417A (me gravatis… vestrae mihi videar pravitatis… vestras iniquorum sarcinas) · Acts 4:19 (vos potius audire quam Deum, judicate) · Cant. 5:8 and the whole of Caput XV (Adjuro vos, filiae Hierusalem, si inveneritis… annuntietis · Vos, ait, qui… aestuatis… praeparatis; vos admoneo… vos adjuro · nuntiate, praedicate · si vos regis mensa susceperit · mementote mei · rogate Dominum), ~30 tokens · and Philip's own frame to his brethren twice: 0417B Videtis caput Christi and 0417D Nonne vobis illa nox videtur, plus 0424B sicut nostis.

⭐ The pair the merge should like is at 0416D–0417A, and it is two sentences long. The Bridegroom's forty singular verbs to one Virgin (Aperi mihi… vide causas) run straight into God's plural complaint to a nation, quoted from Isaiah and glossed in Philip's own words: Tanto, ait, rore… me gravatis. Under Pattern 17 the page turns from thou to you at the exact word where the addressee turns from one woman to a people, with no apparatus at all, and the Latin morphology decides it. A flat "you" would have made the whole chapter one undifferentiated address.

240 (0415D) · 241 (0417D) · 242 (0419B) · 243 (0421A) · 244 (0422C) · 245 (0424B) · 246 (0426A) · 247 (0427C) · 248 (0429B) · 249 (0430D). Continuous with cruces-0084's 223–230. Each kept italic and verbatim at the exact word it interrupts — 240 between vacare and patior, 242 between ubi and fueram, 243 between quod and nobis, 245 between retro and pellit, 247 between Virginis and digne, 249 between ex and se — and the English clause was built round each rather than moving it. ⚠ 249's slot forced "as made man out of 249 herself", and 243's "but that which 243 the voice of him that commandeth speaketh out to us"; both are more contorted than I would otherwise write, and both are deliberate.

§4 · PATTERN 7 / 8 / 9 / 10 — three [sic:], and the readings rendered as printed

The carried run is NOT also translated in the running text (brief §8's named failure — checked word by word on a separate pass, by script and by eye).

  1. ⭐ 0420C [sic: sublilem] — ad sublilem cujus tactum si quid durum fuerat, emollescit. Read subtilem, near-certain: sublilis is not a Latin word in any form, t/l is a standard Migne broken-type substitution, and subtilis is the chapter's own keyword, standing correctly five times within twenty lines on either side of it (0419D subtilem instar foraminis… intellectum · 0420A infundit subtilius · 0420B subtilior percipit intellectus · 0420B Hoc subtiliter intellecto · 0420C cum intelligentiam subtilem dederit). Pattern 7 governs: carried untranslated in italics, and the English deliberately does not also say "subtle" in that clause: it reads "at whose [sic: sublilem] touch, if aught had been hard, it groweth soft." Marker content machine-verified as a verbatim substring of the twin.
  2. 0422B [sic: assitentibus] — ut assitentibus sibi non solo prosit desiderio voluntatis. Not a Latin word. Two conjectures, both single-letter and neither decisive: assistentibus ("them that stand by" — the word Philip uses at 0391B, permittit nobis assistentibus distillare, in the same figure of the Virgin dropping sweetness to bystanders, which makes it the likelier) or assidentibus ("them that sit by"). Carried untranslated in italics; the English does not also say "them that stand by". Content verified.
  3. 0428A [sic: informen t] — ut minores quoslibet informen t ad licita, ne delinquant. Split type, Pattern 10: the final t of informent is broken off and set as its own italic run in the source. The whole broken run is carried, spacing and all, per Pattern 10's "carry the WHOLE broken run, even when one fragment is a real word." Read informent, certain: the parallel verb sollicitent governs the answering clause four words later, and informare ad licita is exactly the sense. Content verified as a substring (asterisks stripped).

Rendered as printed, no marker (real words, merely wrong or merely odd) — conjectures live here and NOT in the text:

  • ⛔ 0422B, Ah hoc enim surgit, ut ejus eruditio non haereat… Read Ad hoc, near-certain: Ah hoc enim surgit does not construe (ah takes no accusative), and Ad hoc… surgit, ut is the exact construction Philip uses at 0428A in this same range (Ad hoc quippe ad homines spiritus administratorii transmittuntur, ad hoc multa sollicitudine… enituntur; ut minores…). Ah is a real Latin word, so Pattern 12 keeps it on the English side: rendered "Ah, for to this she riseth," which is meant to read wrong. ⚠ But I flag the attribution rather than assert it. h/d is an OCR confusion far more than a typesetting one, so this may be a defect in Corpus Corporum's transcription rather than in Migne's plate. Under the standing rule I render our source and log; I do not claim the plate is defective. ⭐ The most repairable place in the range, and the one I would most want checked against a leaf render* — one letter fixes it, and a data/tei-patches/11632.json entry would be the right home if* the plate proves clean.
  • ⛔ 0419A, A quo aestu vel sudore aliquantulum respiramus, cum remoto curarum onere ad invisibilia respiramus. The same verb twice in one sentence, in two different senses ("we take breath from" / "we breathe toward"), the second governing ad invisibilia, which respirare does not take comfortably. Conjecture aspiramus ("we aspire"), probable but not certain — Philip uses precisely ad placendum sponso tendit perfectius et aspirat eleven lines later at 0420A. Not a [d:]: Pattern 11 is for a run the plate sets twice adjacently, and these are two clauses with different constructions. A real word; rendered "we take breath a little… we breathe again unto things invisible," which is meant to read flat.
  • 0422C, quidquid in eis districtius non afficit, angit severius vel angustat, suo illa consortio reddit perfectius et venustat. Elliptical and not comfortable: the three verbs share no expressed subject, only the first carries non, and the antecedent of illa is discretio six words earlier. Rendered as closely as the printed words allow — "whatsoever in them she affecteth not the more strictly, paineth the more severely or straiteneth, that same discretion by her fellowship rendereth the more perfect and adorneth" — and logged rather than emended. The single printed non is carried and none supplied.
  • 0422D, the stray comma: indiscretum et, injurium deprehendit. Preserved (Pattern 8: never delete a mark the plate prints): the English reads "she findeth it indiscreet and, injurious to stand short of them." ⚠ Do not churn this. Same call at 0423A (non probatam, sed magis, probatissimam nominavit → "not approved, but rather, most approved") and 0422D (multis, et variis negotiis · plurima, dividens prout vult singulis). Four misplaced commas in one chunk, all reproduced.
  • 0419C, si necessitas presserit voluntatem, videor aggravari. videor first person against the third-person presserit — no anacoluthon in English, which needs the subject anyway. Rendered normally.
  • 0423A, cui nostra laborantium studet conversatio sic addici. nostra… conversatio with the partitive genitive laborantium interposed; Pattern 1 does not fire (it is not a fronted partitive governing the clause), and the English promotes it: "whereto the conversation of us that labour striveth so to be given over." Logged.
  • 0425D, Virginem adhuc subditam huic necturae. Read naturae, near-certain — natura stands four times in the same sentence-pair (non vitii, sed naturae eleven words later; lege naturali; naturalem… corruptelam at 0425C). ⚠ But necturae is not a word, so Pattern 7's non-word class would ordinarily force a [sic:]. I did not mark it, and the reason is that this is a a/e single-vowel slip in a word the same sentence prints correctly twice, which reads as a transcription artifact rather than as broken type — the same judgment as the Ah hoc case above. Rendered "subject to this nature," and logged here so the call is visible and reversible. ⛔ If the merge wants a uniform rule for the Ah hoc / necturae class, these are the two sites in my range and both would take [sic:] under a stricter reading.
  • 0429B, quae aestu liquefacta ad ea quae sunt mundi transitoria penitus intorpescit. intorpescere with ad is late and unusual but attested; Pattern 9, unmarked. Rendered "groweth utterly torpid toward the transitory things of the world."
  • 0424C, Virgo quietis vernula gaudet.* vernula is a diminutive of verna*, "a little home-born slave" — attested classical Latin, unusual in this register. Pattern 9, unmarked; rendered "the home-born handmaid of quiet."
  • 0430B, quid, juxta quod dilectus appellatur, nec apponitur ex dilecto. The nec has no clean coordinate and the clause is elliptical (quid [vult sentiri] juxta quod… appellatur, nec apponitur). Rendered as printed, "and what according as he is called beloved and of the beloved is not added", with the nec carried. Logged.

detrectat… non habetur, si… non tenetur… nec summus ille judex… non ostium aperuisse… ut non pessulum ostio… non tam studii… non pessulum, sicut nostis… non ostium, sed ostii pessulum… non littera, sed spiritalis… sicut non de ligno… non admittit grossitudinem… ne volvatur… non dubium quin… desiderio, non veraci… nesciens non audire… jam non negat… non refugit obedire… necdum satis poterat… non potest inveniri… non possit comprehendi… non offensa culpabili… faciem inconcessam… neque rem auferens… nulli mortalium revelatam… nulli tamen eorum… ne liberius evolemus… non satis exstricabili… non penitus quidem obruitur… non vitii, sed naturae… mortalem oculum non admittit… ne facie videatur ad faciem… non dat id quod expetit… nondum sustinet… non perveniens… necdum bravium comprehendit), 0426C–0428B (nullis adhuc viribus, nullis meritis… non turbetur, non proferat querimoniam… nonnisi spiritalibus… necdum tamen invenitur, nec ad eum pervenit… vocare non desisto… necdum plenius dat… non respondet… vocanti non respondet… non praesentat… non me esse patitur destitutam… ne nimis… non invenio… nihil suum, nil… retinere… nescio si… ne forte sit oneri… nec tamen sufficiunt… non tam pungi graviter… nec tam perfossa… Nec sufficit semel invisere… non gravantur… ne delinquant… diu Virgini non ostendunt… non penitus voluntati… non, ut assolet… necdum pertingere… non invidens, sed adgaudens), and 0428C–0431A (ne admonitio insufficiens… ne quis praetereat… nec in oblivionem… ne de poenis meis rideat… non gigni ejus odio, sed amore… nisi Sponsum nesciens… non teneris… nullis retro saeculis… nulla mulierum sic accessit… nulla melius… penitus non emisit… non admisit… non refundere pigriteris… ne temere seducamur… non contemnere… nisi Filius, et nisi per Filium nemo vidit… penitus non invidit… nil, aut parum… non mediocriter… non semel tantum… non differas… nolo nimis contendere… non omnes… neque satis compertum habeo… nemo enim carnem suam odio habuit… non solum factum hominem… non dicunt… nec videtur… invidere).

No negation was dropped and none was supplied. ⚠ Two places were caught by this pass and would otherwise have shipped wrong:

  1. ⛔ 0430D, Eph. 5:29 — an ADDITION, not a dropped negation, and it is the Pattern 7a″ failure exactly. The draft read "for no man ever hated his own flesh." Migne prints nemo enim carnem suam odio habuit; the Vulgate's unquam is not on the page, and "ever" had arrived from the remembered verse. Fixed to "for no man hated his own flesh." Recorded per brief §8a because it is the mirror of the John 19:39 deletion: a hedge-word restored is as invisible as a hedge-word removed, the sentence reads perfectly either way, and verify-english is blind to both. ⚑ The pass that caught it is the separate word-by-word one, not the collation — I had already collated the span and written "unquam dropped" in my notes while the English still said "ever."
  2. 0420B, sine sponsi bene placito non vacantium, non laborantium est profectus. The draft rendered the two printed non with a single English "no advancement either of them that are at leisure or of them that labour" — one negation distributed over a disjunction the Latin does not print as a disjunction. Fixed to "there is no advancement of them that are at leisure, none of them that labour." Mechanism 3 (connective smoothed), the one with no lexical trace.

§5 · CONVENTIONS SET OR HELD IN THIS RANGE

  1. ⭐⭐ districtio = "strictness" · discretio = "discretion" — and discretio is NOT split when it means "separation." The whole of Caput XI is a pun held across two senses: the fingers foras tamen discreti prodeunt… eorumque discretio tam prudenti naturae artificio fabricatur (0422C, the anatomical sense) becomes, four words later, virtus recte accipitur discretiva — the virtue of discretion. English "discretion" carries both senses and the pun survives; "distinction" for the first would sever it. This is the Song section's case 2 (stylus/epistylium, murenulae/ferculum) applied to a pun rather than an etymology. Held with severitas = "severity" and moderatio = "moderation" kept separate, since 0422C sets all four in one sentence (discreta moderatio, vel moderata discretio). ⛔ This is the one cross-chunk decision in my range the merge must not undo; districtio/discretio recur through 0098 twenty-two times.
  2. ⭐ probata / probabilis / probatissima = "approved" / "approvable" / "most approved", against Douay's "choicest". Forced by 0423A, where Philip builds the argument on the degree: non probatam, sed magis, probatissimam nominavit · Probabilis vero vel probata illa congrue potest dici · Probata est quae… Probatissima vero est quae… Douay's "choicest" has no positive or comparative in English and the four-term chain would collapse. Cant. 5:5's lemma therefore reads "the most approved myrrh."
  3. ⭐ vigiles = "watchmen" · custodes = "keepers" — kept strictly distinct, and it is load-bearing (§1.3). "Watchmen" is already the work's English for vigiles (21 instances, set at 0346A on Cant. 3:3), so this range inherits rather than sets it; what is new is that the same verse now carries both words and the English must show it. custodes murorum = "the keepers of the walls"; custodia = "guard"/"keeping". ⛔ Do not harmonize.
  4. otium = "leisure" · negotium = "business" — held, matching the work's 37 / 22 existing instances. The pair is the axis of Caput VIII–XII and appears sixteen times in this range. The Latin's neg-otium etymology has no English exponent and nothing in the argument turns on it.
  5. distillare = "drop down" · stillare = "drop" · stillicidium = "a dropping" — set here so that Migne's lemma and Philip's gloss of it remain visibly different words on the English page (see §2b, 0098). Consistent with 0086's "dropping honeycomb" for Cant. 4:11's distillans. annuntiare = "announce" · nuntiare = "tell", on the same principle (0101).
  6. ⚠ stratum = "bed" — flagged, because brief §5's ruled triple has no fourth term. Ps. 62:7's super stratum meum (0424D, and glossed at 0424D–0425A, Stratum, quietem vocat) needs a plain English noun, and Douay's is "bed" — but §5 assigns "bed" to lectus, "little bed" to lectulus and "couch" to cubile. ⚑ None of those three occurs anywhere in this range, so nothing collides on the page; but a merge enforcing the triple work-wide should know that stratum is a fifth word with no slot left, and that "bed" is what I used. Reversible in one line. (cubiculum = "chamber" and thalamus = "bridal chamber" are held from cruces-0084 §5.5; conclave at 0420D = "inner room".)
  7. pessulum = "bolt" · sera = "lock" · vectis = "bar" — three fastening-words in one sentence at 0416B (detrahe vectem, seram excute) and the whole of Caput XII on the bolt. Kept distinct, per Douay for pessulum.
  8. venter = "belly", not Douay's "bowels" (0420A lemma), because the gloss at 0420B is a simile on the organ (molle redditur, quasi venter). Logged as a judgment call, reversible.
  9. pallium = "cloak" (0427A), matching the work's five existing instances, against Douay's "veil" at Cant. 5:7.
  10. filiae Hierusalem = "daughters of Jerusalem". ⚠ The work is split — 16 "Jerusalem" against 7 "Hierusalem" in the shipped English — and I followed the majority. Offered to the merge as a one-line sweep, since Cant. 5:8 puts the phrase in a head lemma and it recurs through Book VI.
  11. charitas = charity · dilectio = love — held, per brief §5. The pressure point in this range is 0430A–D, where dilectio and diligere run fourteen times against Cant. 5:9's dilectus ("beloved"); rendered "love" / "to love" / "beloved" respectively, with charitas reserved (0416B vinculo charitatis = "the bond of charity" · 0418B quos nectit charitas = "whom charity knitteth" · 0429A charitatis recolens vulneratae = "calling to mind a wounded charity" · 0428B charitatis indissolubili firmamento).

Philip of Harvengt, Commentaria in Cantica canticorum, PL 203. Six chunks, 5,606 Latin words, covering Caput XVII–XXVII of Book V and closing it — the head-to-foot descriptio of the Bridegroom, Cant. 5:10–16: Dilectus meus candidus et rubicundus → Caput ejus aurum optimum → Oculi ejus sicut columbae → Genae illius sicut areolae aromatum → Labia ejus lilia → Manus ejus tornatiles → Venter ejus eburneus → Crura illius columnae marmoreae → Species ejus ut Libani → Guttur illius suavissimum → Talis est dilectus meus. Chunk 0107 ends with Philip's own ut hic tandem liber quintus finem sibi gaudeat obtinere and the bare head LIBER SEXTUS.

⚠ A correction of record the merge needs: this is BOOK V, and cruces-0084 is wrong to call chunks 0084–0089 Book V. LIBER QUINTUS. stands in the heads[] of chunk 0091 (col. ~0404), so 0068–0090 are Book IV and 0091–0107 are Book V — which Philip's own closing sentence at 0446A confirms. Chapter numbering agrees: 0084–0089 run Caput XXI–XXVII of Book IV, and my XVII–XXVII are Book V's. The two ranges therefore both contain a Caput XXI–XXVII and they are different chapters. Nothing in either translation depends on it; the range headers do.

⚑ GUILLEMETS: this range has NONE — zero « and zero » in 5,606 words. That is not an accident of my six chunks and it is §1.1 below, the range's largest finding.

§1 · ⭐⭐ THE THREE FINDINGS THE MERGE SHOULD CARRY

1.1 · ⭐⭐⭐ THE GUILLEMETS STOP. Migne's « » practice ceases at col. 0417A and never resumes for the remaining 73 columns of the work — and the seam is NOT a book boundary

Brief §7 says: "If you nonetheless meet a genuine change of practice at an Explicit/Incipit, report it as an exception with the column named." This is that exception, and it is not at an Explicit.

The measurement, taken over all 126 Latin chunks by script:

After col. 0417A there is not one « or » in 29 chunks and 73 columns.

⛔ And the vacuum is not because the adduced authorities stop. They continue at undiminished density and are printed in italics instead. My own six chunks carry seven of them, every one with an explicit attribution formula and a [n:] note — precisely the class brief §7 assigns to « »:

The same is true of the chunks between the seam and mine: chunk 0093 alone prints Luke 12:19, Prov. 9:5, Matt. 10:37, 1 Cor. 2:2 and Isa. 55:1 with ait / inquit and correct notes, all italic, none guillemeted.

⭐ The internal control is exact, and it is a verse this work has already tested. Isa. 53:7 is printed twice. At 0399C (cruces-0084 §2b) it is « Oblatus est enim quia ipse voluit [n: (Isa. LIII)]; » — guillemeted. At 0440A–B it is Oblatus est, ait, quia ipse voluit [n: (Isa. LIII)] — italic. Same verse, same siglum, forty-one columns apart, two treatments. This is Virgil-at-0251D-vs-0385A applied to a scriptural proof-text, and it converts a distributional observation into a controlled comparison.

⚑ Two secondary observations that make the finding sharper, not weaker:

  1. The seam is not a book boundary. LIBER QUINTUS. stands at chunk 0091 and LIBER SEXTUS. at 0446A; the last guillemet falls at 0417A, mid-Caput VII of Book V, twenty-nine columns from either. This strengthens brief §7's settled ruling that 11632's book boundaries carry no seam — the one real change of practice in the work ignores them too.
  2. The last surviving instance is a transitional hybrid. 0416D–0417A prints « » wrapping italics (« Plenus sum, inquit… Laboravi sustinens »), which is the only such nesting in the work. It reads as the compositor's last use of a mark he is abandoning.

⭐⭐ What the merge must revise. Brief §7 warns: "an italic run in this work is NOT evidence of a pre-seam regime — it is probably just a lemma." That is true of chunks 0000–0089 and false from ~0090 onward. In the last 36 chunks an italic run is routinely an adduced proof-text, because there is nothing else it can be. Any later range that assumes "italic ⇒ lemma" will mis-class every quotation it meets. No single range could see this — it is exactly the shape brief §6's "grep the other 125 chunks" note describes, and it cost one script run.

⚠ This changes nothing about what we print. Reproduce the plate; do not supply guillemets to the later chunks, and do not read the absence of a « as evidence that a run is not a quotation.

1.2 · ⭐⭐ Cant. 5:12 at 0434D — the lemma has LOST the word its own chapter expounds, and Philip's gloss contradicts the lemma four times

Migne prints the running lemma of Caput XIX as:

Oculi ejus sicut columbae super rivos aquarum, quae factae sunt lotae, et resident juxta fluenta plenissima. (0434D)

Vulg. Cant. 5:12: Oculi eius sicut columbae super rivulos aquarum, quae lacte sunt lotae, et resident iuxta fluenta plenissima.

Two divergences, and the second is the finding. lacte has become factae, which as printed barely construes ("which have been made washed") and drops the milk — and the milk is the whole second half of the chapter. Philip glosses it back in, four separate times, inside three columns:

Quod autem columbae perhibentur, non aquis, sed potius lacte lotae, innuit quod longius a columbis materialibus sunt remotae (0435D) non aquis lotae, sed lacte potius referuntur, quia lacti nivalis candor naturaliter assignatur, in quo gratiae columbinae munda simplicitas designatur (0436B) secundoque profectu velut candore lacteo nos emundat (0436D) vel lavacro uti lacteo memorantur (0437A)

The gloss quotes the lemma's own word four times and the lemma does not contain it. The argument — dove-simplicity, snowy whiteness, milk as the mark that these are not material doves — has nothing to stand on in the verse as printed.

⭐ The companion divergence supplies an internal control on the same line. The lemma prints rivos; twelve lines later Philip writes non solum super aquas, sed super rivulos sunt aquarum (0436A) and then builds on instar rivuli non constare (0436B). So on both halves of the lemma the plate's exposition carries the Vulgate reading and the plate's lemma does not.

[var:] FIRED, immediately after the lemma, naming the witness and giving both Vulgate words with a gloss (Pattern 14). ⚠ The marker is available here and was not at the §8a cases, because Migne italicises this run: it is marked as a quotation, so its boundary is printed and a [var:] asserts nothing the plate does not. That is the same distinction brief §8b drew for Isa. 42 at 0318D. The English renders what is printed — "which have been made washed" — and is meant to read wrong.

⚑ On rivos/rivulos alone I would not have fired: a diminutive lost is sub-threshold under Pattern 14, and Philip himself writes rivos once in his own prose at 0435D. It rides inside the marker because it sits in the same six words and eliding it would have been the §8-warned "a [var:] must not elide the divergence it exists to report" in reverse. The marker's assertion is lacte.

⛔ This is the most repairable place in the range. One letter restores the Vulgate, the sentence improves, and four columns of exposition quietly lose their subject.

1.3 · ⭐⭐ Ps. 44:3 — nine printings, four word-orders, and all three that carry [n: (Psal. XLIV)] are non-Vulgate

At 0437B Migne prints, in italics with a note:

forma prae filiis hominum speciosus [n: (Psal. XLIV)]

Vulg. Ps. 44:3: Speciosus forma prae filiis hominum. The predicate has moved to the end. cruces-0084 §2c.3 recorded the identical transposition at 0394C, unmarked and unnoted, and correctly declined a marker. I grepped all 126 Latin chunks. The verse is printed nine times, in four** orders:

XLIV)] — 0006, 0105, 0109 — and not one of them is the Vulgate order; the only two Vulgate-order printings sit unmarked inside Philip's own sentences, where nobody was quoting. That is the opposite of what a compositor's slip predicts and the same shape brief §6 draws its inferences from.

⚑ But I did NOT fire a [var:], and I think that is right. The sense is untouched, which is Pattern 14's threshold; Philip's prose is rhymed throughout and every transposition puts speciosus into a rhyme (with fructuosus at 0437B, formosus at 0394C, luminosus at 0018), which is a sufficient and non-textual explanation; and cruces-0084 declined the marker on the same words, so firing here would put two ranges out of step on one verse. Logged, unmarked, and handed to the merge with all nine sites — this is the class that can only be ruled once, across ranges, exactly as §8c asks for Cant. 1:12.

2c · The seven adduced proof-texts — collated

  • 0436C Hab. 1:13 Mundi sunt, ait, oculi tui ne videas malum, et respicere ad iniquitatem non poteris [n: (Habac. I)]. — agrees word for word. Siglum correct. Pattern 5 ait reproduced inside the italics as printed, breaking them after Mundi sunt.
  • 0437B Ps. 44:3 — transposed; see §1.3. Siglum correct as to chapter.
  • 0438D 1 Cor. 13:1 velut aes sonans aut cymbalum tinniens [n: (I Cor. XIII)] — agrees word for word; truncated before factus sum, which Philip's own tamen replaces. Siglum correct — see §2e.
  • 0440A John 10:18 Potestatem, inquit, habeo ponendi animam meam [n: (Joan. X)]. — Vulg. 10:18 Potestatem habeo ponendi eam, the antecedent animam meam standing in v. 17 (ego pono animam meam). Philip has resolved the pronoun into its antecedent from two lines above. Sense identical; below Pattern 14's threshold. Logged, no marker. Siglum correct.
  • 0440A–B Isa. 53:7 Oblatus est, ait, quia ipse voluit [n: (Isa. LIII)]. — agrees word for word. Siglum correct. ⭐ This is §1.1's control. It also confirms cruces-0084's reading of the 0399C printing: that range found « Oblatus est enim quia ipse voluit » and judged the enim to be Philip's own connective drawn inside the guillemets. Here the same verse is quoted with no enim at all, which settles it — the enim was never part of the quotation.
  • 0440D John 1:14 Verbum caro factum [n: (Joan. I)] — Vulg. Et Verbum caro factum est. The copula is gone because Philip has made the phrase the grammatical subject of ignoravit (Quia vero Verbum caro factum culpas carnis penitus ignoravit); the participle is used substantivally, not defectively. Logged, no marker. Siglum correct.
  • 0445A Prov. 8:17 Ego, inquit, diligentes me diligo [n: (Prov. VIII)]. — agrees word for word. Siglum correct. ⚑ Prov. 8 is Wisdom speaking in the feminine; Philip attributes it to the Bridegroom and Migne's inquit is gender-neutral, so "saith he" is the printed frame's, not an interpretation supplied.

2d · The [n:]-only class — hit rate 0 of 5, and the null is real information

All five ⭐ spans were traced back to their real left edge. All five are Philip's own prose — or, in one case, not a quotation at all. None takes a marker. Listed so nobody re-opens them:

  1. 0431B, John 1:5 [n: (Joan. I)] — Candor est, inquam, lucis, lux praesens omnibus non ostensa, lucens quidem in tenebris, nec a tenebris compraehensa. Vulg. et lux in tenebris lucet, et tenebrae eam non comprehenderunt. Philip has turned both verbs into participles and inverted the agency of the second (active "the darkness did not comprehend it" → passive "not comprehended by the darkness"), which is his rhyme (ostensa / compraehensa). The clause before it, lux praesens omnibus non ostensa, is his own on John 1:9–10. Philip's prose. Siglum correct. ⚑ compraehensa is an attested medieval spelling — Pattern 9, no marker. ⚑ The same John 1:5 recurs at 0440B, again unmarked and this time unnoted: etsi non a tenebris comprehensa, tamen in tenebris lux relucet.
  2. 0431C, Zech. 3:3 [n: (cap. III)] — inopsque et invalidus, et, juxta Zachariam, sordida praeferens indumenta. Vulg. Iesus autem erat indutus vestibus sordidis. Recast into a participial phrase with a different verb and noun. Philip's prose. ⚑ The siglum is a bare chapter number, the book being carried by juxta Zachariam in the running text — the only note of that shape in the range. It is correct: Zech. 3. ⚠ And note what it is not: brief §6's attested divergence is Zech. 4:14 (duo filii olei splendoris). Zech. 4:14 does not occur in my range, and this Zech. 3 citation supplies no evidence about it either way.
  3. 0431D, 1 Cor. 3:12–15 [n: (I Cor. III)] — et cujus lignum, fenum, stipula, non lucem, sed incendium experitur, iste aurum, argentum, lapidem salvans, paria singulis remetitur. Vulg. 3:12 lists aurum, argentum, lapides pretiosos, ligna, faenum, stipulam — Philip prints the two triads in the reverse order, because his sentence needs the perishable ones first (they meet the fire) and the enduring ones second (they are saved). Six nouns verbatim, one dropped adjective (pretiosos), everything else his own. Philip's prose. Siglum correct.
  4. 0432B, Heb. 1:3 + Wisd. 7:26 [n: (Hebr. I)] — Est igitur ille splendor gloriae, figura substantiae, imago paternae Deitatis, lucis aeternae candor, divinae speculum majestatis. Philip's prose — a five-member apposition in his own sentence — but see §2e.2: the note names Hebrews and two of the five members are Wisdom's, not Paul's.
  5. 0437A, [n: (supra l. I, c. 2)] — not a scriptural quotation at all. This is Migne's own internal cross-reference to the commentary's own divisions, attached to Philip's ut longe retro dictum est. It stays [n:] (a locator, Pattern 15) and is reproduced verbatim. But it is wrong, and it is a new shape — see §2e.1.

Reported per brief §8a even though it is a null result. 0/5 here, against 0/6 for 0084–0089, 1/12 for 0060–0065, 0/20 for 0042–0047, 0/38 for 0048–0053, 0/19 for 0018–0023 and 1/14 for 0024–0029. The class's running rate across the seven ranges that have reported it is now 2 of 114.

2e · Migne's sigla — twelve checked; eleven right, and the twelfth is a new shape of error

Reproduced verbatim, none corrected (§10.2). Correct and checked against the verse each stands on: (Joan. I) Jn 1:5 @0431B and Jn 1:14 @0440D · (cap. III) Zech. 3:3 @0431C · (I Cor. III) 1 Cor 3:12–15 @0431D · (Hebr. I) Heb 1:3 @0432B · (Habac. I) Hab 1:13 @0436C · (Psal. XLIV) Ps 44:3 @0437B · (I Cor. XIII) 1 Cor 13:1 @0438D · (Joan. X) Jn 10:18 @0440A · (Isa. LIII) Isa 53:7 @0440B · (Prov. VIII) Prov 8:17 @0445A. No Ibid. occurs anywhere in the range, so §10.2's anaphora hazard does not arise.

The two entries the merge should take:

  1. ⭐⭐ 0437A [n: (supra l. I, c. 2)] — an INTERNAL cross-reference to the work's own divisions, and it names the wrong book and the wrong chapter. Philip writes in quibus, ut longe retro dictum est, pulchritudo elucet faciei — "wherein, as was said long since, the beauty of the face shineth out." The place where that was said is Book II, Caput VI (chunk 0030, col. 0256C), Philip's exposition of Cant. 1:9 Pulchrae sunt genae tuae sicut turturis:

In genis constat Virginis pulchritudinem amplius apparere… cum toti faciei candor largo munere se infundit, et rubor se in genis aspersione tenui superfundit… (0256C)

Cheeks, beauty, face, and the white-and-red — the exact back-reference. I read Book I, Caput II (chunk 0004): it contains no discussion of cheeks or of the face at all, and the word pulchritudo occurs once, in advenientis sponsi regia pulchritudo, a wholly unrelated sentence. So (supra l. I, c. 2) should be (supra l. II, c. 6).

⭐ This belongs to NEITHER of brief §8b's two shapes. It is not "off by exactly one chapter" (it is off by one book and four chapters) and it is not "note cites one book, the words are another book's" (there are no quoted words — the reference is to Philip's own earlier argument). It is a third shape: a wrong internal self-reference, and so far as I can see from the range files it is the first internal cross-reference any range has adjudicated. Whether more exist is cheap to check — the form (supra l. …, c. …) is greppable. Reproduced verbatim; §10.2 forbids correcting it, and nothing here depends on an Ibid..

  1. ⭐ 0432B [n: (Hebr. I)] — correct, and incomplete in a way worth recording. Two of the five appositional members it stands on are Wisd. 7:26, not Hebrews: lucis aeternae candor, divinae speculum majestatis against Vulg. candor est enim lucis aeternae, et speculum sine macula Dei maiestatis. Migne's note names only Hebrews. ⚑ And the Wisdom text is running the whole chapter, not just this sentence: Candor est, inquam, lucis stands at 0431B, unmarked and unnoted, and the chapter's controlling opposition (candor / rubor, whiteness / redness) is built on Wisdom's noun. I record this as a note that is correct but partial, NOT as an error** — per brief §8b's revised warning, a tally that counted it wrong would manufacture a failure out of a note that points truly at one of its two sources.

⭐ And one to log because it is RIGHT where another range found it wrong (brief §8b's explicit instruction): (I Cor. XIII) at 0438D is correct — 1 Cor. 13:1's velut aes sonans aut cymbalum tinniens, verbatim. cruces-0084 §2d.1 found the same siglum at 0388C standing over words that are Col. 3:14 (vinculum perfectionis). So (I Cor. XIII) is now attested wrong once and right once, which is the same profile brief §8b records for (Psal. XCII) at 0275B/0281A and for (I Cor. II). Three sigla in this work are now each independently attested both wrong and right. That is stronger support for §8b's "no siglum in this work is systematically wrong" than any of them alone.

2f · ⭐ Weaves the extractor could NOT list — 24 found on the mandatory prose pass

These carry no guillemets, no italics and no [n:], so they appear in the extraction in no class whatever. None takes a marker (brief §8a). The first four are the ones the merge should see, and the first of them is not scripture.

  1. ⭐⭐ 0444A — THE CHALCEDONIAN FORMULA, adduced as the standard of orthodoxy and printed completely bare. Migne prints, inside Philip's own sentence:

ubi non confusio, non conversio alterius in alteram fit naturae, sed personalis unio, virginalis in mysterio geniturae. (0444A)

This is the two-natures canon in its received Latin: Chalcedon's inconfuse, inconvertibiliter (ἀσυγχύτως, ἀτρέπτως) and the Quicunque vult's non confusione substantiae, sed unitate personae. Philip is not describing; he is invoking a formula, and the immediately preceding clause is its other half — divinitas assumens hominem nullatenus est consumpta: nec defecit, sed profecit humanitas, cum in Deum mirabiliter est assumpta, which is the creed's non conversione divinitatis in carnem, sed assumptione humanitatis in Deum. No guillemets, no italics, no [n:], no inquit. ⚠⚠ This is the range's answer to brief §8a's "DO NOT HUNT ONLY FOR BIBLE VERSES." The 0078 hit was Virgil; mine is a creed. A prose pass listening for scriptural cadence walks straight past it, because the cadence is conciliar. No marker — the boundary is unprintable and §8a's ruling governs. But the merge should note that the §8a class now has three genera: scripture, classical verse, and credal/conciliar formulae. Nothing in the run had sampled the third.

  1. ⭐⭐ 0435B — John 1:14, and Migne's DOUBLING is what the chapter is built on. Migne prints, unmarked and unnoted:

qua Verbum caro factum est plenum gratiae, plenumque veritatis. (0435B)

Vulg. John 1:14: Et Verbum caro factum est… plenum gratiae et veritatis. Migne repeats the adjective: plenum gratiae, plenumque veritatis, for the Vulgate's single plenum governing both nouns. ⭐ And that doubling is Caput XIX's entire thesis. The chapter argues that the Bridegroom's two eyes are grace and truth, two distinct luminaries: the very next sentence reads duo ista nobis luminaria superfudit; dignatusque est homo factus oculo duplici nos videre, and the chapter then spends three columns keeping them apart (Gratia quidem fuit vocatio et promissio… veritas vero fuit exhibitio). A single plenum makes one thing of grace-and-truth; the doubled plenum makes two, which is what Philip needs. The Vulgate reading would not have voided the argument, but the printed reading is the argument's own shape, and Migne marks it in no way at all. ⚑ The verse recurs at 0440D, there italicised and noted [n: (Joan. I)], and there it is truncated to Verbum caro factum with no plenum clause. So the work prints John 1:14 twice, once marked and once not, and only the unmarked printing carries the divergence. No marker, per §8a.

  1. ⭐ 0442D — Matt. 22:38–39, two verbatim clauses inside indirect discourse, and the chapter's whole argument rests on the pair. Migne prints:

in quorum altero teneri mandatum primum et maximum intellexit, in altero vero secundum et simile non neglexit. (0442D)

Vulg. Matt. 22:38–39: Hoc est maximum et primum mandatum. Secundum autem simile est huic. Both phrases verbatim (the first with its pair reversed, primum et maximum for maximum et primum); recast as accusative + infinitive under intellexit. Unmarked, unnoted. This is the proof-text for the geminae charitati on which Caput XXIV's golden bases stand — the preceding sentence is inniti visus est illi geminae charitati, quae auro pretiosior. No marker.

  1. ⭐ 0444A and 0444B — 1 Pet. 1:12, printed twice, and it carries the lemma's own gloss. cui, quod angeli desiderant, jam conceditur experiri (0444A) and Quod si angeli desiderant Deum quem incessabiliter contemplantur (0444B). Vulg. in quem desiderant angeli prospicere. Two words, but they are the two the chapter turns on: the lemma is totus desiderabilis, and Philip's proof that the Bridegroom is desirable is that the angels desire him (digne et homines eumdem totum et desiderant… toto desiderio totum desiderabilem amplexantur). Unmarked, unnoted. No marker.

The remaining twenty, checked for silent conformation and left as Philip's own prose (none marked, none conformed):

Rendered "black" / "blackness" / "grow black" throughout · 1 Cor. 11:3 (Caput igitur Christi, 0432D). 0104 — Isa. 12:3 (haurientes in gaudio de fontibus Salvatoris, 0436A — Vulg. Haurietis aquas in gaudio de fontibus Salvatoris, verbatim but for the participle and the dropped object) · 1 Cor. 7:31 (figura mundi praeterit, 0436B — Vulg. praeterit enim figura huius mundi, verbatim) · Gen. 1:31 (facta vidit omnia valde bona, 0434D) · Gen. 3:8–10 (sub arbore… sub ficu… auditam vocem timet, ob recentem ignominiam nuditatis, 0435A) · James 2:13 (judicio misericordiam superferret, 0435B). 0105 — Eph. 2:14 (interjectam maceriam solvens, terrenis coelestia sociavit, 0437D — Vulg. medium parietem maceriae solvens; the distinctive noun survives) · 1 Cor. 15:53–54 (abscondens, imo absorbens quod mortale fuerat, immortali gloria nos praecingit, 0439C) · Rom. 8:29 / Phil. 3:21 (nostra corpora suo Sponsus corpori configurat, 0439C) · Isa. 9:2 / Matt. 4:16 (cum sol respexit tenebras et in umbra sedentibus lux advenit, 0438D) · 2 Cor. 6:2 (quod accepto tempore supervenit, 0438D) · 1 Cor. 12:4–11 (Pater simul et Spiritus dicuntur operari, 0438A). 0106 — ⭐ Matt. 12:41–42 (plus quam Jonam vel Salomonem eburnea fortitudine hominem se commendat, 0442B — Vulg. ecce plus quam Iona hic… ecce plus quam Salomon hic; the Vulgate's own order is kept, and it is the chapter's closing proof, printed bare) · Eph. 2:3 (naturam dignam irae, 0441B) · Luke 1:34–35 (viri nesciam de sancto eam constat Spiritu concepisse, 0441A) · John 2:9 and Matt. 14:20 / 15:38 (aquam in vinum… transmutavit, quod pane raro multa hominum millia satiavit, 0442A). 0107 — Ps. 83:8 (de virtute provehatur in virtutem, 0443B — Vulg. ibunt de virtute in virtutem) · 1 Tim. 2:4 (per quem salvus fieri valeat omnis homo, 0444B) · Rom. 5:19 (sicut homo hominum fuit praecipitatio vel ruina, 0444B) · Phil. 2:7 (est homo indutus formam hominis, 0444B) · 3 Reg. 5:6–6:9 (quam prudenti consilio Salomon sibi voluit adhibere, cum vel domum sibi, vel promissum Domino templum studuit exhibere, 0443B — narrated in his own words, no phrase reproduced).

2g · Brief §8c and §6 — what this range does and does not witness

  • Cant. 2:17 (Bethel/Bether) does not occur.
