§3 · TYPOGRAPHY

3a · Guillemets — none, and see §1.1

0 « and 0 » in all six chunks, matching the Latin twins exactly. Pattern 6's parity check passes trivially; all quotation marks on the English pages of this range are ours (" ") or none at all, and every proof-text is carried by Migne's italics. There is no asymmetry to mirror because there is no mark.

3b · §7a mirroring — the drift point — held word by word

Migne's mixed case runs through this range and none of it was regularized. Diffed mechanically against the Latin twins after drafting; I would check it first in any review.

  • ⭐ Chunk 0105 is the specimen, and both cases sit inside single paragraphs. Thirteen spouse-words in 1,011 words, six capital and seven lower-case, and the shipped English mirrors each one in order — verified by an ordered positional diff, not by eye: 0437A Sponsi→Bridegroom · 0437B Sponsi→Bridegroom [see §3b′] · 0437D sponsi→bridegroom · 0437D sponsum→bridegroom · 0438B sponsi→ bridegroom · 0438B sponsus→bridegroom · 0438C Sponsi→Bridegroom · 0438D Sponsi→Bridegroom · 0438D Sponsi→Bridegroom · 0439A sponsi→ bridegroom · 0439A sponsus→bridegroom · 0439B sponsi→bridegroom · 0439C Sponsus→Bridegroom. ⚑ Note 0438B–0438C, where four lower-case instances are followed immediately by three capitals with no change of subject, and 0437A–0437B, where two capitals open a paragraph whose remainder is entirely lower-case.
  • Chunk 0107, seven spouse-words, four lower-case and three capital, mirrored in order: 0442B Sponsi→Bridegroom · 0443A sponsum→bridegroom · 0443B sponsi→bridegroom · 0443C sponsus→bridegroom · 0443C sponsum→bridegroom · 0443D sponsi→bridegroom · 0445A Sponsi→Bridegroom. ⭐ Note 0443C, where sponsus Virginis is lower-case eleven words after capital Virginis in the same clause — the two words are cased independently, in the same breath.
  • Chunks 0104 and 0106 capitalize throughout (6 and 4 instances, all Sponsi / Sponsus), and 0102–0103 contain none at all. Recorded so the merge can see there is nothing to reconcile in those four.
  • Virgo is capital at every one of its 18 occurrences in the range and there is not one lower-case virgo; the sole lower-case form is the adjective virginalis (0444A), rendered "virginal". So the virgo/Virgo alternation cruces-0084 recorded at 0395A–0396C does not continue into Book V's close.
  • Spiritus is capital at all six occurrences (0437D, 0438A, 0441A ×2, 0441B ×2) and the only lower-case form is the adjective spirituali (0438D). The Spiritus sanctus / sancti Spiritus order does not arise — Philip writes sancto… Spiritu and sanctus ei Spiritus and eorum Spiritus, never the fixed pair, so brief §7a's worked example has no instance here.
  • Pattern 3 fires eight times, and TWICE on the bare form brief §5 flags. 0436A continentiam Scripturarum → "the content of the Scriptures" · 0436B Scripturarum speculum → "the mirror of the Scriptures" · 0436D plenissima fluenta Scripturarum → "the fullest streams of the Scriptures" · 0436C Scripturas evangelicas → "the Scriptures of the Gospel" · 0436C Scripturae propheticae → "the prophetic Scriptures" · 0436D Scripturis veteribus → "the old Scriptures" and evangelicis → "the Scriptures of the Gospel" · ⚑ 0438C nonnunquam in Scripturis efficiens ponitur pro effectu → "sometimes in the Scriptures the efficient is put for the effect" — no divina, no sacra, the exact bare form 11638's sweep missed · 0441C quae hujusmodi pertulisse illum Scriptura memoravit → "such things as Scripture hath recorded him to have borne", the canon in the singular with no adjective, a ninth and slightly different bare form. No divina Scriptura or sacra Scriptura occurs in the range at all, so every instance here is of the bare type.
  • Heads: CAPUT XVII. through CAPUT XXVII. all carry the full stop and all are numerals, matching cruces-0060's and cruces-0084's ranges and contrasting cruces-0048's stop-less pair. LIBER SEXTUS. likewise carries the stop.

3b′ · ⚠ The one mirroring slip caught on the second pass, and how

0437B's Sic et Sponsi, id est ejus divina pulchritudo is capital on the plate and my draft had rendered it "the bridegroom's", lower-case, because the four lower-case instances that follow it at 0437D–0438B had set the paragraph's tone in my ear. It was caught by the ordered script diff described above and not by reading. ⛔ Recorded because brief §7a names this as the likeliest drift point across twenty-one agents and this is what the failure actually looks like: not a decision, an assimilation to the surrounding instances. The mechanical check is cheap and it is the only thing that found it. Fixed; the shipped file mirrors all thirteen.

3c · Pattern 17

Decided by morphology throughout, never by who is addressed. The range is unusually clean on this and gives the merge a usable pair.

  • Singular → thou. One instance only, and it is a quotation: Hab. 1:13 @0436C, Mundi sunt oculi tui ne videas malum, et respicere… non poteris → "Thy eyes are clean, that thou mayest not behold evil, and thou canst not look upon iniquity."
  • Plural → you. All eleven remaining second persons, and every one of them is the Virgin addressing the filiae Hierusalem: 0431A notitiam acquisistis… jam sollicite requisistis · 0432B vobisque… digne requirentibus vult largiri, quibus non invideo… gaudeo vos efficaciter erudiri · 0444D ut ipse quem diligo, vobis aliquatenus innotescat, et in amorem ejus vester quoque animus incalescat · 0445A Vos igitur filiae Hierusalem hunc amare et amari ab illo totis viribus laborate.
  • ⭐ The pair the merge should like is at 0436C–0445A, and it is the widest one the work has produced: the Virgin's whole peroration is plural — she is speaking to a company and the vocative filiae Hierusalem says so — while the single scriptural quotation embedded in the same book is singular, God to the prophet. Under Pattern 17 a reader sees the address change number without apparatus and without ever meeting an archaism in Philip's own voice. Under a flat "thou" the daughters would become one woman; under a flat "you" the Habacuc verse loses the prophet.

3d · Marginal source-edition numbers

250 (0432C) · 251 (0434B) · 252 (0435D) · 253 (0437C) · 254 (0439B) · 255 (0441A) · 256 (0442D) · 257 (0444B). Continuous with cruces-0084's 223–230 (which ended at 0399A), so the 0090–0101 range carries 231–249. Each kept italic and verbatim at the exact word it interrupts, with the English clause built around it rather than moving it: 252 falls between ratio non and admittit, 253 between Nulla and quippe areola, 254 between parum and quid rubeum, 255 between penitus and expedire, 256 between si and quod bene videtur, 257 between non solum and quia homo. ⚠ 253's and 254's slots forced "For no 253 bed is set by a hand so prudent" and "in the midst whereof somewhat 254 a little red is found"; both are more contorted than I would otherwise write, and both are deliberate.

3e · ⚑ An anchor observation NOT reported as a defect (brief §10.1)

Chunk 0107 runs …exspectat [0446A] responsa filiarum… and ends at 0446A; chunk 0108's colFirst is 0445A, so the column sequence across our chunk boundary reads …0445A, 0446A ‖ 0445A, 0445B…

I am recording this and NOT reporting it. Brief §10.1 names recurring column numbers and non-monotonic band marks as the phantom-gap class, examined 49 times corpus-wide with none real, and states that the only real signal is text broken mid-word or mid-construction across an anchor. There is none: exspectat [0446A] responsa filiarum construes perfectly across the mark, and 0108 opens a fresh sentence at 0445B. No [ed:], no patch, no plate check. Noted only so a later reader can see the check was made rather than skipped.

§4 · PATTERN 7 / 8 / 9 / 10 — no [sic:], and the readings rendered as printed

No type in these six chunks is a non-word, so Pattern 12 fires nowhere; every odd reading below is a real Latin word merely wrong or merely odd, which Pattern 12's own boundary clause keeps on the English side. Conjectures live here and NOT in the text.

  • ⛔ 0431B, lux candorem nivem supergressa. Two bare accusatives in apposition where the sense wants a comparison; read candore nivem supergressa ("having surpassed snow in whiteness") or candorem nivis, neither certain. As printed the clause says "a light that hath gone beyond whiteness, snow", and that is how it is rendered. Both candidates are single-letter changes and I decline to pick one in the text. ⚠ The most repairable sentence in the range after §1.2.
  • ⛔ 0441C, Remora igitur necessitate apud nos generaliter coactiva, sua usus est voluntate potentialiter effectiva. Read Remota, probable: the sentence needs necessity to be taken away from Christ, which is exactly what the preceding clause says (legem nobis insitam vi quadam ingenita potentialiter supergressus) and what the following one says (potuit non sufferre molestias, neque laedi). But remora is a real Latin noun, so Pattern 12 keeps it on the English side: rendered "Necessity therefore being a delay generally compulsive among us, he used his own will, powerfully effective", taking Remora as an ablative in apposition to necessitate. It construes and it is flat. Not emended. ⚑ The one place in the range where I would most welcome a second opinion, and it is the same call shape cruces-0084 §4 made for relectio at 0390B.
  • ⛔ 0440A, in praeferendo, non ut videbatur defectus fuit virium, sed potestas. Read perferendo ("in bearing them through"), probable: the clause it depends on is pertulit et molestas, with per- in the verb, and praeferre ("to carry in front, to prefer") makes no sense of enduring troubles. A real word; rendered "in the bringing of them forward", which is meant to read flat. Not supplied.
  • ⛔ 0439B, ut vitare valeat praesentiam penitus ustionem. Two accusatives again; read praesentem… ustionem ("the present burning"), which the antithesis requires — praesentia stands against futuram gloriam four lines later, and the whole lily gloss is present-red against future-white. As printed the clause reads "avoid the presence, the burning, utterly", and that is how it is rendered.
  • 0441A, the misplaced full stop: Quam legem dure insitam. Virgo sola concipiens creditur non sensisse. Migne breaks a single sentence between its object and its verb, and the following word is a proper name so the capital tells us nothing. Preserved (Pattern 8: never delete a mark the plate prints): the English reads "Which law, harshly implanted. The Virgin alone in conceiving is believed not to have felt, forasmuch as…", deliberately as broken as the plate. ⚠ Do not churn this.
  • 0435C, the missing full stop: meritorum praemiis non coronat Vidit ergo nos gratia. The inverse defect, twelve columns earlier: a sentence ends and the next begins with a capital and no stop at all. Preserved: "…crowneth none with the rewards of deserts but the deserving Therefore he saw us with grace…". Same call cruces-0084 §4 made for inquam favus at 0391C and cruces-0060 for Domine, ait si tu sustulisti at 0335A. ⚑ Worth recording together with the 0441A case: this range has one supernumerary stop and one missing stop, six columns apart, and both are inside the same argument.
  • 0439A, the missing stop before ut justus: sint non immemores aeternorum ut justus quisque sic manus inserat. A third instance of the same class in the same chunk-pair. Preserved.
  • 0437A, ad genas, quos a laudandi merito nequaquam judicat alienas. Masculine relative for feminine genas, with the feminine alienas two words later proving the gender. ⚑ Pattern 9, and it is the clean case: English "which" carries no gender, so there is no emendation to make and none to undo. Rendered normally. Logged and marked here so a later sweep does not churn it.
  • 0432D, in unam personam habent duplex natura convenire. Singular subject, plural verb. English can show it ("a twofold nature have to come together") and it is so rendered; Pattern 9, no marker.
  • 0434A, elatis palmarum proceris et rutilantibus similis gaudent esse. Singular similis with a plural subject. No English exponent — "like" is numberless. Pattern 9, rendered normally, logged.
  • 0432C, ex infinite omnium numero. Adverb where an adjective (infinito) is expected. No English exponent for the part-of-speech slip; rendered "out of the infinite number of them all". Pattern 9, logged, no marker.
  • 0431B compraehensa · 0441D agritudo · 0433D ramusculi. Attested medieval spellings (ae/e interchange in both directions); Pattern 9 exempts them explicitly. Translated normally, no italics, no crux beyond this line. ⚠ Recorded only because comprehensa stands correctly at 0440B and aegritudo nowhere, which makes the first look like a defect at first sight.
  • 0437B, Sic et Sponsi, id est ejus divina pulchritudo, in qua nihil inquinatum… A genitive with no governing noun and a sentence with no main verb — the whole period is an anacoluthon depending on sunt hortuli two sentences back. Rendered as closely as the printed words allow ("So also is the Bridegroom's, that is, his divine beauty, wherein is nothing defiled…") and logged rather than repaired.
  • 0441A, Quod vitium quae transitio, quae velut altera jam natura… ventrem omnium … infirmat. Three nominative relatives resumed by nothing, then a singular verb. Rendered literally ("Which vice, which passing over, which now as it were a second nature… weakeneth the belly of all"), logged; the same Latin anacoluthon class cruces-0084 §4 recorded for Quos… nos at 0388D.
  • 0440D, quia modum et ordinem ejus, quam si noverat geniturae, non laeserat mollities. quam si will not construe; quam sic or quam ipsa are both possible and neither is certain. Rendered as closely as the words allow — "the manner and the order of that begetting, such as she had known it" — and logged, not emended.

Negation audit (brief §9), second pass, against the Latin. Every printed non / nec / neque / nisi / nihil / nil / nullus / nunquam / nondum / necdum / nescire / nequaquam / nequire / nonnisi / nullatenus / ne in the six Latin chunks was extracted by script after the prose was drafted and matched one by one against the English. Totals: 0102 30 · 0103 23 · 0104 36 · 0105 35 · 0106 44 · 0107 55 — 223 in all. The dense clusters are 0431C–0432B (non decor illi maneat, non aspectus… mens non caligat, non hebet intellectus… de culpa nil praesumere nisi poenam… non sordet… nec est culpae laesio… Nec solum genae… non nisi gratia… non sustinet, si non misericordia praevenitur… non lucem, sed incendium… non ab aliquo facile potest sciri, nisi cui… quibus non invideo… nulla respersus macula… non desinit… non gigas potentior, non quisquam illi similis), 0433B–0434C (promotum illuminat, non consumit… non decalvat turpitudo, calvities indecens non deturpat… non quibusvis arboribus… non declinant… non ostendunt… non admittit… non aufert praesentiam sed promittit… non solum homines… non incongrue… nec nisi per alterum caret fine, non comparatur… non derogat, non detrahit… non coronae), 0435A–0436D (qui non fuerant… non deesse… nec superba caderent pravitate, ut cadere jam non possent… non respexit… gradum stabilem non accepit… nonnisi immeritis merita prima donat, et item nisi meritos… non coronat… nonnisi gratis… nec est satis utile… veritas non respondet… non invidet… durius nos non vident… non rapinam meditantur… non aquis, sed potius lacte lotae… usus vel ratio non admittit… non solum super aquas… non cessant… nihil stare sinit… non aquis lotae… non noceat, et nos velit alteri non nocere… ne videas malum… non poteris… eligant non videre… non possunt intuitum retorquere… Quis istos non commendet… mala nostra nesciens… non frivolum, sed utile, non superfluum), 0437A–0439C (nequaquam judicat alienas… nil omnino comparandum… non auro, non argento, non hujusmodi… nihil inquinatum, nulla indecens turpitudo… immortalitas finem nescit… non civibus, sed virtutibus… non invalida, non inutilis… Nulla quippe areola… non quisquam pigmentarius… non contrivit… non homo, non angelus praevaleret… Nec alii pigmentarii… nonnisi Filius incarnari… non caret intellectu… nisi ore et labiis… non venimus… non dolum, non fallaciam, non noverunt utique falsitatem… tempus nondum gratiae… non invenit… non immemores aeternorum… non remordet… non excedunt… nec est tam felix quispiam… non vacillat), 0439D–0442B (nondum natus… nil obesse… nihil torno facilius… relabi nesciens in defectum… non angeli, non hominis, non est cujuslibet… non homo simpliciter… non natura… non plumbum, non stannum… etsi non a tenebris comprehensa… non apparens… non tenentur… non solum aureas… Nihil enim aliud… nonnisi ad coelestia bona tendit… non naturae vitio… non carneum appellavit… creditur non sensisse… viri nesciam… non praevenit… non pervenit… non solum nihil intulit detrimenti… vitio non carnalis… non culpae, sed culparum merito… non defectu virium… nihil horum, nisi quia, quando, quantum… potuit non sufferre molestias, neque laedi… non solum indutus… motus nescit… non uratur… nihilominus adhibere… ne plus vel minus valeant… Neque enim vel humana semper), and *0442C–0445A (viandi nescios… non incongrue… nulli dubium… super basim solidam non fundatur… commendabiles non negantur… creditur non coactus… non neglexit… nulli sanctorum… nescit uri vitiis… defectus nesciens repentinos… nesciens culpa laedi… nihil penitus operetur, quod non hujus benevolentia… nequit stare, si… non munitur… non ruinam invenit, nullum sustinet detrimentum… non tam suavior… ne, si minus dictum… dulcedo suavior, suavitas dulcior non habetur… nihil subtilius, nihil mirabilius, nil suavius… nullatenus est consumpta: nec defecit… non confusio, non conversio… non angustat… nec est alius praeter ipsum… non solum quia Deus, non solum quia homo… non qualis alias quivis homo… non totum desideret, non totum diligat, non totum admiretur… non quaerat studiosius, non teneat avidius… non studeat… nescit aemulam, vel pellicem non veretur… non vult caeteris invidere… non sum deceptorie circumventa, nec amor intemperans… non laudavit… necdum tamen valeo… necdum satis congrue sunt expressa… Nec enim potest diligi, si non fuerit intellectus, nec videtur intelligi si non fuerit et dilectus… nihil sanctius… nihil beatius quam ab illo diligi qui nescit non diligere* diligentem).

No negation was dropped and none was supplied. ⚠ Two places were caught by this pass and would otherwise have shipped weakened:

  1. 0434C, nec nisi per alterum caret fine. The draft had rendered the pair idiomatically as "and lacketh an end only through another", which is defensible English for non nisi but leaves neither particle visible. Rewritten to "and lacketh not an end save through another" — the standard nisi → "save" mapping the corpus already uses, with the nec carried. This is the shape of mechanism 3 (connective smoothed), which the audit note in Pattern 7a says leaves no lexical trace at all; here it left one only because the Latin was in front of me.
  2. 0444C, quis talem non quaerat studiosius, non teneat avidius… et alios ad quaerendum non studeat erudire? The draft had let a single "would not" distribute across all three verbs — grammatical in English, but two of the three printed nons were then invisible. Rewritten so each verb carries its own: "would not seek… would not hold… would not be zealous to instruct."

⭐ And one place where the double negation was deliberately kept, because it is the range's best sentence: 0445A ab illo diligi qui nescit non diligere diligentem → "to be loved by him who knoweth not how not to love him that loveth." An English ear wants "who cannot but love"; that would drop one of two printed negations and flatten the figure Philip is closing his book with.

§5 · CONVENTIONS SET OR HELD IN THIS RANGE

  1. ⭐⭐ elatae palmarum (Cant. 5:11) IS translated — "the raised boughs of palm trees" — against Douay's "branches of palm trees", and Caput XVIII depends on it. This is the vermiculatas argento call, not the muraenula call: English has the exponent, so italic Latin is not available. Philip's whole gloss is the participle. Elatae vero illi palmarum esse ramusculi perhibentur, qui in altum prae caeteris procera rectitudine promoventur (0433C) · Sic virtutes coelorum in altum prae caeteris sunt elatae (0433C) · ad intuendam cujus faciem semper erigere se festinant (0433D) · quasi triumphantes elatam palmae gestare gratulantur (0433D) · palmarum, ut jam dictum est, similes sunt elatis (0434B) · elatis palmarum proceris… similes (0434A). Six occurrences of the root across one chapter, and every one is the argument: raised bough → raised on high → the angels lift themselves → they bear the raised bough in triumph. "Branches of palm trees" is botanical and severs the chain exactly as "thy plants" severed emissio. ⛔ This is the one cross-chunk decision in my range the merge must not undo, and the lemma does not recur after 0434C, so it is a closed set.
  2. ⭐ distinctus/distinguitur/distinctio (Cant. 5:14) = "distinguished", NOT Douay's "set with". Same argument, smaller: Venter ejus eburneus, distinctus sapphiris (0440D) → sapphiris… est distinctus (0441D) → venter eburneus… distinguitur sapphiris (0442B) → sed operandi seriem distinctionis gratia decorari (0442B). Philip's closing move in Caput XXIII is that God's works are distinguished — set apart from one another in a series — and "set with sapphires" makes the last sentence explain nothing. The lemma does not recur after 0442B.
  3. ⭐ electus = "chosen" everywhere, at both lemmata, against Douay's "excellent" at Cant. 5:15. electus ex millibus (Cant. 5:10, 0431A) and electus ut cedri (Cant. 5:15, 0443A) are the same word and Philip glosses both with the verb: solus ille sit electus ad ministerium offerendi… iste singulariter est electus (0432C) and Quem nimirum Deus Pater elegit… Propter quod electus est ut in aedificio collocetur (0443B–C). One English word, both places. Douay's "excellent as the cedars" would have broken the second chapter's whole argument from election.
  4. The taste-words split, and the split is forced by one chiasmus. suavis = sweet · dulcis = delightful / delightfulness. Set at 0443D–0444A, where Migne prints dulcedo suavior, suavitas dulcior non habetur — a chiasmus that collapses into "no sweetness is sweeter, no sweetness more sweet" under any single equivalent. "Sweet" is kept for the lemma word (suavissimum, suavior, suavitas, suavius — five occurrences) and dulcis takes the second slot. Logged as a judgment call, reversible, and flagged as the one I am least sure of* — a merge that prefers "sweet" for dulcis must change suavis* everywhere, including the printed lemma.
  5. species takes a THIRD sense here, extending cruces-0084 §5.3. That range split it "spice" (aromatic catalogue) / "kind" (garden). This range adds "fairness" for the Cant. 5:15 lemma Species ejus ut Libani (0443A) and for laudari digna est facies merito speciei (0437A) — the face's beauty, which is speciosus = "fair" territory (cruces-0084 §5.2) and not spice or kind. ⚠ And "spice" also occurs in this range, four times in 0105's perfumer passage (multimodis divites speciebus 0437B · herbas sive species non contrivit 0437D · salutis species collegerunt 0438A · aromaticas species attulerunt 0438B), so both senses stand within six columns. The word has three English exponents in this work and no single one; logged so a merge sweep does not flatten them.
  6. charitas = charity — held, and the range is thin on the pressure point. Two instances only: 0437C ardet praesentia charitatis → "the presence of charity burneth" and 0442D inniti visus est illi geminae charitati → "that twin charity", which is the same phrase cruces-0084 §5.6 recorded at 0400B and is rendered identically. No dilectio occurs in the range, so the doublet is not tested here.
  7. ⭐ amicus meus (Cant. 5:16) = "my friend" — the masculine counterpart of brief §5's ruled amica mea, and it is confirmed by the same mechanism. Migne prints ipse est amicus meus, filiae Hierusalem at 0444C and Philip glosses it in his own voice at 0445A: quem fieri et amicum vere diligentibus intellexi. §5's ruling was proved from John 15:14's amici mei; this lemma is the word in the masculine, in the same book, glossed the same way. "My beloved" is already taken by dilectus meus in the same verse — Talis est dilectus meus, et ipse est amicus meus — so the two must differ in English, which is the §5 argument in miniature. Offered to the merge as the completion of that rule, not a new one.
  8. Beauty-words: cruces-0084 §5.2's set held unchanged. formosus = comely · speciosus = fair · pulcher = beautiful · decor = comeliness. All four are live in this range (0431C non decor illi maneat · 0437A pulchritudo elucet faciei · 0437B forma prae filiis hominum speciosus · 0434A comarum pulchritudo), and formosus does not occur. Nothing to reconcile.
  9. The colour triple held: niger = black throughout 0103, candor = whiteness, rubor = redness. fuscus occurs nowhere in the range, so brief §5's "fusca is never black" rule is untested here. ⚑ candidus at 0431A/0432B is rendered "white" (the Cant. 5:10 lemma candidus et rubicundus), and candidatio does not occur — but brief §5's ruling that candidatio is translated governs the same field and is consistent with this.
  10. Bed- and chamber-words: none occur in this range, so brief §5's cubile = "couch" ruling and cruces-0060's lectulus/lectus pair are untouched. thalamus does not occur either, so cruces-0084 §5.5's open question is not advanced.

Philip of Harvengt, Commentaria in Cantica canticorum, PL 203. Six chunks, 5,444 Latin words, opening Book VI and running Caput I–XII of it — Cant. 6:1–11: Quo abiit dilectus tuus → Dilectus meus descendit in hortum suum → Ego dilecto meo → Pulchra es, amica mea → Averte oculos tuos a me → Capilli tui sicut grex caprarum → Sexaginta sunt reginae → Una est columba mea → Viderunt illam filiae Sion → Quae est ista quae progreditur → Descendi in hortum nucum → Nescivi: anima mea conturbata est. LIBER SEXTUS. stands at the end of chunk 0107 with no text under it (cruces-0102 §3e); CAPUT PRIMUM. at 0445B is the book's first head, so this range opens Book VI.

§1 · ⭐⭐ THE FINDINGS THE MERGE SHOULD CARRY

1.1 · ⭐⭐⭐ Cant. 6:8b at 0454B — Migne ADDS Sion to the lemma, and Philip's very next clause expounds the added word

Viderunt illam, filiae Sion, et beatissimam praedicaverunt: reginae et concubinae, et laudaverunt eam. (0454B, head lemma of Caput IX)

Vulg. Cant. 6:8: Viderunt eam filiae, et beatissimam praedicaverunt; reginae et concubinae, et laudaverunt eam. The Vulgate's filiae is bare — no place-name anywhere in the verse.

⭐⭐ And the addition is load-bearing in the first six words of the exposition. Philip's opening sentence is:

Filiae Sion supra filiae Hierusalem appellantur, quae Virginem, ut ante dictum est, in hoc epithalamio comitantur… (0454B)

— "The daughters of Sion are above called the daughters of Jerusalem." His whole first paragraph is an identification of two named groups, and it identifies a name the Vulgate's lemma does not contain. On the Vulgate text the sentence has nothing to identify: filiae and filiae Hierusalem are not two names. He then keeps the added name in play twice more (hanc attollunt filiae Sion, et beatissimam praedicant confidenter, 0454C).

[var:] FIRED at the lemma, naming both readings. The marker is available because Migne italicises the run — the quotation's boundary is printed, so the marker asserts nothing the plate does not (the same distinction cruces-0102 §1.2 drew, and the reason §8a's unmarked class takes no marker).

⚑ The companion divergence rides inside the same marker and is not elided: Migne prints illam for the Vulgate's eam in the first clause while keeping eam in the last (laudaverunt eam), so the verse uses two pronouns where the Vulgate uses one. Sense untouched; it is inside the marker only because it sits in the same six words.

⚑ Copy-text shape, and the evidence is in the plate. Viderunt illam is printed three times — the chunk's incipit, the lemma at 0454B, and the forward citation De qua subditur: Viderunt illam, etc. at 0454A (chunk 0111) — and never Viderunt eam. And filiae Sion is a phrase this work prints elsewhere in its own right: at 0073 it is the head lemma of Cant. 3:11 (Egredimini, filiae Sion) and at 0023 in Philip's prose. So the Song supplies the name twenty-eight columns earlier, and the natural mechanism is conformation to Cant. 3:11 — exactly the shape of §6's Cant. 5:7 vigiles/custodes case, where Migne's 5:7 was conformed to 3:3. Two members of that shape are now attested in Book V–VI alone.

1.2 · ⭐⭐ Cant. 6:8a at 0451D — matri suae (dative) for the Vulgate's matris suae (genitive), printed four times, and the whole chapter is built on the dative

Una est columba mea, perfecta mea; una est matri suae, electa genitrici suae. (0451D)

Vulg. Cant. 6:8: …una est matris suae, electa genetrici suae.

One letter, and it changes the construction: the Vulgate's genitive says she is the one of her mother (the mother's only child, the Hebrew sense); Migne's dative says she is one unto her mother. Philip reads the dative and builds on it. The phrase is printed four times in the chunk, always dative:

colprinted
0451Duna est matri suae (head lemma)
0452BHaec igitur matri suae una est, et in hac excellentia singularis
0452DUna est igitur matri suae, quia mater gratia, nec primam visa est habere similem nec secundam
0452Dsicut una matri suae, sic et genitrici electa perhibetur

⭐ And the mother he means is gratia, not Anne — quia mater gratia (0452D), quae tam digne, quae tam recte, quam ipsa gratia praedicatur (0452C). That reading needs the dative: grace is the one to whom the Virgin is one and for whom she is unique, and the four columns of Caput VIII run una uni jungitur → in amorem unius… collecta → unitatis hujus merito… perfecta. The genitive would make the sentence a statement about parentage, which is not what he expounds.

⚑ The work knows the genitive. matris suae is printed correctly at 0020 and 0120 — in Philip's own prose, on other verses. So the form is available to the compositor and does not appear at this verse.

[var:] FIRED at the lemma (italicised, boundary printed). ⚠ This is the marker in my range a merge is likeliest to weigh again, and I say so plainly: one letter, and the English "one unto her mother" / "the one of her mother" is a small shift. I fired it because it is a change of case, not of orthography, because it is printed four times, and because §7a mechanism 5 (reference or agency mis-bound) is precisely the class no negation-aware check can see.

1.3 · ⭐⭐ Cant. 6:11 at 0457D — conturbata est (passive) for the Vulgate's conturbavit me (active), and Philip's gloss carries BOTH readings

Nescivi: anima mea conturbata est propter quadrigas Aminadab. (0457D)

Vulg. Cant. 6:11: Nescivi: anima mea conturbavit me propter quadrigas Aminadab. The Vulgate makes the soul the agent troubling the speaker; Migne's passive makes the soul the patient.

The gloss is the interesting part, and it runs both ways inside one column:

  • passive, twice — sum turbata, expavi, obstupui (0458A) · Virgo prius nescia conturbatur (0458D, the chapter's closing sentence)
  • active, once, and it is the Vulgate's own construction — labore salutifero deficiens, vel magis, proficiens me turbavit (0458B)

⭐ So at 0458B Philip writes me turbavit for a soul that troubles her, which is the reading his own lemma does not print. [var:] FIRED (the lemma is italicised), and the crux records the internal control that runs against firing, exactly as cruces-0096 §2b did for distillaverunt: the Vulgate reading survives in the exposition. I fired anyway because unlike distillaverunt (compound for simple, sense untouched) this is a change of voice and of agency, which is Pattern 14's own threshold.

1.4 · ⭐⭐ Exod. 3 at 0456B — the note says Exodus and the words are Acts 7:34's, verbatim

Videns vidi, inquit, afflictionem populi mei, et descendi liberare eos [n: (Exod. III)]. (0456B)

  • Vulg. Exod. 3:7–8: Vidi afflictionem populi mei in Aegypto… et sciens dolorem eius, descendi ut liberarem eum de manibus Aegyptiorum.
  • Vulg. Acts 7:34: Videns vidi afflictionem populi mei qui est in Aegypto, et gemitum eorum audivi, et descendi liberare eos.

Every printed word is Acts 7:34's, including the two things Exodus does not have: the LXX Hebraism Videns vidi (ἰδὼν εἶδον) and the bare infinitive with a plural object, liberare eos, against Exodus' ut liberarem eum. Philip frames it as God's own act in Aegypto and Migne's note names Exodus.

[var:] FIRED — the span is italicised, so the boundary is printed. This is brief §8b's second attested shape ("note cites one book, the words are another book's"), and it is now the fourth instance of it (Luke 9/Matt. 8; Deut. 32/Ps. 91; Isa. 42/Matt. 12 at 0318D; this). ⚑ It is also the cleanest of the four, because the Old Testament verse it names and the New Testament verse it prints are the same verse quoted twice in the canon — so nothing here depends on our judgment of what Philip "meant". The two Latin texts are simply different, and the plate prints one under the other's name.

1.5 · ⭐⭐ 0445B [n: (l. IV, c. 10-12)] — a second wrong internal self-reference, and both known instances are off by exactly ONE BOOK

Philip writes:

Cui cum pessulum ostii sui festinaret Virgo superius [n: (l. IV, c. 10-12)] aperire; sperans eum, cujus vocem pulsantis audierat in januis, propius invenire: Ille, inquit, declinaverat atque transierat. (0445B)

That is Cant. 5:6, and the place it was expounded is Book V, Caput XII–XIII — chunk 0099, col. 0423D, whose head lemma is Pessulum ostii mei aperui dilecto meo: at ille declinaverat, atque transierat, continuing into chunk 0100. (l. IV, c. 10-12) resolves instead to chunks 0076–0077 (Book IV Caput X–XII, cols 0369D–0374A), whose lemmata are Cant. 4:3–4 — Sicut vitta coccinea labia tua and Sicut fragmen mali Punici — no bolt, no door, nothing that turns aside.

⭐⭐ The merge should put this beside cruces-0102 §2e.1. That range found (supra l. I, c. 2) at 0437A pointing where Book II, Caput VI was meant, and called it a third shape — a wrong internal self-reference, the first such adjudicated. Mine is the second, and the two agree on their book error:

colprintedresolves tobook errorchapter error
0437A(supra l. I, c. 2)l. II, c. 6−1 book−4
0445B(l. IV, c. 10-12)l. V, c. 12–13−1 book−2

Both name the book immediately before the right one. Two instances is not a profile, but it is the shape §8b asks ranges to log, and it is the sort of thing only the merge can rule on. ⚑ And the class is not uniformly wrong — three internal cross-references are now attested correct: (sup. l. III, c. 22) @0427A (cruces-0096 §1.3) and both of mine, §1.6 below. So the running tally for (l. …, c. …) is 3 right, 2 wrong, and the two wrong ones are the two that are off by a book.

Reproduced verbatim; §10.2 forbids correcting it, and no Ibid. depends on it (there is none in the range).

1.6 · ⭐ The two internal cross-references that are RIGHT — logged because §8b asks for those too

  • 0449D [n: (l. IV, c. 8)], on Cujusmodi laudes, quia supra… fere verbis eisdem sunt positae. Book IV Caput VIII is chunk 0075, whose incipit is Capilli tui sicut grex caprarum, quae ascenderunt de [monte Galaad] — the very praises being repeated at 0449D. Exactly right, and Philip's own fere verbis eisdem ("in wellnigh the same words") is vindicated by the plate: see §2b's apparuerunt/ascenderunt note.
  • 0453B [n: (l. II, c. 13)], on De quibus, quia loqui longe supra invenior distulisse, cum in secundo libro primum columbas ad medium videtur hoc epithalamium protulisse. Book II Caput XIII is chunk 0036, col. 0274D, whose lemma is Cant. 1:14 Ecce tu pulchra es, amica mea… oculi tui columbarum — the Song's first mention of doves, exactly as Philip says. And chunk 0036 carries septem, septenario, septempliciter, columbina, naturas: the deferred promise is where he says it is. Exactly right, in both the book and the chapter, across a 179-column back-reference.

⭐ Both of these are harder to get right than the two that are wrong — one reaches back 179 columns and lands on the correct chapter of the correct book. That is a strong argument against reading the two failures as a systematic defect, and it is the same correction §8b already applied to (I Cor. II).

§2 · THE COLLATION — all 59 listed spans, plus 26 found on the prose pass

Every span in data/quotations/11632/0108-0113.md was collated word by word against the Vulgate. Spans recorded as AGREES were collated and found to agree; the absence of a marker on them is a finding, not a silence.

  • 0445B Cant. 6:1a Quo abiit dilectus tuus, o pulcherrima mulierum, quo declinavit dilectus tuus, et quaeremus eum tecum. — agrees word for word. ⚑ Migne prints a comma where the Vulgate has the first ? and a full stop where it has the second; preserved (Pattern 8), so the English lemma is not a question.

VI.] is reproduced verbatim inside the italic run, per the [CAP. V.]/[CANT. I.] precedent (cruces-0090 §, cruces-0072, cruces-0036).

Sicut cortex mali Punici, ita genae tuae absque occultis tuis. — agrees word for word except the last connective. Vulg. Cant. 6:6: Sicut cortex mali punici, sic genae tuae, absque occultis tuis. ⭐ ita is Cant. 4:3's word, and this work prints Cant. 4:3 with it: chunk 0077's head lemma is Sicut fragmen mali Punici, ita genae tuae, absque eo quod intrinsecus latet. 2c · The adduced proof-texts — collated, and this is where §7c bites

Ten italicised runs in this range are proof-texts, not lemmata. Under the pre-0090 regime every one of them would have been guillemeted; here there is no mark but the italics, so each was collated on function alone.

I confirm the reading exactly and follow that range in declining a marker: the sense is untouched, Philip's rhyme is a sufficient non-textual explanation (hominum / relucescit / contemplatur), and firing here would put two ranges out of step on one verse. ⚑ But my printing is the third of the three that carry [n: (Psal. XLIV)], and cruces-0102's observation now stands complete: not one of the three noted printings is the Vulgate order, while both Vulgate-order printings are unnoted prose.** The merge has all nine sites and can rule the class once.

All seven ⭐ spans were traced back to their real left edge. None is a quotation with divergences; three are not quotations at all but Migne's own internal cross-references. None takes a marker. Listed so nobody re-opens them:

XII)] — qui Sponsi, vel filii digne fecerit voluntatem; ille frater hujus, et soror, et mater merebitur appellari, sicut ipse idem invenitur in Evangelio protestari. Vulg. Quicumque enim fecerit voluntatem Patris mei… ipse meus frater, et soror, et mater est. Reported per brief §8a even though it is a null result. 0/7 here, against 0/5 for 0102–0107, 1/5 for 0096–0101, 0/6 for 0084–0089, 1/12 for 0060–0065, 0/20 for 0042–0047, 0/38 for 0048–0053, 0/19 for 0018–0023 and 1/14 for 0024–0029. The class's running rate across the nine ranges that have reported it is now 3 of 126.

⚑ A shape worth the merge's notice: three of my seven are internal cross-references, not scripture at all. No earlier range reports more than one. Book VI opens by looking backwards — Philip is closing promises made in Books II and IV — and that is why the class is loaded with locators here. It is also why the class's "hit rate" understates its value in this range: two of the three locators had never been resolved, and one of them is §1.5.

2e · ⭐ Weaves the extractor could NOT list — 26 found on the mandatory prose pass

These carry no guillemets, no italics and no [n:], so they appear in the extraction in no class whatever. None takes a marker (brief §8a). The first four are the ones the merge should see, and the first of them is not scripture.

  1. ⭐⭐⭐ 0447D — HORACE, and this is brief §7b's own internal control, verified in place. Migne prints, run into Philip's sentence:

Virgo autem recte Sponsum diligens, non novit invidere majus quo nec Siculi, juxta quemdam ethnicum, tormentum invenere. (0447D)

Horace, Epist. I.ii.58–59: Invidia Siculi non invenere tyranni / maius tormentum. Printed bare — no guillemets, no italics, no [n:] — and adduced with an explicit attribution formula (juxta quemdam ethnicum). ⭐ Brief §7b names this column as half of the display-rule proof, against the displayed and italicised printing of the same line at chunk 0022 (Invidia, inquit, Siculi non invenere tyranni / Tormentum majus.). I confirm the reading word for word at the column named, which is the half of the control that had not been checked inside a translated range. No marker (§8a). ⚑ Note that Philip has recast it into a comparative relative (majus quo… invenere) round his own non novit invidere, so the only verbatim run is Siculi… tormentum invenere — which is why the scripture-shaped search of §8a's warning walks past it twice over.

  1. ⭐⭐ 0451A — BOETHIUS, displayed on four lines and italicised, with NO note and NO name, and it is the second half of §7b's rule. Migne prints:

Gaudia, inquit, pelle, Pelle timorem, Spemque fugato, Nec dolor adsit.

Boethius, De consolatione I, m. vii.25–28: Gaudia pelle, / pelle timorem / spemque fugato / nec dolor adsit. — agrees word for word. Introduced only as prudens ille philosophus, and carrying an inquit. ⭐⭐ This is the strongest single confirmation of §7b any range can supply, because both variables sit four lines apart in one chunk: the same author quotes a pagan poet twice within 0109–0110, once run-in and bare (Horace, 0447D) and once displayed and italicised (Boethius, 0451A). Same book, same page-run, same function, two treatments, and the discriminator is display. ⚑ And it adds a datum §7b did not have: a displayed quotation is italicised even when it carries no note and names no author. The italics are doing the work of the guillemets that are no longer available (§7c), on a quotation the apparatus does not identify at all. ⚑ Rendered as four italic lines with the Pattern 5 inquit kept inside the first — "Joys, saith he, drive away, / Drive away fear, / And put hope to flight, / Nor let grief be present."

  1. ⭐⭐ 0458D — Dan. 7:10, verbatim, unmarked and unnoted, and it is the chapter's closing image. Migne prints:

cum introducta in ejus sanctuarium ministrantia ei millia millium admiratur. (0458D)

Vulg. Dan. 7:10: millia millium ministrabant ei, et decies millies centena millia assistebant ei. Three words verbatim with the finite verb turned into a participle. This is what the Virgin is troubled by — the quadrigae Aminadab of the lemma are resolved into the angelic host, and the sentence that says so is the chapter's last. No guillemets, no italics, no [n:], no inquit*. No marker (§8a: the boundary is not printed).

  1. ⭐ 0454D–0455A — 2 Tim. 3:5, and it is the DEFINITION of the concubines. Migne prints: et multi virtutem abnegantes, pietatis specie colorati. Vulg. habentes speciem quidem pietatis, virtutem autem eius abnegantes. Four of the verse's words verbatim, in reverse order, inside Philip's own antithesis — and the whole point of Caput IX's second half is that the later concubinae are the teachers non amantes, sed amorem simulantes. Unmarked, unnoted. No marker. ⚑ In the same sentence, Matt. 24:12 with a substituted noun: apud nonnullos vero abundante malitia charitas refrigescit against Vulg. et quoniam abundavit iniquitas, refrigescet caritas multorum. The distinctive verb refrigescit survives; iniquitas has become malitia. Bare, unnoted, and therefore logged unmarked — but recorded because a substituted noun inside an otherwise verbatim run is §8a's commonest shape.

§3 · TYPOGRAPHY

3a · Guillemets — none, and §7c is confirmed a third time

0 « and 0 » in all six chunks, matching the Latin twins exactly. Pattern 6's parity check passes trivially; every quotation mark on the English pages of this range is ours (" ") or none at all, and there are in fact no " " either — every quotation Migne marks, he marks with italics, and every one is carried by italics in the English.

⭐ The range adds one thing §7c did not have: a positive account of what the italics are now doing. Ten adduced proof-texts (§2c), eleven Song lemmata (§2b), one displayed classical quotation (§2e.2), the sub-lemmata columba mea / perfecta mea discussed as words, one printed locator [CAP. VI.], one etymological spontaneus, and nine marginal source numbers — seven distinct functions, one mark. Nothing but function separates them, and the lemma/ proof-text line in particular has to be drawn by asking is this the verse under exposition, or is it adduced? — never by the mark. Chunk 0109 is the specimen: its three italic runs at 0448B–0448D are a lemma-fragment, a Psalm proof-text and a Genesis proof-text, and they look identical on the page.

3b · §7a mirroring — the drift point — held word by word

Migne's mixed case was diffed mechanically against the Latin twins after drafting, as an ordered positional string, not by eye. All six chunks match 1:1.

  • ⭐⭐ Chunk 0113 is the specimen of the range, and it is the cleanest spouse-word alternation the work has produced: six capitals followed by five lower-case, with no change of subject and no chapter boundary between them. In order: 0456A Sponsus → Bridegroom · 0456C Sponsam → Bride · 0456C Sponsus → Bridegroom · 0457A Sponso → Bridegroom · 0457A Sponsus → Bridegroom · 0457A Sponsus → Bridegroom · 0457B sponsus → bridegroom · 0457C sponsus → bridegroom · 0457D sponsus → bridegroom · 0457D sponsum → bridegroom · 0458B sponsum → bridegroom. The switch falls inside Caput XI, between videt Sponsus, et approbat (0457A) and amat sponsus nihilominus pervidere (0457B) — twelve lines apart, same paragraph, same sentence-shape, same verb of seeing. ⛔ Nothing licenses regularizing it and nothing explains it; it is mirrored.
  • Chunks 0108 (5), 0109 (9), 0110 (4), 0111 (3) and 0112 (1) capitalize every spouse-word, so there is nothing to reconcile in those five. Recorded so the merge can see the check was made.
  • Virgo is capital at every one of its 54 occurrences across the six chunks, and the sole lower-case form in the whole range is the adjective virginalem (0458A), rendered "virginal". So cruces-0102's finding that the virgo/Virgo alternation does not continue past Book IV holds through Book VI c. XII too.
  • Dilectus/dilectus: capital twice, both times sentence-initial inside a printed lemma citation (Ad haec Virgo respondet: Dilectus, etc. 0446B; [CAP. VI.] Dilectus meus descendit 0446B) and lower-case at all fourteen other occurrences. ⚠ English capitalizes sentence-initially anyway, so this particular alternation has NO English exponent and nothing was mirrored or could be. Recorded because cruces-0096 §3b reports a genuine mid-sentence Dilecti/dilectum alternation at 0428C–0429B; mine is not that, and a merge comparing the two should not read them as the same phenomenon.
  • Spiritus is capital at both its divine occurrences (0453B sanctus ei Spiritus, 0458A sanctus mihi Spiritus) with lower-case sanctus both times, and lower-case at non habui ultra spiritum (0458B, of the Virgin's own breath) and in spiritualium / spiritaliter. ⚠ The Spiritus sanctus / sancti Spiritus order does not arise — Philip writes the adjective before the noun both times with the noun's own possessor between them. English has no exponent for the lower-case sanctus: "the Holy Spirit" capitalizes regardless, so cruces-0096 §2b's ruling governs and nothing was regularized in either direction. Both are rendered "the Holy Spirit"; the lower-case spiritum is "spirit".
  • Pattern 3 fires twice, and BOTH are the bare form brief §5 flags. 0453D diligenter fluentis incumbit scripturarum → "the streams of the Scriptures" — ⚑ Migne prints it lower-case, with no divina and no sacra; and 0453D–0454A dum curam vel studium adhibet in Scripturis → "in the Scriptures", the exact bare form 11638's sweep missed and brief §5 names at 0260A. No divina Scriptura, no sacra Scriptura and no Scriptura singular occurs anywhere in the range, so both instances here are of the bare type and one of them is bare and lower-case — which is the hardest version of the form to catch by pattern-matching.
  • Heads: CAPUT PRIMUM. then CAPUT II. → CAPUT XII. continuously, every one carrying the full stop. ⭐ CAPUT PRIMUM. is rendered "CHAPTER THE FIRST." per brief §7a's ⭐ ruling of 2026-08-08 — this is Book VI's opening, the last of the work's six book-openings, and it is the first time the ruling has been applied since the sweep. The numerals that follow are kept as numerals; nothing was tidied into one style.

3b′ · ⚑ The mirroring slip that did NOT happen, and why it is worth a line

cruces-0102 §3b′ records that its one slip was an assimilation — a capital Sponsi flattened to lower case because four lower-case instances followed it — and that only the ordered script diff found it. This range presented the same trap in a worse form: 0113 runs six capitals and then five lower-case in one chapter, which is exactly the gradient that produces assimilation in either direction. The ordered diff was therefore run before the file was considered finished rather than after, and it came back clean on the first pass. ⛔ Recorded because the cheap mechanical check is the only thing that can establish this, and a range that reports "mirrored carefully" without running it has reported nothing. The check is four lines of node and it is in §3b.

3c · Pattern 17 — the range gives the merge two clean in-chunk pairs

Decided by morphology throughout, never by who is addressed.

  • ⭐ Chunk 0113 carries both numbers in one chapter, eleven lines apart. Plural: Nostis quod arcam Domini… (0458B) → "You know that the men of Azotus…" — Philip turning to his readers. Singular, inside the quotation two lines earlier: Hab. 3:8 Qui ascendis super equos tuos, et quadrigae tuae salvatio (0458B) → "Thou that ridest upon thy horses, and thy chariots are salvation". A reader sees the address change number across the quotation boundary with no apparatus.
  • ⭐ Chunk 0108 carries the reverse pair across a chapter boundary. The daughters address the Virgin as one woman throughout Caput I — quo abiit dilectus tuus · quaeremus eum tecum · Dic ergo… dic, si nosti · cujus laudes tam multimodas texuisti… tam sollicite monuisti · quam tu, quae dono gratiae illius sanctuarium introisti — thirteen singulars, all thou/thy/thee. The Virgin answers in Caput II addressing them as a company — Scire vultis · ad vestrum desiderium · cum vobis quasi esurientibus — all you/your. ⚑ This is the mirror of cruces-0102 §3c's pair, which had the Virgin plural and a quotation singular; here the number switches between two consecutive chapters of the running dialogue, and under a flat "you" the whole o pulcherrima mulierum address would collapse into the chorus that speaks it.
  • The remaining second persons are all singular and all the Bridegroom to the Virgin — the whole of Caput IV–V (0447C–0449D): Tu, ait, quae tanto aestuas… pasceris… formas… te conformas · volo tamen ut altiora te… non scruteris, neque putes · Averte oculos tuos a me · quo… attentius in lucem figis oculos inaccessam — thou throughout. Plus Luke 10:23 at 0454D, quae vos videtis, plural inside a quotation in a chunk that otherwise has no second person at all: "the eyes that see the things which you see".
  • God addressed in the singular at 0452B: licet tuis, Deus, in oculis merito non despectos → "though in thine eyes, O God, deservedly not despised" — and Ps. 138:16 in the same sentence, viderunt oculi tui → "thine eyes did see". Both singular, both thou-family, and the ruling's point is that they take it for the same reason a monk would.

3d · Marginal source-edition numbers

258 (0445D) · 259 (0447B) · 260 (0449A) · 261 (0450C) · 262 (0452A) · 263 (0454A) · 264 (0455C) · 265 (0457A) · 266 (0458D). Continuous with cruces-0102's 250–257, which ended at 0444B. Each kept italic and verbatim at the exact word it interrupts, with the English clause built around it rather than moving it: 258 between quaerentes, and errore devio; 261 between sexies deni, and sic decies seni; 263 between nondum revelata and facie contemplatur; 264 between pulchrior est quam and luna; 265 between et approbat and et facit omnia prosperari. ⚠ 263's slot forced "because him whom she loveth she contemplateth not yet with a revealed 263 face", which inverts the Latin's participle order to keep the number between the two words it actually sits between; deliberate. ⚑ 259, 260 and 266 fall at the very end of their chapters and sit at the end of the English paragraph, as printed.

3e · ⚑ An anchor observation NOT reported as a defect (brief §10.1)

Chunk 0108 opens with a bare [0445A] on its own line — chunk 0107 already ran through 0445A and ended at 0446A — and 0108 then runs …0446A, 0446B… while 0107's last anchor is 0446A. So the sequence across our chunk boundary reads …0445A, 0446A ‖ 0445A, 0445B, …0446A, 0446B…

Recorded and NOT reported. cruces-0102 §3e made the identical observation from the other side of the same boundary and cited brief §10.1; I confirm it from mine and add the only thing that would matter: there is no text broken mid-word or mid-construction. Chunk 0107 ends on a completed sentence (ut hic tandem liber quintus finem sibi gaudeat obtinere) followed by the bare head LIBER SEXTUS.; chunk 0108 opens a fresh head and a fresh lemma. No [ed:], no patch, no plate check.

§4 · PATTERN 7 / 8 / 9 / 10 — three [sic:], and the readings rendered as printed

4a · Carried type — [sic: …] fired three times

All three contents were machine-checked as verbatim substrings of their Latin twins. Conjectures live here and NOT in the text.

  1. ⭐ 0451C, [sic: a dolescentulae] — Pattern 10 split type, the clearest in the range: novitatis vel imperfectionis merito, a dolescentulae nominantur. The word is adolescentulae, and it is the lemma's own word — Cant. 6:7's adolescentularum, printed correctly four lines above at 0451B and in the head lemma at 0450B. Carried whole, spacing included, per Pattern 10's "carry the WHOLE broken run" rule, even though a is a real Latin word: the defect is the division. The crux is here; the conjecture is certain.
  2. ⭐ 0456B, [sic: invados] — a non-word: quos cum invados et rerum spiritualium inopes intellexit. Read invalidos ("weak"), which the doublet requires — it is paired with inopes ("poor") and the whole clause is about the multitudes' incapacity. Nothing else construes: invado is a verb and has no form invados in any voice. Carried into the English untranslated, in italics, under Pattern 7's non-word ruling. ⚑ Pattern 7a′ observed: the run governs an accusative-and-infinitive, and the governed clause is translated ("that they were… and poor in spiritual things"). The marker quarantines the fragment, not what it governs.
  3. ⭐ 0458B, [sic: Videos] — a non-word: Videos enim sponsum non inopem, non indigum… descendisse… non habui ultra spiritum. Read Videns, near-certain: the sentence needs a nominative participle governing descendisse / advenisse, and the Virgin is the subject of non habui. ⚠ Recorded with an internal control that makes the conjecture nearly mechanical: Videns is printed correctly at 0457D, eight lines above, in the parallel sentence Videns Virgo in hortum suum sponsum mirabiliter descendisse — same participle, same accusative, same verb, same subject. So the plate prints the word right and then prints it wrong within one column. Carried untranslated, in italics.**

4b · Real words merely wrong or merely odd — rendered, logged, not emended

  • ⛔ 0446D, quae ubera, quam mortem denique sit perpessus. Read verbera ("stripes"), probable: perpeti takes verbera naturally, the paired noun is mortem, and Stephen is contemplating quid pro salvandis salvator miserans sit aggressus — what the Saviour underwent. ubera ("paps, breasts") is a real Latin word, so Pattern 12's boundary clause keeps it on the English side: rendered "what breasts, what death at last he endured", which is meant to read wrong. Not emended. ⚠ The single most repairable place in the range, and the one I would most welcome a second opinion on — it is the same call shape cruces-0102 §4 made for Remora at 0441C.
  • ⛔ 0451C, Non sive boni sunt, qui in vasa postmodum eliguntur, sive mali qui emissi forinsecus respuuntur… cuivis hominum numerabiles non habentur. Read Nam for Non, probable: sive… sive wants a positive frame, and the sentence's own non habentur already carries the negation the sense needs. As printed there are two negations governing one predicate. Both are carried (brief §9), giving "Not whether they be good… or evil… are they held numerable by any man." It construes, it is flat, and it is deliberate. ⚑ Recorded as a candidate for the merge's polarity ledger, because a supernumerary non is the mirror of the class §9 exists to protect.
  • ⛔⛔ 0452B, quae videlicet si curam adhibeat seipsam intueri, dum vivit mortaliter perfectam audeat se fateri. This is the range's one candidate DROPPED NEGATION, and it is logged rather than repaired. The clause as printed says the Virgin would dare to confess herself perfect while she lives mortally — and the next two sentences are Phil. 3:12 and Ps. 138:16 adduced to prove the exact opposite (Quod si Paulus et David se cognoscunt veraciter imperfectos…). A vix, a non, or a rhetorical ? would each rescue it, and Migne prints none of the three. Rendered as printed — "who, to wit, if she should apply care to behold herself, might dare, while she liveth mortally, to confess herself perfect" — with the subjunctive left potential rather than smoothed into a negative. ⛔ Not emended, and the reason is Pattern 7a′ exactly: a crux that describes a repair does not make the repair honest. The merge should have it as a candidate; I decline to pick among three conjectures in the text.
  • ⛔ 0457B, quae cum novo genere tumorem ad nos protulit uterinum, longe tamen illicitae suspicionis maculam, et virus protulit serpentinum. The same verb governs two clauses with opposite senses — she brought forth the swelling of the womb, and she [put] far off the stain of suspicion. longe… protulit will bear "carried far off" only under pressure; the argument wants something like proturbavit or abstulit, and Philip's rhyme (uterinum / serpentinum) explains why the verb was not varied. Rendered as closely as the words allow — "yet far off brought forth the stain of unlawful suspicion and the serpent's venom" — and logged. ⚑ Not a [d:]: the repetition is rhetorical, not a compositor's doubling, and both occurrences are needed.
  • ⛔ 0457B, si odore florido a suis finibus omne virus noxium prohibere. The third of three si clauses under amat sponsus pervidere, and it drops into a bare infinitive where the first two have finite verbs (accelerat respondere / invenitur refulgere). An anacoluthon. Rendered literally — "whether with a flowery odour to forbid all hurtful venom from her borders" — and logged, not repaired.
  • 0448B, tanto decore conspicuat.* conspicuo* is attested but rare and is here used intransitively with an ablative of manner. Rendered "is conspicuous with so great beauty"; Pattern 9, no marker.
  • 0448C, recte, sicut Hierusalem, formoso praedicatur. Masculine (or neuter) ablative where the subject is the feminine Virgin; the parallel clauses round it are all feminine. ⚑ Pattern 9's clean case: English carries no gender on "comely", so there is no emendation to make and none to undo. Rendered normally. Logged and marked here so a later sweep does not churn it.
  • 0450C, the misplaced full stop: qui juxta legis formam disponit quidquid temporaliter operatur. is profecto digne in sexagenario continetur. Migne breaks a relative clause from its apodosis and the following word is lower-case. Preserved in both respects (Pattern 8, and brief §5's ruling that Migne's lower-case after a misplaced stop STANDS): the English reads "…whatsoever he worketh in time. he assuredly is worthily contained in the number sixty". ⚠ Do not churn this; cruces-0102 §4 preserved the identical shape at 0441A.
  • 0453C, the missing full stop: Alienos pullos nutrit columba Virgo quidem in hujus vitae salo animum retinet tam serenum. The inverse defect, and it falls at the head of one of the seven dove-properties, where the other six all carry their stop (Columba felle caret. · Non rostro lacerat columba. · Columba secus fluenta libenter habitat. · Meliora grana eligit columba. · Columba libenter in petra nidificat. · Columba pro cantu gemit.). Preserved: "The dove nourisheth another's young The Virgin indeed keepeth…" ⚑ Recorded with its six controls, because a stop missing from one member of a seven-member parallel series is as close to a demonstrable plate defect as Pattern 8 cases get — and it is still not emended.
  • 0451B, non est forma dilectionis geminam invenire. A nominative forma with an accusative attribute geminam, under an impersonal non est… invenire. Read formam. Rendered "it is not possible to find the twofold form of love"; the case slip has no English exponent (English nouns carry no case), Pattern 9, logged, no marker.
  • 0451B, nulli quidem hominum, Deo soli potius numerosa. numerosus ("numerous") where the sense wants numerabilis ("numerable") — and numerabiles is printed correctly eight lines later at 0451C. A real word merely wrong; rendered "numerous indeed unto no man, but rather unto God alone"**, which is meant to read slightly off. Not emended.
  • 0446C representat · 0453A praecognitae · 0447C similandi · 0455D incoepto. Attested medieval spellings and formations (ae/e interchange, similare for simulare, incoeptum for inceptum); Pattern 9 exempts them explicitly. Translated normally, no italics, no crux beyond this line. ⚠ Recorded only because simulantes stands correctly at 0454D, eight columns from similandi, which makes the first look like a defect at first sight.

4c · ⭐ One editorial judgment I want the merge to see: castra left in italic Latin at 0449A

quia et angelos caro vel carnis copula nunquam laedit, et remotis a complexu domestico castris, castitas nomen dedit. (0449A)

This is an etymology: castra ("camp") from castitas ("chastity"), the standard patristic derivation, and Philip makes it the hinge on which the lemma's terribilis ut castrorum acies becomes a statement about the Virgin's virginity. English shares no root. Rendered "chastity gave its name unto the castra, the camps that are removed from the household embrace" — the Latin noun shown once, italic, with its English gloss beside it, so that the inference is available to a reader who cannot see the Latin column.

⚑ Why this and not the muraenula treatment. castra is translated "camps" at all nine of its other occurrences in the range, including the lemma itself, because there the word is doing no etymological work. Leaving it Latin throughout would make the lemma unreadable; leaving it English throughout makes one sentence explain nothing. This follows translation-style.md's Song ruling case 2 (stylus/epistylium, murenulae/ferculum) rather than brief §5's blanket-italic list. It is the reason 0109's asterisk count runs +2 against its twin, and it is reversible in one edit if the merge prefers uniform English.

4d · Negation audit (brief §9), run as a separate pass AFTER the prose was drafted

Every printed non / nec / neque / nisi / nihil / nil / nullus / nunquam / nondum / necdum / nescire / nequaquam / nullatenus / nonnisi / ne in the six Latin chunks was extracted by script after drafting and matched one by one against the English. Totals: 0108 21 · 0109 53 · 0110 18 · 0111 40 · 0112 24 · 0113 50 — 206 in all.

⛔ The pass found four of my own defects, and every one was an OMISSION of a printed word, not an addition. Recorded rather than quietly fixed, because brief §8a's whole argument is that this pass earns its cost:

  1. 0108 @0445B — necdum sinit ad liquidum se videri had been drafted "he suffereth not himself to be seen clearly". necdum is "not yet", and the whole clause is about a deferral, not a refusal. Fixed to "not himself as yet to be seen clearly".
  2. 0108 @0446B — cum necdum penitus ad vestrum desiderium se inclinat, the same word, the same loss, eleven lines later. Fixed.
  3. 0109 @0449C — quod affectant necdum penitus apprehendunt drafted as "and yet do not fully apprehend", where "and yet" was carrying tamen and necdum had vanished. Fixed to "do not as yet fully apprehend". ⚑ Three instances of one word, in one range. necdum is the range's characteristic particle (10 occurrences) and it is the easiest of the whole list to lose, because English "not yet" splits and the "not" alone reads complete. A merge sweeping this work for dropped negations should grep necdum and nondum first.
  4. 0111 @0454A — nihil Virgo meritis, nihil suae detrahit sanctitati, nihil ei… unitati nil subtrahit columbae gemitus. Four negations and I had written three, having collapsed nihil ei… unitati and nil subtrahit into one English clause. Fixed to carry all four; the sentence is clumsier for it and correctly so.

No negation appears in the English that the Latin does not print. The two places where that was a live risk are §4b's Non sive boni sunt (where the temptation is to drop the supernumerary Non and read Nam) and §4b's audeat se fateri (where the temptation is to supply the missing one). Both are rendered exactly as printed.

4e · ⭐ The conformation audit, run against my OWN English (brief §8a's ⭐ instruction)

Every quotation in §2b and §2c was re-read against the plate after the collation was written, on the ground that cruces-0096 §2b's Eph. 5:29 case proves the two acts come apart. One real trap and two near ones:

  • ⛔ Phil. 3:12 @0452B — the trap, and it was defused before drafting, not after. Migne prints Non quia jam acceperim… aut perfectus sim; the Vulgate and every English have aut iam perfectus sim, "or were already perfect". The English says "or am perfect". Checked twice, on the plate both times.
  • Exod. 33:20 @0449C — the remembered English is "For man shall not see me, and live"; Migne prints neither the enim nor that word order. The English mirrors the printed order (Non me… videbit homo) and carries no for.
  • Cant. 6:9 @0455A — Douay gives "Who is she that cometh forth as the morning rising fair as the moon, bright as the sun"; Migne prints electa ut sol, and Philip's exposition turns on election (ad hoc divinitus est electa, 0455D). The English reads "chosen as the sun" and the chapter is coherent because of it.

Philip of Harvengt, Commentaria in Cantica canticorum, PL 203. Six chunks, 6,459 Latin words, covering Caput XIII–XXXII of Book VI — the Bridegroom's foot-to-head descriptio of the Bride, Cant. 6:12–7:13, answering the Bride's head-to-foot descriptio of him in Book V (chunks 0102–0107). The range runs: Revertere, revertere, Sunamitis → Quid videbis in Sunamite → Quam pulchri sunt gressus tui → Junctura feminum → Umbilicus tuus → Venter tuus → Duo ubera tua / collum tuum sicut turris eburnea → Oculi tui sicut piscinae in Hesebon → Nasus tuus sicut turris Libani → Caput tuum ut Carmelus → Quam pulchra es → Dixi: Ascendam in palmam → Guttur tuum → Dignum Dilecto meo → Ego dilecto meo → Veni, dilecte mi → Mane surgamus ad vineas → Ibi dabo tibi ubera mea → Mandragorae dederunt odorem → Omnia poma nova et vetera.

⚑ Book VI is confirmed from inside the range, not inferred: at 0461A Philip writes Ipsa autem Virgo in praecedenti libro of the Cant. 5:10–16 descriptio, and Migne's note there is [n: (l. V a c. 18 ad 27)] — which is cruces-0102's Book V, chunks 0102–0107. So 0114–0119 are Book VI, Caput XIII–XXXII.

§1 · ⭐⭐ THE FOUR FINDINGS THE MERGE SHOULD CARRY

1.1 · ⭐⭐⭐ Cant. 7:13 at 0473B — Migne DIVIDES THE VERSE differently from the Vulgate, and Caput XXXI has nothing else to stand on

This is the range's largest finding and the only one that reshapes a chapter.

Migne prints two lemmata, heading two chapters:

CAPUT XXXI — Mandragorae dederunt odorem in portis nostris. (0473B) CAPUT XXXII — Omnia poma nova et vetera, Dilecte mi, servavi tibi. (0474A)

Vulg. Cant. 7:13: Mandragorae dederunt odorem. In portis nostris omnia poma: nova et vetera, dilecte mi, servavi tibi.

Every word is present; the division is not. The Vulgate's in portis nostris belongs to the apples; Migne's belongs to the mandrakes, and Caput XXXII's lemma accordingly opens at Omnia poma with the gates already spent.

⭐ And the whole of Caput XXXI is an exposition of the gates as the mandrakes'. Philip re-quotes the divided lemma with his own jam wedged into it — Odorem, inquit, in portis nostris mandragorae jam dederunt, the roman jam standing inside the italic run and reproduced there as printed — and then builds:

Et ii quidem necdum in aedibus, necdum in thalamo fructum proferunt pleniorem, sed in portis, id est sensibus spiritalibus gratum virgini dant odorem (0473D)

The Jews-as-mandrakes are not yet in the house or the bridechamber; what they give in the gates is a smell. Under the Vulgate's division the gates hold apples and the mandrakes' smell has no location at all, and the antithesis aedibus / thalamo / portis — the chapter's frame — is unwritable.

[var:] FIRED, immediately after the lemma, naming the Vulgate's division and what it gives to which fruit. The marker is available here for the reason cruces-0102 §1.2 gives: Migne italicises the run, so the quotation's boundary is printed and the [var:] asserts nothing the plate does not.

⚠ This is a division, not a wording divergence, and I want the merge to see it as its own shape. Pattern 8 governs punctuation and says mirror the plate; Pattern 14 governs scripture divergence and says mark what changes the sense. Here they meet: the only difference from the Vulgate is where the sentence breaks, and the sense changes completely. I judged Pattern 14 to govern because what diverges is the extent of the quotation, which is a textual fact, not a compositor's comma. If the merge rules the other way the fix is a one-line deletion; nothing in the English depends on it.

1.2 · ⭐⭐ Cant. 6:12 at 0458D — Sunamitis for the Vulgate's Sulamitis, seven printings, and the whole chapter is an etymology of the divergent name

Migne prints, as the running lemma of Caput XIII:

Revertere, revertere, Sunamitis: revertere, revertere, ut intueamur te.

Vulg. Cant. 6:12 (6:13 Heb.): Revertere, revertere, Sulamitis; revertere, revertere, ut intueamur te. And Cant. 6:12b at 0459D: Quid videbis, aiunt, in Sunamite, nisi choros castrorum? for Vulg. in Sulamite.

Three lines later Philip glosses the divergent form:

Sunamitis interpretatur captiva vel despecta, sive coccinea. (0459A)

Those are Jerome's interpretations of Sunamitis (coccinea sive despecta), not of Sulamitis, which is the peace-name. And they are not decoration: they are the chapter's three-part architecture, and Philip works each one —

naturaliter filia fuit irae… adhuc tamen gravatur vinculo, et naturae legibus est captiva · infectionis merito mundioribus Dei oculis est despecta · et coccinea digna sit nominari merito, non colore. Coccus ignis speciem tenet, amorem significans … ut coccus sit bis tinctus, ad hunc amorem geminum bis invitat (0459A–C)

— and the coccus bis tinctus leg then carries the chapter to its end, twinning the Bridegroom's two natures with the two dyeings and the two Revertere's. Conform the lemma to Sulamitis and there is no captive, no despised, no scarlet, and the twice-dyed scarlet has no verse to hang from.

⭐ I greped all 126 Latin chunks. Sulamit- occurs nowhere in the work; the verse is printed only here, and the name seven times in the body of one chunk (four Sunamitis, three Sunamite). So there is no internal control — this is unlike Eccles. 9:1, which contradicts itself at 0049, and unlike Ps. 44:3, which Migne prints nine times in four orders. What it has instead is the authorial witness: the exposition names the form and derives from it. That is §6's Zech. 4:14 shape (Philip builds on the addition) rather than its distributional shape.

[var:] FIRED at the lemma, once, naming Vulg. Sulamitis. The English carries Sunamite throughout, including in the gloss.

1.3 · ⭐⭐ Cant. 7:5 at 0465B — the lemma prints juncta canalibus, and Philip's own gloss twice keeps the Vulgate's vincta

Migne prints:

Caput tuum ut Carmelus, et comae capitis tui sicut purpura regis juncta canalibus. (0465B)

Vulg. Cant. 7:5: …sicut purpura regis vincta canalibus — "bound in channels." Migne repeats the divergent word in the exposition: purpurae regis junctae canalibus similantur (0465D).

⭐ But the dyer's excursus that immediately follows is written on vincta. Philip explains the craft twice, and both times the verb is binding or straitening, never joining:

solet purpura per fasciculos in angustis canalibus alligari, cui alligatae aqua superfunditur (0465D) lana subtilis et candida in canalibus angustatur (0465D) Comae autem capitis in angustis canalibus disponuntur (0466A) Quos in canalia, id est in depressas et humiles angustias voluit introduci (0466C)

Four times the channel constricts the purple. Junctus ("joined to") says the opposite thing about the same preposition-less ablative, and the moral it carries — thoughts driven down into humble narrows — needs the binding.

[var:] FIRED, naming Vulg. vincta and pointing at Philip's alligari. ⚑ Iuncta is not a phantom: it is a known variant in the Vulgate tradition. That is an argument for [var:]'s wording ("Vulg. vincta"), not against firing — Pattern 14 states two readings and lets the crux argue.

⭐ Grep result, offered because it is the cheap kind: canalibus occurs in this work only in chunk 0116, five times, all in this chapter. There is no second printing anywhere to control against.

1.4 · ⭐⭐ 0464C — Migne prints cinis where his own etymology, six lines above, requires cingulum — and it stands inside the only autobiographical paragraph in the range

At 0464A Philip gives the name's meaning, italicised:

Hesebon interpretatur cingulum moeroris. — "the girdle of sorrow"

He then applies it: ingressos portae angustias moeror necessarius nos accingit ("a necessary sorrow girdeth us", 0464A–B) — the verb built on the same root. Twelve lines later, in the personal passage, Migne prints:

hujus [0464C] cinis Hesebon mea ipsius moestitia cogeret deperire, si non Virgo dignaretur extenta manu citius subvenire.

cinis, ash, is a real Latin word, so Pattern 12's own boundary clause keeps it on the English side and no [sic:] fires. Rendered as printed — "the ash of this Hesebon, mine own sadness, would have compelled me to perish" — taking cinis and moestitia as the two nominatives in apposition that the plate supplies. ⛔ The conjecture is cinguli / cingulo, and it is close to certain: the sentence is the payoff of the cingulum moeroris gloss, the girdle is what the whole chapter has built, and ash has appeared nowhere in the book. Not emended. ⚠ This is the range's most repairable place: one word restores the argument and destroys the evidence.

⭐ And note what the paragraph is. Expertus sum quod aio — "I have experienced what I say" — introduces Philip speaking in his own person about being turned on by his own community: Cum divino perurgente judicio filii matris meae contra me pugnaverunt, cum exteris parcentibus, ii quos mea credebam viscera, me laeserunt. That clause is Cant. 1:5 (filii matris meae pugnaverunt contra me), taken out of the lemma-machinery entirely and turned on his own life, with no marks and no note. See §2f.1.

2d · The [n:]-only class — hit rate 1 of 10, and the hit is the range's best §8a candidate

All ten ⭐ spans were traced back to their real left edge. Nine are Philip's own prose or bare cross-references. One is a genuine quotation with a genuine divergence, and it is unmarked, so per brief §8a it is LOGGED AND NOT MARKED.

  1. ⭐⭐ 0469A, Deut. 32:33 — THE HIT. Migne prints, naked inside Philip's own sentence:

Sitit enim ille, et nostra omnium bona sitit, qui tamen fel draconum et vinum aspidum non admittit [n: (Deut. XXXII)]

Vulg. Deut. 32:33: Fel draconum vinum eorum, et venenum aspidum insanabile. Migne has vinum aspidum for the Vulgate's venenum aspidum — asps' wine for asps' poison — and has dropped eorum, which is what made vinum the predicate of the dragons' gall in the first place. Two words re-soldered into one phrase.

⭐ And the divergence is the chapter's own subject. Caput XXVI is a wine chapter from end to end: the Bride offers the Bridegroom vinum optimum, in a grato calice, merum… vinum, not a faeculentus calix. What Philip needs at this exact sentence is a counter-wine — the one drink the thirsting Christ refuses — and venenum aspidum does not supply one. The very next clause confirms it: non acetum Judaeorum, non oblatam bibit amaritudinem, sed recusat. Vinegar, drinking, bitterness. The printed reading is the argument; the Vulgate reading is not.

⛔ NO MARKER, per brief §8a: Migne prints the words in neither guillemets nor italics, so the quotation's left edge is not on the plate and a [var:] would have to assert a boundary Migne does not print. The note is the only thing marking it at all, and §8a's ruling is explicit that a note is not a boundary. Logged with full evidence for the merge to rule once. ⚑ The siglum (Deut. XXXII) is correct.

  1. 0460D, [n: (l. IV, c. 7 et 22)] — not a quotation. Migne's internal cross-reference on qui supra cum laudaret ab oculis voluit inchoare. CORRECT, verified: chunk 0074 is Book IV Caput VII and its lemma is Cant. 4:1, [CAP. IV.] Quam pulchra es amica mea… oculi tui columbarum. See §2e.
  2. 0460D, [n: (l. IV, c. 23)] — not a quotation. On mammas ejus vel ubera non transivit. CORRECT, verified: chunk 0085 is Book IV Caput XXIII and its incipit is Quam pulchrae sunt mammae tuae, soror mea sponsa (Cant. 4:10) — precisely the praise Philip says he did not pass beyond.
  3. 0461A, [n: (l. V a c. 18 ad 27)] — not a quotation. On Ipsa autem Virgo in praecedenti libro laudans eum… a capite ad crura et eorum bases. CORRECT: cruces-0102 places Cant. 5:11 Caput ejus aurum optimum at Book V Caput XVIII and closes the descriptio at Caput XXVII. Start and end both right.
  4. 0461D, Jer. 6:14 / 8:11. dicunt enim plures pax, pax, in quibus pax non potest inveniri. Vulg. dicentes Pax, pax, et non erat pax. Unnoted, unmarked, and recast (present tense, relative clause, non potest inveniri for non erat). ⚠ It sits eleven words after [n: (Isa. IX)] and is NOT covered by it — the note stands on princeps pacis, and the extraction pulled the whole run up to the note. Philip's prose on a proverbial tag. No marker.
  5. 0462A, Ezek. 16:25 conflated with Isa. 51:23 [n: (Isa. LI)] — sicut propheta meminit, pedes suos quibusque transeuntibus divaricat. Vulg. Ezek. 16:25: et divisisti pedes tuos omni transeunti. Vulg. Isa. 51:23: posuisti ut terram corpus tuum et quasi viam transeuntibus. ⭐ I checked the siglum before reporting it wrong, and it is not wrong. The verb and the feet are Ezekiel's; transeuntibus is Isaiah 51's word, and the whole picture — a body laid down for passers-by — is Isaiah 51:23's. Migne names the book that supplies the noun Philip actually reproduces. Logged as CORRECT but partial, exactly the call cruces-0102 §2e.2 made for (Hebr. I) over a Wisdom phrase, and for the same reason brief §8b gives: a tally that counted this wrong would manufacture a failure. Philip's prose. No marker.
